questions.objective: Address possible rubella exposure and an inappropriate live-vaccine plan during pregnancy
questions.stem: A patient at 18 weeks is documented as nonimmune to rubella. A vaccine clinic, unaware of the pregnancy, scheduled MMR vaccination for tomorrow. Today the patient learns that a household member is being evaluated for suspected rubella after a febrile rash and international travel. Which nursing response is best?
questions.clue: Two separate safety issues must be handled: a contraindicated live vaccine and a possible infection exposure.
questions.rationale: Do not administer MMR during pregnancy. Clarify the household contact and promptly involve the obstetric clinician and appropriate public-health resources for individualized exposure assessment. The household illness is not diagnosed from the stem, and nonimmune status alone does not prove maternal or fetal infection. Postpartum vaccination remains a separate preventive plan.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner coordinates two linked but distinct decisions—stopping an unsafe prenatal vaccine plan and escalating a possible exposure without diagnosing infection. This is level 2 application.

options.text: Stop the prenatal MMR plan, clarify the timing and nature of contact, and arrange prompt obstetric and public-health guidance about the possible exposure.
options.reason: MMR is contraindicated during pregnancy, while possible rubella exposure during pregnancy requires prompt clinician evaluation rather than passive observation. Clarifying the contact does not assume the household member has rubella.

options.text: Keep the MMR appointment because vaccination after a possible exposure offers more benefit than risk during pregnancy.
options.reason: Pregnancy is a contraindication to MMR vaccination. Exposure concern does not convert the live vaccine into routine prenatal postexposure treatment.

options.text: Cancel the MMR appointment and notify the obstetric clinician only if the patient develops fever or rash.
options.reason: Deferring MMR is appropriate, but waiting for maternal symptoms delays evaluation of a possible exposure that should be reported promptly during pregnancy.

options.text: Cancel MMR, avoid further household contact, and wait for the relative's final diagnosis before notifying the obstetric clinician.
options.reason: Avoiding further contact is prudent, but waiting for the relative's final diagnosis delays prompt individualized assessment of a possible exposure during pregnancy.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Placenta previa.
questions.stem: A patient at 33 weeks has a first episode of painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding. The uterus is soft, BP is 114/72 mmHg, and the fetal heart rate is 140/min with moderate variability. Placental location is unknown. Which proposed action should the nurse stop and clarify?
questions.clue: Painless bleeding with unknown placental location.
questions.rationale: The immediate safety issue is avoiding a potentially hemorrhage-provoking examination. Reassuring findings allow assessment but do not rule out placenta previa.
questions.difficultyReason: Connect painless bleeding and unknown placental location to a procedure-specific safety decision despite reassuring vital signs.

options.text: Continue fetal monitoring while arranging an ultrasound.
options.reason: Monitoring and ultrasound support safe assessment of bleeding and placental location.

options.text: Measure ongoing blood loss and trend maternal vital signs.
options.reason: Stable initial vital signs do not eliminate the need for continued hemorrhage surveillance.

options.text: Establish IV access and obtain prescribed blood specimens.
options.reason: These prepare for deterioration and do not disturb the placenta.

options.text: Perform a digital cervical examination to determine whether labor has begun.
options.reason: Digital examination can disrupt a placenta covering the cervical opening and provoke major hemorrhage before previa is excluded.

questions.objective: Prioritize vascular access during suspected ectopic rupture while emergency help is being mobilized
questions.stem: A patient with a confirmed tubal ectopic pregnancy is in the emergency department without IV access. The patient develops shoulder-tip pain and dizziness; BP falls from 116/74 to 84/48 mmHg and pulse rises to 132/min. Vaginal spotting remains scant. A second nurse is activating the emergency response and contacting the obstetric team. Which task should the bedside nurse prioritize?
questions.clue: The patient has new shock findings and no IV access; another nurse is already summoning help.
questions.rationale: Respond to the deteriorating perfusion, not the small visible loss. Suspected rupture can produce intraperitoneal hemorrhage. Establish access and continue emergency assessment while resuscitation and surgical evaluation proceed together. This item isolates the bedside task; it does not prescribe a fluid volume, transfusion ratio or operative technique.
questions.difficultyReason: Apply a clear shock pattern to the next available nursing task after team activation is assigned. The findings align, so urgency does not justify an advanced rating.

options.text: Establish large-bore IV access for the anticipated emergency resuscitation.
options.reason: The circulation findings suggest major internal bleeding. Rapid vascular access supports resuscitation while the team arranges definitive care.

options.text: Collect repeat serum hCG by venipuncture to assess pregnancy progression.
options.reason: Serial hCG can guide stable-patient follow-up, but this acute perfusion change makes resuscitation access the higher priority.

options.text: Arrange transport to radiology for a repeat transvaginal ultrasound.
options.reason: Further imaging may help the team, but routine transport should not precede stabilization of this deteriorating patient.

options.text: Prepare the pelvic examination equipment to localize the vaginal bleeding.
options.reason: The amount and location of visible bleeding cannot explain away the shock findings. Examination setup does not restore circulation.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Preeclampsia; Care of patients with severe gestational hypertension and severe preeclampsia.
questions.stem: A patient with gestational hypertension is reviewing when to seek urgent evaluation. Which new findings should the nurse include as warning signs of progression or another serious pregnancy complication? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: New neurologic, hepatic, or respiratory symptoms.
questions.rationale: Teach organ-system warning signs, not just edema or a single BP threshold. Symptoms can justify urgent evaluation even before another BP is obtained.
questions.difficultyReason: Evaluate several independent organ-system warnings and separate them from expected pregnancy changes.

options.text: Shortness of breath at rest.
options.reason: This may indicate pulmonary edema or another cardiopulmonary emergency.

options.text: A persistent severe headache that does not improve with the prescribed measures.
options.reason: Persistent severe headache may reflect neurologic involvement and increased seizure risk.

options.text: Blurred vision with flashing lights.
options.reason: Visual disturbance is a serious neurologic warning sign.

options.text: Symmetric ankle swelling that resolves after overnight rest, without other changes.
options.reason: This isolated pattern is common in pregnancy and is less urgent than the listed organ-dysfunction signs.

options.text: Brief irregular tightening that resolves with rest and has no bleeding or fluid leakage.
options.reason: This description alone does not indicate worsening hypertensive disease, although persistent or changing symptoms need assessment.

options.text: New right-upper-quadrant pain with nausea.
options.reason: Hepatic involvement, including HELLP syndrome, can produce this pattern.

questions.objective: Interpret a painful, sustained uterine-tone pattern with maternal instability and scant visible blood
questions.stem: At 35 weeks, a patient develops persistent abdominal pain and a uterus that remains firm between contractions. Pulse is 122/min, BP is 92/56 mmHg and recurrent late fetal decelerations are present. Only a small amount of dark vaginal blood is visible. The nurse is giving an urgent handoff. Which interpretation best accounts for the combined findings?
questions.clue: Maternal circulation, uterine tone and fetal status all matter more than the amount on the pad.
questions.rationale: Communicate suspected abruption with concealed hemorrhage and support urgent coordinated care. The interpretation guides assessment and escalation; it is not a definitive diagnosis from blood color or permission to independently select the delivery route. Do not let scant external bleeding downgrade the response.
questions.difficultyReason: Integrate several concordant classic findings and distinguish plausible bleeding mechanisms. The cues still point in one direction; the revised estimate remains 2 rather than restoring the former 3 label.

options.text: Placental separation with concealed maternal bleeding and impaired fetal oxygen transfer.
options.reason: Pain, sustained uterine tone, maternal instability and fetal changes fit abruption; external blood loss can underestimate its severity.

options.text: Cervical bleeding during labor with pain-related tachycardia and fetal head compression.
options.reason: Ordinary cervical change does not adequately explain maternal hypotension and persistent uterine firmness; late decelerations are not the usual head-compression pattern.

options.text: Bleeding from a placenta over the cervix with discomfort caused by contractions.
options.reason: Previa can bleed severely, but the constant pain and sustained tone make abruption the better fit here. Blood color alone is insufficient.

options.text: Ruptured fetal vessels in the membranes with blood loss primarily from the fetus.
options.reason: Fetal-vessel bleeding can compromise the fetus, but it does not best explain this maternal shock and sustained painful uterine-tone pattern.

questions.objective: Coordinate prescribed hemorrhage and cause-directed care during suspected abruption-associated DIC
questions.stem: A patient with severe abruption has active bleeding, oozing at venipuncture sites, falling platelets and fibrinogen, and a prolonged clotting time. The bedside team has ordered urgent birth and blood-component support. Which nursing actions support this plan while resuscitation continues? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Clinical bleeding, perfusion, and coagulation findings may change on different timelines during resuscitation.
questions.rationale: Suspected DIC requires attention to the trigger, circulation and impaired coagulation together. Follow the emergency team's orders and continue clinical reassessment. The case does not establish a particular transfusion ratio, laboratory trigger, medication regimen or point at which resuscitation must be complete before birth.
questions.difficultyReason: Apply an explicitly ordered plan to an aligned bleeding/coagulopathy pattern. Distinguishing perfusion improvement from coagulation recovery is application here, not enough alone for an advanced label.

options.text: Maintain the resuscitation IV access and prepare the ordered, released blood components using required safety checks.
options.reason: Reliable access and correctly administered components support circulation and coagulation during active bleeding.

options.text: Trend perfusion findings and puncture-site bleeding alongside repeat coagulation studies, reporting changes to the bedside team.
options.reason: Clinical bleeding and serial laboratory findings together show the evolving response; neither should be interpreted in isolation.

options.text: Continue assigned preparation for urgent birth while other team members provide the prescribed hemorrhage support.
options.reason: The obstetric trigger and bleeding require coordinated care. Preparation can proceed alongside the team's resuscitation plan.

options.text: Interpret improved blood pressure after red cells as evidence that the coagulopathy is resolving.
options.reason: A pressure response reflects improved perfusion but does not establish correction of impaired clotting; clinical bleeding and serial coagulation findings still require joint interpretation.

options.text: Document the quantified vaginal loss as the estimated total blood loss when reporting ongoing hemorrhage severity.
options.reason: Quantified vaginal loss records observed external loss; concealed abruption and bleeding from other sites can make total blood loss greater than that value.

questions.objective: Explain why improving symptoms and one normal hCG do not independently end molar surveillance
questions.stem: After evacuation of a molar pregnancy, a patient's first serum hCG within the laboratory's normal range is reported. Bleeding has stopped, but the specialist's written plan still includes additional hCG testing. The patient asks to cancel those tests and try to conceive now. Which response is best?
questions.clue: There is a documented surveillance plan that extends beyond the first normal result.
questions.rationale: Acknowledge the desire for another pregnancy and explain what the follow-up is protecting against. The treating service determines the endpoint from the disease and response. Do not impose the notes' blanket one-year duration or assume complete and partial moles share one schedule. Support future pregnancy planning after the individualized follow-up is completed.
questions.difficultyReason: Apply the purpose of serial surveillance to a patient who reasonably interprets symptom and laboratory improvement as completion. No complex diagnostic trend or fixed schedule is required.

options.text: Keep the specialist's testing and contraception plan until surveillance is complete; another pregnancy would complicate interpretation of hCG.
options.reason: A single improved result does not override the planned surveillance endpoint. Follow-up checks for persistent disease while avoiding pregnancy-related hCG confusion.

options.text: Replace the scheduled laboratory samples with weekly home pregnancy tests; report a positive result before arranging another clinic visit.
options.reason: Home tests are not an independently interchangeable replacement for the specialist's prescribed surveillance. Laboratory urine sampling may be used when actually ordered.

options.text: Request a pelvic ultrasound instead of the remaining hCG tests; a normal scan can serve as the surveillance endpoint.
options.reason: Imaging alone does not replace the ordered biochemical follow-up or establish that the specialist's endpoint has been reached.

options.text: Continue the hCG tests while trying to conceive; use the date of the next missed period to distinguish pregnancy from persistent disease.
options.reason: A new pregnancy can confound hCG surveillance. Menstrual timing does not reliably separate its contribution from persistent trophoblastic activity.

questions.objective: Evaluate daily self-management teaching when insulin is added for gestational diabetes
questions.stem: At 30 weeks, a patient with gestational diabetes is starting prescribed insulin and has an individualized meal plan, glucose targets and instructions for reporting out-of-range readings. No self-titration schedule was prescribed. Which statements show an appropriate daily self-care plan? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Starting insulin changes the safety plan, but it does not replace nutrition or prescribed glucose monitoring.
questions.rationale: Evaluate the day-to-day plan as a whole: measured glucose, adequate planned food, prescribed medication and a response to lows or repeated abnormalities. This revision narrows the earlier mixed maternal/newborn/postpartum question to daily self-management. It does not set universal glucose targets, doses or a postpartum testing timetable.
questions.difficultyReason: Apply individualized instructions to practical insulin-and-meal decisions. The choices test independent daily-care misconceptions rather than advanced diagnostic synthesis.

options.text: I will bring my complete glucose log to review patterns, including readings that later return to target.
options.reason: The complete pattern helps the team evaluate the plan; later improvement does not erase an earlier out-of-range result.

options.text: I will carry a measured fast-acting glucose source and review how to use it if my glucose becomes low.
options.reason: Insulin introduces hypoglycemia risk. Preparation includes an appropriate rescue source and the individualized treatment instructions.

options.text: I will follow the meal plan's timing and carbohydrate amounts rather than remove meals when a reading is high.
options.reason: Nutrition and insulin must work together. Skipping planned intake can create low-glucose risk and inadequate nutrition.

options.text: I will add an extra insulin dose for an elevated post-meal reading using the previous day's prescribed dose as my guide.
options.reason: A previous scheduled dose is not a correction algorithm. Use the reporting plan and obtain guidance instead of inventing an extra dose.

options.text: I will replace routine glucose checks with symptom checks on days when I eat the planned meals and feel well.
options.reason: Gestational diabetes can be asymptomatic. Following the meal plan does not show whether glucose targets are being met.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Infections during pregnancy: Rubella.
questions.stem: A patient at 12 weeks has a negative rubella immunity result and no symptoms or known recent exposure. Which plan should the nurse reinforce?
questions.clue: Nonimmune means susceptible, not infected; the patient is pregnant.
questions.rationale: Separate susceptibility from infection. Exposure during pregnancy warrants prompt clinician contact, but routine prevention does not include prenatal MMR.
questions.difficultyReason: Recall that rubella nonimmunity is not active infection and prenatal MMR is not routine prevention.

options.text: Give MMR today because the first trimester has the greatest fetal risk.
options.reason: Greater fetal vulnerability does not make a live vaccine safe during pregnancy.

options.text: Document that a negative immunity result confirms active fetal infection.
options.reason: Lack of immunity is not evidence of current maternal or fetal infection.

options.text: Start prophylactic antibiotics for the remainder of pregnancy.
options.reason: Antibiotics do not prevent rubella, a viral infection.

options.text: Avoid exposure and arrange MMR vaccination when eligible after pregnancy.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Preeclampsia: fetal assessment and monitoring of fetal activity.
questions.stem: The prenatal nurse receives four telephone messages. Which patient needs the most urgent callback and immediate evaluation?
questions.clue: A marked change from the patient’s usual fetal movement pattern.
questions.rationale: The highest-priority call identifies a potentially time-sensitive threat. Do not reassure the patient solely because there is no pain or bleeding.
questions.difficultyReason: Compare four calls using a current fetal warning sign rather than routine pregnancy discomforts.

options.text: A patient at 34 weeks with mild bilateral ankle swelling that improves with elevation.
options.reason: This isolated dependent swelling is lower priority than possible fetal compromise.

options.text: A patient at 24 weeks with heartburn after a spicy meal and no chest pain or dyspnea.
options.reason: An isolated meal-related symptom has lower immediate priority.

options.text: A patient at 10 weeks with morning nausea who is drinking fluids and urinating normally.
options.reason: Preserved fluid intake and normal urination make this nausea report lower priority than a new marked reduction in fetal movement.

options.text: A patient at 30 weeks who reports markedly reduced fetal movement compared with the usual pattern today.
options.reason: A clear change in fetal activity can indicate compromise and requires prompt assessment.

questions.objective: Reconsider a previously entered fluid order when oxygen response does not resolve new respiratory findings
questions.stem: A hospitalized patient with severe preeclampsia has a one-time crystalloid challenge ordered earlier for low urine output. Before it starts, the nurse finds new bilateral crackles, RR 28/min and oxygen saturation 91%; the urinary catheter is patent. A second nurse summons the obstetric team. Ordered oxygen raises saturation to 96%, but crackles persist and urine output remains low. What should the nurse do with the fluid order now?
questions.clue: Oxygen corrected one measured result, but the persistent crackles still challenge the safety of additional fluid.
questions.rationale: Reassess an earlier order when the clinical situation changes. Continue oxygenation support and urgent team assessment; oliguria alone does not establish simple volume depletion. The question does not diagnose pulmonary edema with certainty or prescribe diuretics, fluid restriction rates or a replacement regimen. The earlier order is a fictional case fact, not a recommended routine preeclampsia order.
questions.difficultyReason: Reconcile the competing low-output goal, the prior order and partial treatment response: improved saturation does not resolve persistent respiratory findings. Provisional advanced estimate for revising care after discordant response, not for the severe diagnosis itself.

options.text: Pause the planned challenge and obtain urgent review of the changed respiratory findings before starting it.
options.reason: Supplemental oxygen improves saturation without establishing fluid tolerance. The new findings require reassessment of the earlier order.

options.text: Start the full ordered challenge now that saturation is above 95%, then reassess the urine output.
options.reason: A better saturation on oxygen does not show that the lung findings resolved or that the previous fluid plan is safe.

options.text: Give half the ordered challenge as a test, then decide about the remainder from the respiratory response.
options.reason: An independently chosen smaller challenge still exposes a patient with possible fluid intolerance before the needed urgent review.

options.text: Begin the challenge at a slower infusion rate while waiting for imaging to clarify the lung findings.
options.reason: Slowing the rate does not resolve the changed indication or make additional volume appropriate while pulmonary edema is being considered.

questions.objective: Verify procedure safeguards for planned ECV without treating one prior low-transverse cesarean as automatic exclusion
questions.stem: A patient at 37 weeks with a singleton breech fetus is attending a hospital assessment for possible external cephalic version. The history includes one low-transverse cesarean birth. No final eligibility decision has been made. Which nursing actions support safe assessment and the care plan if ECV proceeds? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Prior surgery is one part of eligibility; confirming presentation is one part of procedure safety.
questions.rationale: Support a qualified clinician's individualized eligibility decision, procedure readiness and observation. Do not independently approve the procedure or cancel it using the older ATI blanket prior-cesarean statement. The actual course anchor is Week 5 L&D notes and lecture, not Week 4 pregnancy notes. Its existing Pregnancy blueprint allocation is retained pending final mapping review.
questions.difficultyReason: Apply several independent procedural safeguards and distinguish an individualized assessment from a blanket exclusion. This remains an intermediate care-plan task, not advanced merely because it has six SATA options.

options.text: Review the preprocedure fetal tracing and bring any concerning finding to the clinician before the attempt.
options.reason: Fetal status contributes to eligibility and provides a baseline for assessing tolerance of the procedure.

options.text: Confirm the setting can provide urgent cesarean birth if a complication occurs during the version attempt.
options.reason: Appropriate emergency capability is part of safe procedure planning even when an uncomplicated attempt is expected.

options.text: Continue the ordered fetal observation after a successful turn rather than using fetal position as the discharge criterion.
options.reason: A head-down position shows the maneuver's result; it does not replace assessment of maternal and fetal tolerance afterward.

options.text: Review how to obtain prompt hospital advice for bleeding, persistent abdominal pain or reduced fetal movement after discharge.
options.reason: New symptoms after discharge require assessment rather than reassurance based solely on the earlier successful turn.

options.text: Request cancellation on the basis that one prior low-transverse cesarean birth independently excludes an ECV attempt.
options.reason: One previous cesarean is not an automatic exclusion in the checked guidance. The clinician must assess the complete eligibility picture.

options.text: Substitute abdominal palpation for the planned ultrasound because confirming the breech position completes the screening assessment.
options.reason: Ultrasound also contributes information such as placental location and fluid assessment; palpation does not complete that screening.

questions.objective: Initiate a targeted bedside response to recurrent late decelerations in explicitly defined labor
questions.stem: A patient at 38 weeks is in spontaneous labor at 4 cm dilation, lying supine. The fetal baseline is 140/min. During the last 20 minutes, gradual fetal decelerations follow most contractions: each nadir occurs after the contraction peak and recovery occurs after the contraction ends. Variability is minimal, not absent. Contractions occur four times in 10 minutes. BP is 118/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air; no oxytocin or sedating medication is being given. Another nurse is notifying the clinician. Which bedside action is most appropriate now?
questions.clue: The decelerations are late, but variability remains present; maternal oxygenation is normal.
questions.rationale: Use the entire tracing and maternal context. This category II pattern requires prompt evaluation and response, not a declaration of proven acidemia. Continued or worsening abnormalities may require further team-directed interventions or delivery. No universal response deadline or delivery route is determined by this question. The bonus NST/CST slide is background, not the source for this intrapartum response.
questions.difficultyReason: Apply late-deceleration timing, present-but-minimal variability and maternal findings to the immediate bedside action. The setting is now explicit; the task remains intermediate.

options.text: Turn the patient laterally and reassess the fetal pattern while maintaining continuous monitoring.
options.reason: Position change is an appropriate initial response to the recurrent late pattern while maternal assessment and escalation continue.

options.text: Apply oxygen by face mask and maintain the current position until the fetal tracing improves.
options.reason: Routine maternal oxygen is not supported for a nonhypoxic patient solely to treat the tracing; it does not replace targeted positioning.

options.text: Document a category III tracing and bypass further bedside assessment to prepare immediate operative birth.
options.reason: Minimal variability is not absent variability. The stated pattern warrants assessment and escalation without inventing a category III classification.

options.text: Allow another 30 minutes of undisturbed observation to see whether a fetal sleep cycle ends.
options.reason: A possible sleep contribution to variability does not explain away recurrent late decelerations or justify delaying the initial response.

questions.objective: Select prompt oral treatment with measured reassessment for symptomatic hypoglycemia and safe swallowing
questions.stem: During an antenatal visit, an insulin-treated patient becomes shaky and diaphoretic. Capillary glucose is 54 mg/dL. The patient is alert, can swallow safely and is not vomiting. Oral glucose is available, and the clinic hypoglycemia protocol applies. Which initial plan is most appropriate?
questions.clue: The low glucose is measured, and oral treatment is immediately available with safe swallowing.
questions.rationale: Treat now, measure the response and follow the protocol for further treatment. If consciousness or swallowing deteriorates, oral treatment becomes unsafe and the emergency pathway changes. Review the cause and ongoing meal/insulin plan after recovery. Fifteen grams falls within the checked 15-to-20-g guidance; no universal glucagon product or dose is specified.
questions.difficultyReason: Use measured glucose, symptoms and route safety to choose treatment plus reassessment. This is a standard application task rather than a hard item based on a low number alone.

options.text: Give 15 g of oral glucose now and repeat the glucose measurement in 15 minutes.
options.reason: Rapid oral glucose is appropriate with safe swallowing; prompt repeat measurement determines whether more treatment is required.

options.text: Give a measured glucose source now and end reassessment when the sweating and shaking resolve.
options.reason: Symptoms can improve before the episode is safely resolved. Repeat glucose measurement, not symptoms alone, guides the next step.

options.text: Give the prescribed emergency glucagon first and use oral glucose after reassessing the response.
options.reason: The case supports immediate oral treatment; emergency rescue for inability to self-treat is not the preferred initial route here.

options.text: Draw a venous glucose for confirmation and begin treatment once the laboratory result is available.
options.reason: A symptomatic, measured low glucose calls for prompt treatment. Waiting for laboratory confirmation prolongs the identified problem.

questions.objective: Evaluate complication reporting and follow-up after a transvaginal cervical cerclage
questions.stem: At 22 weeks, a patient with a transvaginal cervical cerclage is preparing for discharge after an uncomplicated assessment. The clinician has supplied individualized activity instructions and a planned follow-up and stitch-removal appointment. Which statements show correct understanding? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: This is a vaginal stitch with an ongoing follow-up plan; labor, infection and possible rupture can require earlier assessment.
questions.rationale: Teach how to reach the maternity team and use teach-back for warning symptoms and appointments. Specify the cerclage type because transabdominal management differs. The clinician determines activity and removal timing; the nurse is not instructing self-removal or declaring that every stitch is managed identically.
questions.difficultyReason: Apply procedure-specific discharge teaching to independent reporting and follow-up decisions. Straightforward warning signs and individualized activity planning support level 2.

options.text: If regular cramping or contractions begin, I will contact the maternity team without waiting for the scheduled removal visit.
options.reason: Labor symptoms with a vaginal stitch need prompt assessment because the plan for the stitch may need to change.

options.text: If green, foul-smelling discharge appears without contractions, I will mention it at the next scheduled prenatal appointment.
options.reason: Possible infection requires prompt contact even without contractions. Waiting for the routine appointment is not the appropriate reporting plan.

options.text: I will keep the planned follow-up and removal appointment even if I feel well and have no vaginal bleeding.
options.reason: An uncomplicated interval does not replace the planned review and management of the stitch before birth.

options.text: I will add continuous bed rest until the stitch is removed to give the procedure the best chance of working.
options.reason: Routine prolonged bed rest is not recommended. Follow the actual individualized recovery and activity instructions rather than adding restrictions.

options.text: If clear fluid leaks but there is no pain, I will wait for contractions before contacting the maternity team.
options.reason: Possible membrane rupture needs prompt assessment on its own; pain or contractions are not prerequisites for reporting leakage.

questions.objective: Escalate a hypertensive pregnancy with hemolysis, liver injury, and thrombocytopenia despite a negative protein dipstick
questions.stem: A patient at 32 weeks who was normotensive before pregnancy has BP readings of 154/98 and 152/96 mmHg four hours apart. The patient reports persistent right-upper-quadrant pain. Platelets are 72,000/microliter, AST is 186 units/L, the blood smear shows fragmented erythrocytes, and LDH is flagged high. A urine dipstick is negative for protein. Which interpretation should the nurse communicate immediately?
questions.clue: Repeated new hypertension accompanies hemolysis, liver injury, and thrombocytopenia even though the protein dipstick is negative.
questions.rationale: Communicate the whole pattern rather than anchoring on absent dipstick protein or waiting for a severe-range blood pressure. The added prior-BP history, repeated readings, and hemolysis evidence support immediate evaluation for possible HELLP syndrome. The nurse is escalating a suspected syndrome; the team must still assess alternative causes and direct management.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies several aligned organ-dysfunction findings while rejecting the discordant negative dipstick. The case does not require trend interpretation or a treatment tradeoff, so the author estimate is level 2.

options.text: Report preeclampsia with severe features, but state HELLP is unlikely without proteinuria.
options.reason: The organ-dysfunction findings support serious preeclampsia concern, but absent proteinuria does not make HELLP unlikely when hemolysis, liver injury, and thrombocytopenia are present.

options.text: Report possible HELLP syndrome, include the complete pattern, and request immediate obstetric evaluation.
options.reason: The case now supplies evidence from all three HELLP components while the negative protein result does not remove the serious hypertensive-pregnancy concern.

options.text: Report gestational hypertension because neither blood-pressure reading reaches the severe range.
options.reason: Classifying the case from blood-pressure magnitude alone underweights the concurrent hemolysis, liver injury, thrombocytopenia, and right-upper-quadrant pain that require an urgent HELLP-focused handoff.

options.text: Report a primary hematologic disorder as the leading concern because hemolysis and thrombocytopenia dominate the pattern.
options.reason: A hematologic disorder can remain in the differential, but making it the leading interpretation underweights the linked new hypertension, right-upper-quadrant pain, liver injury, hemolysis, and thrombocytopenia in pregnancy.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Oxytocin (Pitocin).
questions.stem: A patient receiving oxytocin has six contractions per 10 minutes averaged over 30 minutes, recurrent late decelerations, and minimal variability. Maternal oxygen saturation is 99%. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.clue: Excessive contraction frequency accompanies recurrent late decelerations while maternal oxygen saturation is normal.
questions.rationale: Stop the harmful infusion promptly, then reposition, assess maternal status, notify the team, and implement further ordered measures. Actions may occur concurrently with team help.

options.text: Continue the rate and reassess after another 30-minute averaging period.
options.reason: The concerning fetal pattern makes delay unsafe.

options.text: Stop the oxytocin infusion.
options.reason: Removing the uterine stimulant addresses a reversible cause of tachysystole and reduced placental perfusion.

options.text: Notify the provider and await further orders.
options.reason: The provider should be notified, but waiting for orders delays stopping oxytocin, the immediate action that removes the ongoing uterine stimulus.

options.text: Apply oxygen at 10 L/min while maintaining the current oxytocin rate.
options.reason: Routine oxygen is not recommended without maternal hypoxia and does not remove the uterine stimulus.

questions.objective: Respond immediately to overt magnesium toxicity
questions.stem: A patient at 31 weeks is receiving magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis with severe preeclampsia. The patient is difficult to arouse, respirations are 7/min and shallow, oxygen saturation is 86%, and patellar reflexes are absent. An emergency-response nurse is supporting ventilation, and a PRN IV calcium gluconate order is active for magnesium toxicity. Which action should the assigned nurse take next?
questions.clue: Ventilation is already being supported, overt toxicity is clinically apparent, and a calcium-gluconate order is active.
questions.rationale: Stop magnesium and use the prescribed calcium gluconate while the response team continues airway and ventilatory support. Absent reflexes and severe respiratory depression are clinical toxicity findings; a laboratory result should not become a prerequisite for treatment. Continuing magnesium at any rate or while giving calcium maintains the offending exposure.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies an aligned toxicity cluster to the next action after ventilation has already begun and distinguishes treatment from laboratory confirmation. The item does not require a dose calculation or discordant-cue integration, so the estimate is level 2.

options.text: Stop the magnesium infusion and administer the prescribed calcium gluconate while ventilatory support continues.
options.reason: The patient has overt clinical toxicity with respiratory compromise and absent reflexes. Ongoing exposure should stop, and the ordered calcium antagonist should be used while ventilation continues.

options.text: Stop the infusion and wait for a stat serum magnesium result before using the calcium order.
options.reason: A serum level informs continuing care, but waiting for it would delay prescribed treatment of an already apparent clinical toxicity emergency.

options.text: Reduce the magnesium infusion rate and reassess respirations and reflexes after ventilation improves.
options.reason: A slower infusion is insufficient when severe respiratory depression and absent reflexes are already present. The infusion should be stopped rather than continued at a reduced rate.

options.text: Administer the prescribed calcium gluconate but leave the magnesium running to maintain seizure prophylaxis.
options.reason: Calcium does not justify continued magnesium exposure during overt toxicity. The infusion must be stopped while the emergency is treated.

questions.objective: Escalate PPROM with suspected intraamniotic infection
questions.stem: A patient with PPROM at 31 weeks is receiving expectant inpatient care. New findings are temperature 38.7 C, maternal heart rate 116/min, uterine tenderness, foul-smelling fluid, and fetal heart rate 175/min. Current orders include maternal cultures and laboratory tests plus IV broad-spectrum antibiotics when infection is suspected. Which actions should the nurse take or anticipate? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: A previously stable PPROM course now has a combined maternal-fetal infection pattern, and relevant specimen and antibiotic orders already exist.
questions.rationale: Escalate the full pattern, obtain ordered specimens promptly when feasible, administer prescribed broad-spectrum antibiotics without avoidable delay, and coordinate neonatal readiness and team-directed birth planning. Do not preserve the prior latency goal pending culture confirmation. Infection alone does not mandate cesarean birth; route and timing remain individualized obstetric decisions.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies an aligned clinical deterioration pattern to four coordinated actions and rejects two management-goal errors. The cues are concordant and no regimen or route must be selected, so the corrected estimate is level 2 rather than level 3.

options.text: Report the full change in findings promptly and request bedside obstetric reassessment for suspected intraamniotic infection.
options.reason: The combined maternal, uterine, fluid, and fetal changes warrant prompt reassessment. Reporting suspected infection does not claim that a culture-confirmed diagnosis or sepsis is already established.

options.text: Collect the ordered maternal cultures and laboratory tests promptly when feasible without creating an avoidable antibiotic delay.
options.reason: Ordered specimens support evaluation and should be collected promptly when feasible, but the collection process should not create a meaningful delay in prescribed treatment.

options.text: Administer the prescribed IV broad-spectrum antibiotics without avoidable delay.
options.reason: Prompt prescribed antimicrobial treatment addresses maternal and fetal infection risk in the setting of suspected intraamniotic infection.

options.text: Alert the neonatal team and prepare the patient for the birth plan determined by the obstetric team.
options.reason: Prematurity and suspected infection require neonatal readiness and coordinated birth planning. This wording leaves the route and timing decision with the obstetric team.

options.text: Continue the prior expectant-management plan until a culture identifies a specific organism.
options.reason: The current multisystem clinical pattern warrants action before a culture identifies an organism. Expectant management is appropriate only when no contraindication to continuing pregnancy has emerged.

options.text: Prepare for cesarean birth as the required route solely because intraamniotic infection is suspected.
options.reason: Suspected intraamniotic infection requires timely treatment and birth planning, but infection alone does not make cesarean the mandatory route.

questions.objective: Assess fetal status immediately after high-risk membrane rupture
questions.stem: A laboring patient with polyhydramnios has a cephalic presenting part at -3 station. Immediately after a large spontaneous gush of fluid, the external fetal monitor loses the tracing. Which assessment should the nurse perform first?
questions.clue: A high presenting part, polyhydramnios, a sudden gush, and loss of the tracing create an immediate cord-compromise concern.
questions.rationale: Reestablish and assess the fetal heart rate immediately. The other assessments are appropriate parts of ongoing care, but fluid appearance, contractions, and maternal temperature do not address the most time-sensitive fetal risk first. Because a normal tracing cannot exclude prolapse in every high-risk rupture, the nurse should continue prompt bedside evaluation and escalation if concern remains.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner uses two cord-prolapse risk factors and the immediate post-rupture timing to prioritize among four legitimate bedside assessments. This is applied prioritization without a confirmed prolapse or advanced triage, so the estimate remains level 2.

options.text: Reposition the ultrasound transducer and determine the fetal heart rate immediately.
options.reason: Membrane rupture with polyhydramnios and a high presenting part increases cord-prolapse risk. Immediate fetal heart-rate assessment can reveal acute bradycardia or decelerations that require urgent response.

options.text: Inspect the fluid pad for color, odor, and consistency before replacing the monitor.
options.reason: Fluid characteristics are important after rupture, but they do not take priority over immediately assessing fetal status in this high cord-risk situation.

options.text: Palpate the contraction pattern for frequency and intensity before reestablishing the fetal tracing.
options.reason: Contraction assessment remains part of labor care, but the sudden tracing loss after high-risk rupture requires fetal heart-rate assessment first.

options.text: Measure the maternal temperature before assessing fetal status because the membranes are now ruptured.
options.reason: Temperature surveillance addresses infection risk over time; it does not precede immediate evaluation for acute fetal compromise after this rupture.

questions.objective: Respond to postcesarean respiratory depression after neuraxial opioid
questions.stem: Two hours after cesarean birth with intrathecal morphine, a patient is difficult to arouse, respirations are 7/min and shallow, and oxygen saturation is 86%. The IV is patent, a PRN naloxone order covers significant opioid-related respiratory depression, and another nurse has activated the emergency response. Which action is best now?
questions.clue: The patient has severe hypoventilation and hypoxemia, the emergency response is active, and naloxone is already authorized.
questions.rationale: Begin airway and ventilatory support immediately while the prescribed naloxone is administered. Naloxone is indicated for opioid-induced respiratory depression, but supportive resuscitation remains necessary and cannot wait for the drug response or laboratory testing. Low-flow oxygen and stimulation alone are inadequate for the stated shallow bradypnea.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies airway-breathing priorities to an opioid-specific postoperative context and distinguishes concurrent support from reversal-only or test-first sequencing. Severity does not create competing or discordant cues, so the estimate remains level 2.

options.text: Apply low-flow nasal oxygen and stimulate the patient, then reassess before using the naloxone order.
options.reason: Stimulation and supplemental oxygen alone do not correct severe hypoventilation. Waiting to use the prescribed reversal plan delays treatment of a current airway and breathing emergency.

options.text: Support the airway and ventilation immediately while the prescribed naloxone is administered as the response team arrives.
options.reason: Severe sedation, bradypnea, and hypoxemia require immediate airway and ventilatory support. Prescribed naloxone reverses opioid depression but does not replace resuscitative support.

options.text: Administer the prescribed naloxone first and defer ventilatory support unless the saturation remains low afterward.
options.reason: Naloxone should not become a reason to postpone ventilation in an already hypoventilating, hypoxemic patient. Resuscitative measures and reversal proceed together.

options.text: Obtain an arterial blood gas before starting assisted ventilation or reversal.
options.reason: Laboratory assessment may assist later evaluation, but it must not delay stabilization and prescribed reversal of clinically significant respiratory depression.

questions.objective: Stay and support imminent unplanned birth with the team
questions.stem: A patient arrives in triage with rapidly progressive labor. The fetal head is crowning, an emergency-birth cart is at the bedside, and the birth clinician and newborn nurse are responding. Which actions are appropriate from now through the immediate newborn transition? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Crowning fixes the location and urgency; the responding team allows birth support and immediate maternal-newborn tasks to occur in parallel.
questions.rationale: Stay with the patient, update and coordinate the responding team, use side-lying positioning and panting as appropriate, and support a controlled birth with gloved hands within protocol. Once birth occurs, newborn drying, warming, and assessment can proceed while another team member assesses maternal bleeding and trauma. Do not transfer a crowning patient or use premature cord traction to hurry placental delivery.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner separates appropriate actions before birth from coordinated actions immediately afterward and applies team roles across the transition. The cues are aligned and no complex complication is introduced, so the estimate remains level 2.

options.text: Remain at the bedside and use the call system to update the responding team that birth is occurring in triage.
options.reason: Crowning makes birth imminent. The patient should not be left while additional birth and newborn support is mobilized and updated.

options.text: Assist the patient to a side-lying position and coach open-mouth panting between contractions as birth support is organized.
options.reason: The course and supplied ATI material support side-lying positioning and panting to promote controlled support during a rapid, unavoidable birth.

options.text: Use gloved hands and light pressure according to the emergency-birth protocol to control rapid expulsion without trying to stop birth.
options.reason: A controlled supportive approach can reduce abrupt expulsion and trauma. It is different from forcefully obstructing or reversing an imminent birth.

options.text: After birth, have the newborn nurse begin drying, warming, and assessment while maternal bleeding and trauma are assessed concurrently.
options.reason: The stem explicitly includes the immediate newborn transition. Team members can provide prompt thermal/newborn care while maternal assessment continues in parallel.

options.text: Move the patient by wheelchair to the delivery suite between contractions before permitting any further pushing.
options.reason: With crowning, transfer can create an uncontrolled birth during movement. The nurse should prepare for birth at the current location rather than make transport a prerequisite.

options.text: After birth, begin pulling on the umbilical cord before signs of placental separation appear to shorten the third stage.
options.reason: Placental care begins with assessment for separation. Premature or excessive cord traction is a uterine-inversion risk and is not a safe way to shorten the third stage.

questions.objective: Maintain immediate relief of cord compression after help is activated
questions.stem: After membrane rupture, the fetal heart rate falls to 70/min. During examination, the nurse feels a pulsating cord below the presenting part. Another nurse has activated the obstetric emergency response, and the team is preparing urgent transfer for birth. What should the examining nurse do now?
questions.clue: Help is already activated, cord compression is confirmed, and the fetal heart rate is severely low; the tested task is maintaining decompression through transfer.
questions.rationale: Use the gloved hand to elevate the presenting part and maintain that relief during transfer until a qualified clinician takes over or birth occurs. Positioning and protection of an exposed cord can be coordinated by the team, but neither replaces continuous decompression. Do not attempt routine cord replacement or withdraw the hand because transport has begun.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a confirmed cord-prolapse finding to the examining nurse's continuing role and distinguishes decompression from three plausible sequencing errors. No competing diagnosis or route-of-birth decision is required, so the estimate remains level 2.

options.text: Place the patient in knee-chest position, then remove the examining hand to help move the bed.
options.reason: Positioning can assist decompression, but it does not replace establishing and maintaining manual elevation. Other team members should manage the bed while relief is maintained.

options.text: Elevate the presenting part with the gloved hand and maintain that relief during transfer until a qualified handoff or birth.
options.reason: Manual elevation relieves cord compression and must continue as a bridge to urgent birth. The examining nurse should not release pressure merely because help and transfer are underway.

options.text: Guide the cord above the presenting part, remove the hand, and then reassess the fetal heart rate.
options.reason: Routine cord replacement is not the decompression maneuver. Removing the hand after manipulating the cord can restore compression and delay definitive care.

options.text: Cover the cord with sterile saline-moistened gauze before applying pressure to the presenting part.
options.reason: Protecting an exposed cord is appropriate when needed, but it should not precede immediate relief of the compression causing severe fetal bradycardia.

questions.objective: Recognize cardiopulmonary deterioration during terbutaline treatment
questions.stem: During an induction, a patient receives prescribed short-term subcutaneous terbutaline for acute uterine tachysystole. Soon afterward, the patient reports chest tightness and dyspnea; pulse rises from 96 to 138/min, oxygen saturation is 90%, and new bilateral crackles are heard. Which action is best?
questions.clue: Several new maternal cardiopulmonary findings appeared together after a subcutaneous beta-agonist dose.
questions.rationale: Treat the pattern as possible serious terbutaline-related cardiopulmonary deterioration: withhold any additional exposure, obtain urgent evaluation, and maintain maternal-fetal surveillance. The current label lists increased heart rate, arrhythmias, pulmonary edema, and myocardial ischemia among serious maternal adverse reactions and warns against prolonged or outpatient maintenance tocolysis. This item uses a prescribed, short-term monitored dose for an acute obstetric indication; it does not endorse a routine regimen or imply an FDA-approved tocolysis indication.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a concordant cluster of medication-related findings to an urgent response. The cues do not require reconciliation of competing data, so the estimate is level 2 rather than level 3.

options.text: Withhold any additional terbutaline, activate urgent cardiopulmonary evaluation, and continue close maternal-fetal monitoring during the response.
options.reason: The clustered respiratory and cardiovascular findings suggest a serious adverse response rather than an isolated expected effect. Further exposure should be withheld while the nurse escalates and supports ongoing assessment.

options.text: Document that the contraction pattern improved and ask pharmacy to review the medication before notifying the obstetric team.
options.reason: Improvement in uterine activity does not reduce the urgency of new hypoxemia, chest symptoms, tachycardia, and crackles. A pharmacy review can assist later but should not delay clinical escalation.

options.text: Obtain an electrocardiogram and metabolic panel before reporting the change because the fetal tracing remains reassuring.
options.reason: Electrocardiography and laboratory studies may be ordered during evaluation, but completing tests first would delay the response to current maternal cardiopulmonary deterioration. A reassuring fetal tracing does not make the maternal findings benign.

options.text: Request a different medication for the remaining contractions and report only if the oxygen saturation falls further.
options.reason: The immediate problem is the patient's current cardiopulmonary status, not selection of another uterine-relaxing drug. Waiting for greater desaturation would delay assessment of a potentially serious reaction.

questions.objective: Assess severe perineal pressure and occult bleeding after forceps
questions.stem: One hour after a forceps-assisted birth, a patient reports worsening unilateral perineal pain and deep rectal pressure despite analgesia. The fundus is firm and midline, lochia is scant, pulse has risen from 92 to 122/min, and blood pressure has fallen from 116/72 to 94/58 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take next?
questions.clue: The uterus and lochia do not explain the focal pressure, while the pulse and blood pressure suggest declining perfusion.
questions.rationale: Assess beyond uterine tone when postpartum blood loss may be concealed. Operative vaginal birth is a hematoma risk, and severe localized pain or rectal pressure can occur despite scant lochia. Inspect and palpate the perineum, reassess hemodynamic status, and urgently report the suspected hematoma so the team can evaluate the bleeding source and stabilize the patient.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner integrates local symptoms, birth history, uterine findings, and a hemodynamic trend to choose focused assessment and escalation. The pattern is strongly aligned, so the estimate is level 2.

options.text: Inspect and palpate the perineum, reassess perfusion, and urgently report a suspected concealed hematoma.
options.reason: Forceps birth, focal pain and pressure, scant external bleeding, and worsening hemodynamics fit a possible vaginal or vulvar hematoma. Focused assessment and urgent escalation are needed without claiming a confirmed diagnosis.

options.text: Massage the firm fundus, quantify lochia, and defer perineal inspection until external bleeding increases.
options.reason: Fundal massage addresses uterine atony, but the uterus is already firm and lochia may remain scant when blood is collecting in pelvic soft tissue. Waiting for visible bleeding can miss worsening concealed loss.

options.text: Assist the patient to a bedside commode for possible bladder pressure, then repeat vital signs after voiding.
options.reason: Urinary retention can cause pressure, but mobilizing a patient with worsening tachycardia and hypotension delays evaluation and increases fall risk. The unilateral severe pain after forceps requires direct perineal and perfusion assessment.

options.text: Apply ice and give the prescribed analgesic for tissue trauma, then reassess before contacting the provider.
options.reason: Ice and analgesia can be appropriate for a small, stable hematoma, but the evolving vital signs and disproportionate pressure make symptom treatment alone insufficient and unsafe as the next step.

questions.objective: Recognize postpartum warning symptoms despite completed birth
questions.stem: On postpartum day 2 after a cesarean birth, a patient with recent preeclampsia reviews discharge teaching. Which statements show correct understanding of when to seek immediate medical care? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Postpartum discharge teaching must address neurologic, cardiopulmonary, bleeding, thrombotic, wound, and mental-health changes without assuming birth ended the risk.
questions.rationale: The patient should seek immediate care for a severe persistent headache with visual change, sudden chest pain or breathing difficulty, or heavy bleeding at the stated threshold. Worsening wound changes and unilateral leg symptoms should be reported promptly rather than deferred, and harm thoughts require immediate help. Cesarean recovery and recent preeclampsia shape risk, but these warning-sign decisions belong to broader postpartum safety rather than a cesarean-only mastery claim.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner evaluates six realistic discharge statements across several postpartum complication families and distinguishes immediate escalation from plausible but unsafe self-monitoring or delay. The estimate is level 2.

options.text: "I will seek care now for a severe headache that persists after medicine and fluids or occurs with blurred vision."
options.reason: A persistent severe headache and visual change are urgent maternal warning symptoms after birth, including in a patient with recent hypertensive disease.

options.text: "Sudden chest pain or trouble breathing needs emergency evaluation even after I have returned home."
options.reason: Chest pain and difficulty breathing are urgent postpartum warning symptoms that require immediate medical evaluation rather than routine follow-up.

options.text: "I need immediate care if bleeding soaks through a pad in an hour or I pass a clot larger than an egg."
options.reason: The CDC warning-sign guidance identifies this degree of postpartum bleeding or large clots as requiring immediate care.

options.text: "If my incision becomes red and starts draining without a fever, I can wait until my scheduled postpartum visit."
options.reason: New redness and drainage can signal a wound complication even before fever appears. The patient should contact the obstetric team promptly rather than wait for the routine visit.

options.text: "If one calf becomes newly swollen and tender, I should walk for a while before deciding whether to call."
options.reason: New one-sided leg swelling or tenderness is an urgent postpartum warning pattern. Walking as a self-test delays evaluation and is not an appropriate way to rule out thrombosis.

options.text: "If I develop thoughts of harming myself or my baby, family supervision is enough until the routine follow-up visit."
options.reason: Thoughts of harming self or baby require immediate help. Family presence can support safety but does not replace urgent professional evaluation.

questions.objective: Explain fetal benefit rather than a tocolytic purpose of betamethasone
questions.stem: A patient at 30 weeks is still considered likely to give birth within the next 7 days, although contractions decreased after other treatment. Betamethasone is prescribed. Which explanation by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The contraction treatment and the medication intended to improve neonatal outcomes have different purposes.
questions.rationale: Betamethasone is given for fetal maturation and reduction of neonatal respiratory morbidity when preterm birth remains likely; it is not the medication used to stop contractions or treat infection. The benefit is probabilistic, not a promise that the newborn will avoid respiratory support. Eligibility and timing are established in the case rather than generalized to every gestation or clinical situation.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner identifies the basic purpose of a named antenatal corticosteroid from direct cues and distinguishes it from three parallel medication purposes. The estimate remains level 1.

options.text: "It reduces the baby's risk of respiratory complications by promoting fetal lung maturation."
options.reason: Antenatal corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturation and reduce respiratory morbidity when preterm birth remains likely. They improve risk; they do not guarantee that respiratory support will be unnecessary.

options.text: "It treats organisms that could ascend after the membranes rupture before labor."
options.reason: Betamethasone is not an antimicrobial and does not replace indicated antibiotic management for membrane rupture or infection risk.

options.text: "It stops the contractions by reducing calcium entry into uterine smooth muscle."
options.reason: This describes a tocolytic mechanism associated with calcium-channel blockade, not the fetal-maturation purpose of betamethasone.

options.text: "It prevents neonatal hypoglycemia by stabilizing fetal insulin release before birth."
options.reason: That is not the purpose of antenatal betamethasone. Corticosteroid exposure can instead require maternal glucose monitoring, especially when diabetes is present.

questions.objective: Select surveillance and prescribed support for stable PPROM
questions.stem: A stable patient at 29 weeks with confirmed PPROM is admitted for expectant management. There is no fever, bleeding, labor, or nonreassuring fetal pattern. The written plan includes prescribed latency antibiotics, antenatal corticosteroids, and ongoing fetal assessment. Which nursing measures are appropriate? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Expectant management is active: preserve the ordered plan while repeatedly reassessing for infection, labor, bleeding, and fetal compromise.
questions.rationale: For this stable 29-week patient, appropriate care includes maternal infection surveillance, ordered fetal assessment, prompt reporting of movement changes, limited routine digital examinations, and administration of the prescribed antibiotics and corticosteroids. Stability must be reassessed over time. The case does not prescribe universal bed rest or extend this medication plan to every gestational age or PPROM presentation.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies an explicitly documented expectant-management plan while selecting four independent surveillance or treatment actions and rejecting an isolated-test inference and routine strict bed rest. The estimate remains level 2.

options.text: Trend maternal temperature and pulse, and assess for uterine tenderness or a change in fluid odor.
options.reason: These are relevant clinical findings during surveillance for evolving intraamniotic infection; no single finding should be interpreted in isolation.

options.text: Administer the prescribed antibiotics and corticosteroids after verifying allergies and the current orders.
options.reason: At the stated gestation, these prescribed therapies fit the documented expectant-management plan. The item does not turn them into an all-gestation or nurse-initiated regimen.

options.text: Continue the ordered fetal surveillance and ask the patient to report any decrease in fetal movement.
options.reason: PPROM carries continuing fetal risks, including cord-related compromise. Ongoing prescribed assessment and attention to movement changes help detect a change in status.

options.text: Avoid routine digital cervical examinations while continuing to assess for new contractions or bleeding.
options.reason: Limiting routine digital examinations reduces avoidable infection exposure in stable PPROM, while new labor or bleeding symptoms still require prompt clinical reassessment.

options.text: Use the absence of fever and one normal white blood cell count to rule out evolving intraamniotic infection.
options.reason: Neither absence of one clinical sign nor a single normal laboratory value excludes evolving infection; interpret serial clinical findings, maternal tests, and fetal status together.

options.text: Begin strict bed rest as the standard method to prevent birth until the antibiotic course is completed.
options.reason: Routine strict bed rest is not an evidence-based universal PPROM intervention and can cause harm. Activity decisions should follow the individualized plan and current maternal-fetal status.

questions.objective: Select and evaluate safe nursing care: Shoulder dystocia.
questions.stem: After the fetal head delivers, it retracts against the perineum and the shoulders do not deliver. The birth clinician announces shoulder dystocia. Which actions should the nurse perform or assist with? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: The head has delivered but the shoulders are impacted, and the clinician has announced the emergency.
questions.rationale: Coordinated maneuvers, not forceful pushing or traction, address shoulder impaction. Follow the clinician's directions and document the sequence accurately.
questions.difficultyReason: Select coordinated shoulder-dystocia maneuvers after the diagnosis has been announced.

options.text: Call the additional obstetric and neonatal team members specified by protocol.
options.reason: Extra personnel and newborn resuscitation readiness are needed for this time-critical emergency.

options.text: Apply suprapubic pressure when directed by the birth clinician.
options.reason: Correctly directed suprapubic pressure can help dislodge the impacted shoulder.

options.text: Apply fundal pressure to increase the expulsive force.
options.reason: Fundal pressure can worsen impaction and injury.

options.text: Assist with McRoberts positioning as directed.
options.reason: Hyperflexing the patient's thighs can improve the pelvic relationship for shoulder release.

options.text: Pull forcefully on the delivered head between maneuvers.
options.reason: Excessive traction increases brachial plexus and other birth-injury risks.

questions.objective: Communicate suspected uterine rupture and resuscitation needs
questions.stem: During a trial of labor after cesarean, a patient develops sudden persistent fetal bradycardia, loss of fetal station, constant abdominal pain, pulse 132/min, and blood pressure 86/50 mm Hg. Oxytocin has been stopped, IV access is patent, and the emergency team is arriving. Which handoff best communicates the priority?
questions.clue: The prior uterine scar, loss of station, persistent bradycardia, constant pain, and maternal shock form one time-critical pattern.
questions.rationale: Use a concise handoff that communicates suspected uterine rupture, the supporting maternal-fetal findings, and the need for immediate operative birth plus maternal resuscitation. Current cesarean guidance classifies suspected rupture or persistent fetal bradycardia as an immediate threat. Oxygenation, IV fluids, blood preparation, and other resuscitative measures proceed with surgical preparation rather than replacing it.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner synthesizes several aligned findings into an emergency handoff and distinguishes it from plausible but incomplete alternative explanations. Because the evidence is concordant, the estimate is level 2 rather than level 3.

options.text: "Suspected uterine rupture: fetal bradycardia and loss of station with maternal pain and shock. Prepare immediate operative birth and resuscitation."
options.reason: This handoff names the suspected emergency, reports the aligned maternal-fetal evidence, and requests the time-critical operative and resuscitation response.

options.text: "Persistent bradycardia followed oxytocin use. Continue intrauterine resuscitation and reassess fetal station after the tracing recovers."
options.reason: Initial resuscitative actions should continue, but the full pattern suggests rupture and should not be reduced to a tracing problem that can wait for recovery before operative preparation.

options.text: "Possible epidural-related hypotension is affecting the fetus. Correct the blood pressure before requesting an immediate operative response."
options.reason: Hypotension requires resuscitation, but an epidural explanation does not account for the loss of station and constant abdominal pain. Treating one finding must not delay response to suspected rupture.

options.text: "Arrest of descent may be developing. Perform a cervical examination and reconsider oxytocin if the tracing returns to baseline."
options.reason: The patient has an acute maternal-fetal emergency, not routine arrest of descent. Examination and renewed uterine stimulation would delay or worsen the response to possible rupture.

questions.objective: Escalate symptomatic hypoglycemia when oral intake is unsafe
questions.stem: A 3-hour-old newborn of a patient with diabetes is lethargic, has a weak suck, and has shallow respirations with brief apnea. A repeat bedside glucose is 26 mg/dL. Airway support is underway, and the neonatal team is at the bedside. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate next?
questions.clue: The newborn has neurologic and respiratory symptoms plus an unsafe suck, so oral rescue cannot be the definitive route.
questions.rationale: Treat the symptomatic newborn promptly while maintaining airway and breathing support. Route safety matters: feeding and gel have roles in selected stable or asymptomatic situations, and gel may bridge a delay in IV access, but this newborn requires parenteral treatment and reassessment under the local protocol.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies symptoms and feeding safety to choose the treatment route after emergency support has already begun. The cues are aligned, so the author estimate is level 2 rather than advanced.

options.text: Begin IV dextrose treatment under the neonatal hypoglycemia protocol and reassess the response.
options.reason: The newborn is symptomatic and cannot safely rely on oral intake. IV dextrose provides prompt treatment while airway support and glucose reassessment continue.

options.text: Use buccal dextrose gel as definitive therapy while respiratory support continues.
options.reason: Gel can be a temporary bridge while IV access is established, but it should not replace IV treatment in this symptomatic, unwell newborn.

options.text: Give the prescribed feeding by bottle before starting another glucose intervention.
options.reason: Lethargy, weak suck, and apnea make bottle feeding unsafe and unreliable as the immediate glucose treatment.

options.text: Obtain laboratory confirmation before beginning glucose replacement or changing the current plan.
options.reason: A confirmatory sample can be obtained, but acute treatment should not be delayed when an at-risk newborn has symptoms and a very low bedside result.

questions.objective: Escalate enlarging scalp swelling with systemic deterioration
questions.stem: Four hours after a vacuum-assisted birth, a newborn's diffuse, fluctuant scalp swelling has extended toward the neck and head circumference has increased 1.5 cm in 90 minutes. The newborn is pale, pulse is 184/min, and capillary refill is 4 seconds. The neonatal practitioner is en route. Which bedside action should the nurse prioritize?
questions.clue: The swelling is enlarging over time and is paired with a deteriorating peripheral-perfusion pattern.
questions.rationale: Trend and systemic status distinguish this emergency pattern from a stable scalp finding. Escalate for suspected subgaleal hemorrhage and prepare to support circulation while the neonatal team evaluates and directs investigations and treatment. The nurse is not diagnosing severity from head size alone or prescribing a particular fluid or blood-product dose.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies an aligned trend in scalp size and perfusion to an urgent care decision. The emergency label and one anatomic feature do not create advanced reasoning, so the revised estimate is level 2.

options.text: Place the newborn under a radiant warmer and repeat temperature and glucose to explain the perfusion changes.
options.reason: Temperature and glucose can identify concurrent problems, but warming and metabolic testing do not address the expanding scalp collection and current poor perfusion.

options.text: Request urgent neonatal evaluation and prepare for continuous monitoring, vascular access, and circulatory support.
options.reason: Expanding diffuse swelling with tachycardia, pallor, and delayed refill suggests ongoing blood loss and possible shock. Urgent team evaluation and resuscitation readiness are indicated.

options.text: Mark the swelling margins and repeat head circumference before increasing the current surveillance level.
options.reason: Serial scalp assessment is useful, but another measurement should not precede continuous monitoring and preparation for circulatory support when deterioration is already evident.

options.text: Prepare the newborn for immediate cranial imaging to define the source of the enlarging swelling.
options.reason: Imaging may follow stabilization, but transport and diagnostic clarification do not take priority over monitoring and readiness to restore circulation.

questions.objective: Use the prescribed PKU diet with biochemical monitoring
questions.stem: An infant with confirmed phenylketonuria is preparing for discharge on an individualized plan that includes medical formula and a measured amount of breast milk. The caregiver asks how to handle hunger after a feeding, future monitoring, and new foods or products. Which statements show correct application of the plan? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Daily hunger, normal growth, a laboratory change, and food introduction each require applying—not independently rewriting—the individualized plan.
questions.rationale: PKU care is controlled, individualized nutrition rather than elimination of all protein. Caregivers should prepare the prescribed feeding plan, keep laboratory and growth follow-up, check relevant labels, and coordinate changes with the metabolic team. No universal milk recipe, numerical phenylalanine goal, or rule for every sweetener is introduced.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies an established metabolic plan to realistic home feeding, monitoring, and label decisions. Each choice is independently assessable, supporting level 2.

options.text: If the infant remains hungry after the planned feeding, I will contact the metabolic team before adding standard formula.
options.reason: An extra standard feeding changes phenylalanine and nutrient intake. The team can adjust the plan while still supporting growth and hunger cues.

options.text: I will keep the ordered phenylalanine tests even when weight gain and development appear on track.
options.reason: Expected growth and development do not establish biochemical control. Ordered phenylalanine results help the team adjust nutrition safely.

options.text: As foods and products are introduced, I will check labels for aspartame and discuss uncertain ingredients with the team.
options.reason: Aspartame contains phenylalanine and product labels identify it for people with PKU. Questions about a product belong with the metabolic team.

options.text: If a phenylalanine result rises, I will reduce the measured breast-milk portion until the next clinic visit.
options.reason: The caregiver should not independently change one component of the prescribed mixture. The team interprets the result and balances phenylalanine control with nutrition.

options.text: When solids begin, fruits and vegetables can replace the medical formula on days the infant eats well.
options.reason: Low-protein foods can be part of an individualized plan, but eating them does not make the prescribed medical formula automatically replaceable.
