The item does not create an HSV test, viral-load, membrane-duration, symptom-duration, operative-timing, or neonatal-treatment threshold.
Symptom resolution is not treated as proof of continued viral shedding; it is treated as unable to erase the supplied labor-onset prodrome from clinical history.

questions.objective: Use gestational, renal-sediment, serologic, symptom, maternal end-organ, and fetal data to decide when parallel SLE-flare and preeclampsia pathways must be reconciled in a shared handoff before disposition.
questions.stem: A patient at 31 weeks has systemic lupus erythematosus with previously quiescent lupus nephritis and takes prescribed hydroxychloroquine. At 20 weeks, blood pressure was 118/72 mm Hg, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio was 0.2, and complement and anti-double-stranded DNA results were stable for this patient. Today, repeated blood pressures are 146 to 152/90 to 94 mm Hg and the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 0.8. The patient also reports new arthralgia and a malar rash; urinalysis shows red blood cell casts, C3 and C4 are below the patient's baseline, and anti-double-stranded DNA has risen. Platelet count and AST are normal, fetal growth and surveillance are reassuring, and a blood pressure after resting is 138/86 mm Hg. The triage team is considering disposition before rheumatology has reviewed the new results. Which recommendation should the nurse include in the handoff?
questions.clue: Learning focus: Use gestational, renal-sediment, serologic, symptom, maternal end-organ, and fetal data to decide when parallel SLE-flare and preeclampsia pathways must be reconciled in a shared handoff before disposition.
questions.rationale: The encounter supports neither a flare-only nor a preeclampsia-only pathway. New hypertension and increased proteinuria after 20 weeks require pregnancy-specific surveillance, while new rash and arthralgia, red blood cell casts, falling complement, and rising anti-double-stranded DNA support active SLE or recurrent lupus nephritis. The lower resting pressure, normal platelets and AST, and reassuring fetal assessment are meaningful current findings but do not clear either branch. Every serious option preserves prescribed hydroxychloroquine, both diagnostic pathways, and same-day obstetric/MFM and rheumatology involvement. The distinguishing nursing consequence is whether the two trajectories are integrated before disposition. A shared plan avoids sequential or siloed decisions without asking the nurse to select definitive therapy.
questions.difficultyReason: All four options retain both lupus-flare and preeclampsia pathways, continue hydroxychloroquine, and arrange same-day obstetric/MFM and rheumatology review. c1 uses genuine reassuring data to permit disposition before integrated review; c2 makes a rheumatology label a prerequisite for obstetric planning; c3 completes both reviews but postpones reconciliation. The learner must translate overlapping evidence into an observable coordination sequence, not select the only inclusive plan.

options.text: Continue hydroxychloroquine and obtain a shared same-day obstetric/MFM-rheumatology plan before disposition, linking the blood-pressure/protein trend with the active urine sediment, symptoms, serologies, and fetal assessment.
options.reason: Both pathways are active and can coexist. A lower resting blood pressure, normal platelets and AST, and reassuring fetal assessment are important but do not resolve either the new pregnancy-hypertensive pattern or the patient-specific lupus-nephritis pattern. A shared plan before disposition makes the cross-domain trajectory actionable without requiring the nurse to diagnose or prescribe therapy.

options.text: Continue hydroxychloroquine and arrange both same-day reviews, but let obstetrics complete disposition from the resting pressure, platelets, AST, and fetal results while rheumatology updates the plan afterward.
options.reason: This is the closest rival because it preserves both diagnoses, both specialties, same-day timing, and established therapy. It loses on sequence: the reassuring obstetric findings do not clear new hypertension/proteinuria, and disposition before integrating the active-sediment and serologic change can fragment a potentially coexisting maternal process.

options.text: Continue hydroxychloroquine and arrange both same-day reviews, but ask rheumatology to classify the renal-serologic change before obstetrics sets the hypertension, protein, and fetal follow-up plan.
options.reason: The lupus evidence warrants rheumatology interpretation, but preeclampsia surveillance should not wait for a definitive flare label. The new gestational blood-pressure and protein pattern remains independently relevant, and the supplied data support a shared plan rather than one specialty's conclusion becoming the other's prerequisite.

options.text: Continue hydroxychloroquine and complete both same-day reviews, but document separate specialty follow-up plans and reconcile the renal-serologic and pregnancy-hypertensive trends at the next shared visit.
options.reason: Separate same-day assessments are better than closing either branch, but postponing reconciliation leaves the current coexistence question unresolved at disposition. The same blood pressure, protein, urine sediment, symptoms, and serologies must inform one coordinated near-term plan because each domain can change the meaning of the other.

questions.objective: Use the chronology and partial response to oxygen to maintain parallel acute-chest and infection evaluation while dynamically reassessing analgesia and hydration during a sickle-cell pain admission.
questions.stem: A patient at 29 weeks with sickle cell disease was admitted 3 hours ago for a vaso-occlusive pain episode after 2 days of vomiting and poor intake. On admission, lungs were clear, temperature was 37.1° C (98.8° F), respirations were 18/min, and oxygen saturation was 98% on room air. Prescribed isotonic IV hydration and the patient's individualized opioid regimen were started. Since admission, 1,200 mL has infused and urine output is 350 mL; pain has decreased from 9/10 to 5/10. The patient now has a temperature of 38.2° C (100.8° F), pleuritic chest pain, cough, respirations of 26/min, oxygen saturation of 90% on room air, and fine bibasilar crackles. Fetal surveillance is reassuring. Oxygen is started under the local protocol. Twenty minutes later, the patient is awake, respirations are 24/min, and saturation is 95% on 2 L/min, but the cough, pleuritic pain, and crackles persist. The team has been notified, and urgent hematology and maternal-fetal-medicine evaluation is underway. Which interpretations or actions belong in the nurse's updated plan? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Learning focus: Use the chronology and partial response to oxygen to maintain parallel acute-chest and infection evaluation while dynamically reassessing analgesia and hydration during a sickle-cell pain admission.
questions.rationale: The patient has evolved from an uncomplicated pain episode into a high-risk pulmonary presentation. Improvement from 90% on room air to 95% on supplemental oxygen is an important response but not evidence that persistent fever, cough, pleuritic pain, tachypnea, and crackles have resolved. The updated plan keeps urgent acute-chest and infectious evaluation in parallel, preserves individualized analgesia with respiratory and sedation reassessment, and reconsiders hydration using the actual intake, output, and lung findings. Reassuring fetal surveillance cannot clear maternal deterioration, and neither an oxygen response nor a possible fluid contribution should become a prerequisite for completing the pulmonary evaluation. Hematology and maternal-fetal medicine retain diagnostic and treatment authority.
questions.difficultyReason: The strongest rival uses a real improvement on oxygen plus reassuring fetal surveillance to make recurrent room-air desaturation a diagnostic gate. Another rival uses the actual positive fluid balance and new crackles to sequence pulmonary causes instead of evaluating them in parallel. The learner must distinguish response from resolution and dynamic fluid reassessment from premature single-cause closure; no option depends on contradicting a stated baseline, banning specialist review, or claiming that pain improvement ends sickle disease.

options.text: Carry the pre- and post-oxygen findings forward: 95% on 2 L/min shows response to support, not resolution of the new pulmonary process.
options.reason: The saturation improved only with supplemental oxygen, while tachypnea, pleuritic pain, cough, fever, and crackles persist. The response demonstrates that support is helping; it does not close evaluation for acute chest syndrome, infection, or another serious pulmonary complication.

options.text: Continue prescribed individualized analgesia with close sedation and respiratory reassessment; adequate pain control supports ventilation, while dosing must remain responsive to the changing pulmonary status.
options.reason: Undertreated pain and splinting can impair ventilation, but analgesia must be reassessed when respiratory status changes. Continuing the established individualized plan with repeated assessment avoids both abrupt undertreatment and an automatic unchanged-dose assumption.

options.text: Report the 1,200-mL intake, 350-mL urine output, and new crackles, and ask the team to reassess hydration rather than automatically completing the original replacement rate.
options.reason: The patient began with poor intake, so hydration was appropriate, but the positive balance and new crackles now matter. Sickle care requires hydration without fluid overload; the nurse supplies the trajectory and seeks team-directed adjustment rather than independently stopping or fixing a rate.

options.text: Keep infection and acute chest syndrome in parallel evaluation because fever and cough can identify an infectious trigger without separating it from sickle pulmonary injury.
options.reason: Infection can precipitate or coexist with acute chest syndrome, and their manifestations overlap. The chronology supports evaluation of both pathways rather than declaring that one explains away the other.

options.text: Use the sustained 95% saturation on low-flow oxygen and reassuring fetal tracing to defer chest imaging unless room-air desaturation recurs during the next reassessment.
options.reason: This uses a genuine treatment response and reassuring fetal information, but it makes renewed room-air hypoxemia a gate to evaluating persistent maternal pulmonary findings. Respiratory symptoms plus documented hypoxemia warrant prompt clinician-directed evaluation even when oxygen temporarily improves the displayed saturation.

options.text: Because crackles appeared after a positive fluid balance, prioritize fluid overload and wait for response to hydration reduction before continuing the infection and acute-chest evaluation.
options.reason: Fluid balance and crackles justify immediate reassessment of hydration, making this a plausible rival. They do not establish a single cause or justify sequencing the high-risk sickle and infectious pulmonary evaluation behind a fluid-response trial.

questions.objective: Distinguish an initially plausible vacuum chignon from an evolving subgaleal hemorrhage pattern and escalate before overt shock while preserving serial facts, team authority, and local protocol boundaries.
questions.stem: A term newborn was delivered by vacuum assistance after a prolonged second stage; the cup detached once before birth was completed with a second application. Apgar scores were 8 and 9. At 15 minutes, the newborn was pink and alert with a pulse of 142/min, capillary refill of 2 seconds, head circumference of 35.0 cm, and firm swelling centered at the cup site that crossed one suture line. At 90 minutes, the newborn remains awake and has fed, blood pressure and oxygen saturation are unchanged, but the swelling is now diffuse and fluctuant, extends beyond the cup site toward the nape, and slightly displaces the ears. Head circumference is 35.8 cm, pulse is 158/min, capillary refill is 3 seconds, and the skin appears paler. The neonatal practitioner is coming to the bedside. Which actions or interpretations should the nurse include now? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Learning focus: Distinguish an initially plausible vacuum chignon from an evolving subgaleal hemorrhage pattern and escalate before overt shock while preserving serial facts, team authority, and local protocol boundaries.
questions.rationale: The initial firm cup-site swelling and reassuring adaptation can fit an expected vacuum chignon, and crossing a suture line alone is not decisive. Over the next 75 minutes, however, the swelling becomes diffuse and fluctuant, spreads toward the nape, displaces the ears, and accompanies increased head circumference, rising pulse, slower refill, and pallor. That trajectory is concerning for subgaleal hemorrhage before hypotension or oxygen desaturation appears. The nurse should escalate now, communicate the entire chronology and vacuum exposure without assigning single-maneuver causation, continue serial scalp and perfusion assessment, and prepare for practitioner-directed investigation and circulatory support under the local protocol. Neither another measurement nor imaging should become a prerequisite for hemorrhage readiness.
questions.difficultyReason: The initial firm cup-site swelling that crosses a suture can be an expected chignon, while later diffuse fluctuant expansion, ear displacement, circumference change, and subtle perfusion drift require reinterpretation before overt shock. The strongest rival uses normal blood pressure, normal oxygenation, and alert feeding to justify one more confirmation point. Other rivals appropriately recognize the exposure but fail through unsupported maneuver causation or imaging-first sequencing. The learner must compare serial morphology and systemic response rather than select a rote post-vacuum checklist.

options.text: Escalate the serial pattern as suspected subgaleal hemorrhage now rather than waiting for hypotension, oxygen desaturation, or a larger head-circumference change.
options.reason: The change from localized firm swelling to diffuse fluctuant expansion with ear displacement, increasing circumference, a rising pulse, delayed refill, and pallor supports urgent evaluation before overt shock. Normal blood pressure and oxygen saturation can be falsely reassuring early.

options.text: Report both examinations and the vacuum course; crossing a suture line initially is less decisive than the later change in consistency, distribution, circumference, and perfusion.
options.reason: A vacuum-related chignon can cross sutures and be prominent immediately. The clinically important inference comes from the evolution away from a firm cup-site finding toward diffuse fluctuant enlargement plus perfusion change, so both time points belong in the handoff.

options.text: Continue cardiorespiratory, perfusion, scalp, and head-circumference surveillance and prepare for practitioner-directed laboratory assessment, vascular access, and circulatory support under the local protocol.
options.reason: Suspected subgaleal bleeding can progress rapidly. Ongoing serial assessment and readiness for team-directed investigation and support are appropriate while the practitioner evaluates; the nurse does not independently diagnose severity or prescribe a fluid or blood-product dose.

options.text: Use the unchanged blood pressure and oxygen saturation plus alert feeding to continue routine surveillance until another head measurement confirms that enlargement is continuing.
options.reason: Those findings are genuinely reassuring and make this the closest rival, but they do not outweigh the already supplied change in swelling, circumference, pulse, refill, and color. Requiring one more measurement delays escalation of an evolving hemorrhage pattern.

options.text: Record the single cup detachment as the cause of subgaleal hemorrhage before clinician evaluation because the later swelling developed after vacuum exposure.
options.reason: The vacuum course is relevant exposure history, but temporal association does not let the nurse assign the collection to one detachment or make a final diagnosis before evaluation. The correct response is urgent evidence-based escalation without unsupported maneuver-specific causation.

options.text: Arrange cranial imaging as the confirmation step before activating hemorrhage readiness because stable blood pressure and oxygenation permit an anatomic diagnosis first.
options.reason: Imaging may later help characterize injury, but it should not gate monitoring and resuscitation readiness when serial clinical findings already raise concern for concealed blood loss. Stabilization and urgent neonatal evaluation precede diagnostic transport or confirmation.

questions.objective: Build an immediate post–shoulder dystocia handoff and response that uses serial maternal and newborn findings to time focused evaluation, preserve exposure history, and communicate uncertainty without grammar-cued or uniquely complete answers.
questions.stem: A shoulder dystocia is resolved about 80 seconds after delivery of the head. McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure are attempted first, followed by successful delivery of the posterior arm. Ten minutes later, the newborn's Apgar scores are 7 and 9, respirations are comfortable, and arm movement appears symmetric; a focused post-exposure examination has not yet been completed. The patient has vital signs at the recorded baseline and a firm fundus. Quantified blood loss has increased by about 250 mL during those 10 minutes, no brisk external bleeding is visible, and deep perineal pressure and pain have increased from 3/10 to 7/10; qualified clinician evaluation for internal or concealed trauma has not yet occurred. The patient asks, “Did pulling out the arm hurt the baby or cause this pain?” Which actions and interpretations should the nurse include in the immediate handoff and response? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Learning focus: Build an immediate post–shoulder dystocia handoff and response that uses serial maternal and newborn findings to time focused evaluation, preserve exposure history, and communicate uncertainty without grammar-cued or uniquely complete answers.
questions.rationale: After a resolved shoulder dystocia, the handoff should retain objective timing, personnel, the full maneuver sequence, and each observed response. The currently reassuring newborn findings do not replace a focused examination for clavicle or humerus fracture, brachial plexus injury, and hypoxic effects; further follow-up is driven by findings and local protocol, and the exposure remains relevant even if the first examination is normal. For the patient, a firm fundus, stable vital signs, and no brisk visible bleeding do not explain increasing quantified loss and deep perineal pressure and pain. The nurse continues uterine, bleeding, vital-sign, pain, and visible assessment while promptly coordinating qualified clinician evaluation for vaginal, perineal, rectal, or concealed hematoma injury. The patient's causal question should be answered now with known facts and explicit uncertainty rather than delayed, blamed on one maneuver, or paired with an outcome prediction. Later review supplements rather than replaces immediate factual communication.
questions.difficultyReason: Keyed and unkeyed choices share multi-clause, complete, and conditional forms. c4 is a respectful nonblaming communication plan that loses by postponing a factual uncertainty response to a direct question. c5 performs the full immediate newborn examination and loses only by erasing exposure from a normal-result handoff. c6 preserves all RN-scope hemorrhage and uterine surveillance and loses on whether current reassuring findings justify one more trend point before clinician trauma evaluation. Selection requires case-specific timing, continuity, and communication judgments rather than detecting an adversative clause, an unsafe omission, maneuver blame, or permanent diagnostic closure.

options.text: Give the receiving teams the head-to-body times, personnel present, complete maneuver sequence, and observed response to each attempt; posterior-arm success does not erase earlier attempts.
options.reason: An objective chronology supports both recipients' continuing care and later review. Each attempted maneuver remains part of the exposure and event record even though posterior-arm delivery completed the birth.

options.text: Arrange a focused newborn examination now for clavicle or humerus fracture, brachial plexus injury, and hypoxic effects, although adaptation and symmetric movement are reassuring; later follow-up follows findings and local protocol.
options.reason: The newborn is currently stable, but the known shoulder-dystocia exposure warrants the focused examination that has not yet occurred. Reassuring Apgar scores, respirations, and movement inform that examination without replacing it; subsequent observation, referral, or testing depends on findings and local protocol.

options.text: Continue quantified blood-loss, fundal-tone, vital-sign, pain, and visible-perineal assessment while promptly coordinating qualified clinician evaluation for vaginal, perineal, rectal, or concealed hematoma injury.
options.reason: The firm fundus, stable vital signs, and lack of brisk visible bleeding are important, but they do not explain increasing deep pressure, pain, and blood loss. The nurse continues parallel uterine and hemorrhage surveillance and promptly coordinates clinician-led assessment of internal or concealed trauma.

options.text: Although the examinations are incomplete, answer now with the known sequence and current findings, explain why both patients still need checks and what remains uncertain, and offer later review.
options.reason: The patient's direct question can be answered factually without speculating: the event sequence and current findings are known, while injury and causation are not yet established. Explaining current uncertainty, ongoing assessment, and access to later discussion supports informed care now.

options.text: Explain now that the event resolved, both patients are being checked, and later review is available; reserve discussion of possible causes and uncertainty until the examinations are complete.
options.reason: This response is calm, factual, nonblaming, and preserves continuing checks and later review, so it is a realistic communication alternative. It is incomplete for the patient's direct question: the nurse can state now that current findings do not establish injury or causation and explain why the uncertainty itself requires assessment.

options.text: Complete the focused newborn examination now. If its findings are normal, give a routine newborn handoff without separately carrying the shoulder-dystocia exposure forward.
options.reason: The immediate focused examination is correct and a normal result would be reassuring. The downstream handoff remains too narrow because exposure history and the completed examination provide context for any later finding and for local-protocol follow-up; a normal first examination does not erase the event.

options.text: Maintain quantified loss, uterine tone, vital signs, pain, and visible assessment now; use one additional trend point before clinician trauma evaluation because vital signs and fundal tone remain reassuring.
options.reason: This preserves the complete RN-scope surveillance and uses genuinely reassuring findings, making it a plausible timing rival. The existing trajectory already includes rising loss and sharply increasing deep pressure and pain with no completed internal-trauma evaluation, so another trend point should not precede prompt clinician assessment.

questions.objective: Integrate tick-exposure chronology, serial rash morphology, systemic findings, a competing tinea exposure, and the early serologic window when framing a clinician-directed decision for a possible erythema migrans lesion.
questions.stem: A 10-year-old who lives in a Lyme-endemic county is seen at the pediatric clinic 12 days after a caregiver removed an attached tick from the posterior thigh. A small itchy bump appeared immediately and faded within 2 days. On day 9, a new oval red patch appeared at the same site. Caregiver photographs and border markings show that it has expanded beyond each prior border over 3 days. The patch is warm with partial central clearing, but it is not itchy, painful, scaly, raised at the edge, or draining. Today the child has fatigue, headache, and a temperature of 38.0° C (100.4° F), without edema or red streaking. A wrestling teammate is being treated for ringworm, and the children recently shared practice mats. A two-tier Lyme antibody test drawn on the first day of the new rash was negative. At the same-day clinician evaluation, which synthesis should the nurse present as the leading interpretation?
questions.clue: Learning focus: Integrate tick-exposure chronology, serial rash morphology, systemic findings, a competing tinea exposure, and the early serologic window when framing a clinician-directed decision for a possible erythema migrans lesion.
questions.rationale: The nurse should preserve the entire chronology: an immediate itchy bite-site bump resolved within 2 days, then a separate warm, progressively expanding, nonpruritic and nonpainful patch began 9 days after the tick exposure and was accompanied by fever, headache, and fatigue. That pattern is compatible with erythema migrans. Current guidance supports clinical diagnosis when tick exposure in an endemic area is paired with a compatible erythema migrans lesion, and it cautions that antibody tests may be falsely negative during the first weeks. Partial clearing and wrestling exposure make tinea corporis a credible rival, but the lack of scale or itch and the delayed expansion plus systemic symptoms weigh against it. Cellulitis remains possible but is less consistent without pain, edema, drainage, or streaking. The nurse frames the evidence and its timing for the clinician; the item does not let the nurse independently diagnose, select an antibiotic, or set a dose or duration.
questions.difficultyReason: The strongest rival is supported by a real contact-sport exposure, shared mats, annular shape, and partial central clearing. The learner must nevertheless integrate the resolved immediate reaction, delayed onset, serial expansion, absence of scale and itch, systemic symptoms, and the early false-negative window. No single stated order, unsafe outlier, dose fact, or collaboration wording identifies the key.

options.text: Lead with likely erythema migrans: connect the delayed, progressively expanding, warm, nonpruritic patch and systemic symptoms to the tick exposure, and explain that the early negative antibody result should not postpone the clinician's treatment decision.
options.reason: The immediate itchy bump resolved on the expected short local-reaction timeline, whereas a distinct lesion began 9 days after the bite and progressively expanded with warmth and systemic symptoms. That pattern is compatible with erythema migrans. Antibody testing can be falsely negative during the first weeks, particularly when erythema migrans is present, so the day-1 negative result does not outweigh the clinical and exposure pattern or justify delaying the clinician's treatment decision.

options.text: Lead with tinea corporis: connect the partial central clearing and wrestling exposure, regard the nonscaly nonpruritic edge as atypical but outweighed, and use the negative Lyme test to support a fungal evaluation and treatment decision.
options.reason: The teammate, shared mats, annular shape, and partial clearing make tinea the strongest rival. However, tinea corporis is commonly itchy and scaly, while this lesion is nonscaly and nonpruritic, expands after a characteristic post-tick delay, and accompanies fever, headache, and fatigue. The very early negative Lyme antibody result cannot be used as affirmative support for the fungal interpretation.

options.text: Lead with delayed bite hypersensitivity: connect the lesion to the original site, treat continued expansion as an inflammatory reaction, and ask the clinician to choose symptomatic care while observing for later evidence of infection.
options.reason: A local bite reaction is plausible because the findings share a site, but the child already had an immediate itchy bump that resolved within 2 days. A separate lesion that starts on day 9, expands over several days, is not itchy, and accompanies systemic symptoms is not well explained by simply extending the resolved local-reaction episode.

options.text: Lead with cellulitis: connect the warmth, expansion, and fever to bacterial skin infection, and ask the clinician to choose an antibacterial pathway while treating the tick history and negative Lyme result as secondary.
options.reason: Warmth, expansion, and fever keep bacterial skin infection in the differential. The absence of pain, edema, drainage, or streaking, together with an oval lesion that expands after a tick-bite delay and is associated with headache and fatigue, makes cellulitis less coherent as the leading synthesis. The early negative Lyme test cannot relegate the exposure pattern to a secondary detail.

The item asks for the leading handoff synthesis at an already arranged same-day clinician visit; it does not state that the nurse independently confirms Lyme disease, tinea corporis, hypersensitivity, or cellulitis.
The item does not select an antibiotic or antifungal, calculate a dose, state a duration, infer tick attachment duration, or create a prophylaxis rule.
Central clearing is treated as nondiagnostic: it can support a tinea rival and can occur in erythema migrans, while many erythema migrans lesions do not have a classic target appearance.
The negative result is explicitly tied to the first day of the new rash. It is not generalized into a rule that all negative Lyme tests are uninformative or that no testing is ever appropriate.

The clinician retains responsibility for diagnosis, consideration of alternative illnesses, individualized treatment, and any additional testing; no drug, dose, allergy, contraindication, or universal regimen is imported.
Older course simplifications about a definitive early test or age-based drug exclusions are not used. Current CDC and IDSA guidance controls the early-serology and clinical-diagnosis claims.

questions.objective: Differentiate a stable caput from cephalohematoma and evolving subgaleal hemorrhage
questions.stem: One hour after a vaginal birth, a newborn has soft, edematous scalp swelling that was present at birth and extends across suture lines. During serial assessments, the swelling and head circumference remain unchanged. Color, heart rate, and perfusion are within the nursery's expected ranges. Which plan should the nurse follow?
questions.clue: Use both the suture-line pattern and the absence of progression or systemic deterioration.
questions.rationale: A soft scalp edema that crosses suture lines, is present at birth, and remains stable without perfusion changes is consistent with caput succedaneum. Continue routine serial newborn assessment and give reassuring teaching because caput usually resolves without treatment. A cephalohematoma is confined by suture lines and adds bilirubin-surveillance concerns. Diffuse swelling that enlarges or accompanies pallor, tachycardia, delayed refill, or increasing head circumference requires urgent evaluation for subgaleal hemorrhage. Crossing a suture line alone does not make an emergency; the trajectory and systemic findings complete the distinction.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate anatomy, timing, trend, and systemic status to select the matching care pathway rather than identify one isolated definition, supporting level 2.

options.text: Treat the finding as a cephalohematoma and arrange bilirubin surveillance because the swelling crosses suture lines.
options.reason: A cephalohematoma does not cross suture lines. Bilirubin surveillance is relevant after that diagnosis, but the stated anatomy and stable course fit caput instead.

options.text: Document a finding consistent with caput, continue routine serial assessment, and explain that it usually resolves without treatment.
options.reason: Caput is soft scalp edema that can cross sutures. Stability of the swelling, head circumference, and perfusion supports routine observation and reassuring teaching.

options.text: Activate emergency subgaleal-hemorrhage support solely because the swelling extends across more than one skull bone.
options.reason: Subgaleal swelling can cross sutures, but emergency concern depends on a diffuse progressive collection or systemic blood-loss findings. Those changes are absent here.

options.text: Prepare for skull imaging because any scalp swelling that crosses a suture line indicates an underlying bone injury.
options.reason: Crossing suture lines is expected with caput and does not by itself establish a skull injury or make imaging the priority.

refs.label: Week 5 High-Risk Newborn Instructor Notes — Birth injuries and soft-tissue scalp findings.
Week 5 High-Risk Newborn Student Lecture — slide 18, birth injuries.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — chapter 23, printed p. 163: caput succedaneum and cephalohematoma assessment.

limitations: The case supports a stable caput pattern; it does not claim that every swelling crossing sutures is benign.
No imaging rule, aspiration procedure, bilirubin threshold, surveillance interval, or subgaleal resuscitation protocol is introduced.
A change in swelling, head circumference, color, heart rate, or perfusion would require reassessment rather than continued reassurance.

questions.objective: Recognize a fetal alcohol syndrome pattern and select realistic newborn and family support
questions.stem: A growth-restricted newborn with documented prenatal alcohol exposure has a flat midface, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip, poor suck, and marked sensitivity to light and sound. Cardiorespiratory findings are stable, and the interprofessional team is evaluating for fetal alcohol spectrum disorder. Which nursing plan best addresses the newborn's current and longer-term needs?
questions.clue: The plan should support feeding and regulation now while acknowledging that developmental effects may persist.
questions.rationale: The findings form a taught fetal alcohol syndrome pattern. Nursing care should support safe feeding with suck-and-swallow assessment and small frequent feedings, monitor growth, reduce excess stimulation when the newborn is sensitive, and coordinate developmental and hearing follow-up with nonjudgmental family support. These measures support function and early intervention; they do not imply that established neurodevelopmental effects will disappear when alcohol clears from the newborn's body.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must connect a multi-domain exposure pattern to immediate feeding and regulation care plus longitudinal support while rejecting a transient-withdrawal explanation, supporting level 2.

options.text: Treat the findings as short-lived alcohol withdrawal and reassure the family that the physical and developmental effects should resolve after alcohol clears.
options.reason: Irritability or tremors can occur after alcohol exposure, but the growth, facial, feeding, and developmental risk pattern is not expected to reverse simply when alcohol clears.

options.text: Delay developmental and hearing referrals until a major milestone delay appears, while using routine feeding care without adaptation.
options.reason: The newborn already has a recognized risk pattern and poor suck. Early feeding support and coordinated follow-up are more appropriate than waiting for a severe delay.

options.text: Support small frequent feeds, track growth, reduce excess stimulation, and coordinate developmental and hearing follow-up with the family.
options.reason: This plan addresses poor suck, growth risk, sensory sensitivity, and possible long-term hearing and developmental effects without promising reversibility.

options.text: Use larger scheduled feeds and frequent stimulation to increase intake and accelerate neurologic adaptation before discharge.
options.reason: Larger feeds can increase fatigue or feeding difficulty, and frequent stimulation can worsen hypersensitivity. Neurologic adaptation cannot be accelerated by overstimulation.

refs.label: Week 5 High-Risk Newborn Instructor Notes — Alcohol exposure and fetal alcohol spectrum disorders.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — chapter 27, printed pp. 189–190: fetal alcohol syndrome findings, complications, and supportive newborn care.

limitations: The pattern prompts interprofessional evaluation; the nurse is not independently confirming a fetal alcohol spectrum diagnosis or predicting severity.
No feeding volume, calorie target, developmental prognosis, or mandatory referral schedule is prescribed.
The item addresses newborn recognition and support, not prenatal alcohol-use counseling or blame.

questions.objective: Use a documented non-opioid exposure to focus assessment and supportive care without labeling opioid withdrawal
questions.stem: A newborn with documented prenatal methamphetamine exposure has intermittent tremors, increased muscle tone, and fatigue with feeding. Temperature and bedside glucose are within the nursery's expected ranges, and there is no documented opioid exposure. Which actions should the nurse include now? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Use the exposure history to focus observation and support, but do not let it replace assessment or establish an opioid diagnosis.
questions.rationale: Documented non-opioid exposure can guide focused neurologic, respiratory, feeding, hydration, and growth assessment. Low-stimulation containment and small, paced feeding attempts are appropriate while coordination and physiologic stability remain adequate. The nurse should communicate the complete pattern to the neonatal team so evaluation remains open to concurrent causes. Tremors and poor feeding do not prove neonatal opioid withdrawal or authorize morphine, and the exposure history should not be hidden while awaiting another test.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must select a coordinated assessment-and-support bundle while avoiding both diagnostic closure and an opioid-specific treatment pathway, supporting level 2.

options.text: Trend tone, tremors, state regulation, respirations, feeding tolerance, hydration, and weight.
options.reason: The exposure history supports focused monitoring across neurologic, respiratory, feeding, hydration, and growth domains.

options.text: Start an opioid-withdrawal medication pathway and request morphine because tremors and poor feeding establish neonatal abstinence syndrome.
options.reason: The findings do not establish opioid withdrawal, no opioid exposure is documented, and medication decisions require a diagnosis-specific team plan.

options.text: Use a dim, quiet environment with swaddling or containment and offer small paced feeds while coordination remains safe.
options.reason: Reduced stimulation and supportive feeding can limit stress and fatigue while the nurse continues to observe feeding safety and physiologic tolerance.

options.text: Omit the documented exposure from handoff until a newborn toxicology result independently confirms it.
options.reason: The documented history is relevant to focused assessment and should be communicated. A toxicology result is not required before reporting known clinical context.

options.text: Report the exposure and complete assessment pattern so the neonatal team can evaluate other causes and refine the care plan.
options.reason: Exposure may contribute to the pattern but does not exclude other neonatal problems. Team evaluation preserves diagnostic breadth and guides further care.

options.text: Increase handling and wake the newborn frequently between feeds to reduce abnormal tone and prevent sleep-related symptoms.
options.reason: Frequent handling can increase stress and does not treat abnormal tone. Care should be paced and stimulation reduced when the newborn shows sensitivity or fatigue.

refs.label: Week 5 High-Risk Newborn Instructor Notes — Non-opioid prenatal substance and medication exposure.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — chapter 27, printed pp. 189–190: exposure-related findings and supportive newborn care.

limitations: The item does not claim that methamphetamine exposure always produces withdrawal or that the listed findings are specific to one exposure.
No toxicology order, scoring system, medication, child-protection action, breastfeeding decision, or discharge rule is prescribed.
The case owns post-birth assessment and support; prenatal cessation and maternal-risk counseling remain outside scope.

questions.objective: Recognize net fluid loss in a preterm newborn and escalate for team-directed fluid and environmental reassessment
questions.stem: A 28-week newborn with very thin skin remains tachypneic under a radiant warmer and is receiving prescribed IV fluids. The documented intake has been delivered. Across successive assessments, weight is falling faster than the unit's expected transition trend, urine output is increasing, and serum sodium has moved from within the unit reference range to above it. Blood pressure and perfusion remain stable, with no edema or crackles. Which recommendation should the nurse make?
questions.clue: Interpret the direction of the weight, urine, and sodium changes together with the newborn's sources of insensible fluid loss.
questions.rationale: The aligned weight loss, increasing urine output, and rising sodium support a possible net water-loss trend. Prematurity increases vulnerability because thin skin, tachypnea, heat exposure, and immature renal concentration can all affect fluid balance. The nurse should verify the measurement record, report the trend, and request team reassessment of the prescribed fluid plan and heat/humidity or respiratory-loss contributors. Stable perfusion does not erase an evolving fluid/electrolyte problem. Independent free-water administration, warmer changes, diuretics, or fluid-order changes are not authorized by the case.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate serial data with several preterm loss mechanisms and preserve team authority rather than reacting to one value, supporting level 2.

options.text: Continue the current plan until the next daily weight because increasing urine output and stable perfusion rule out dehydration.
options.reason: Stable perfusion can coexist with an evolving deficit. The combined weight, urine, and sodium trajectory warrants timely reassessment rather than waiting.

options.text: Recommend reducing the IV fluid rate because weight loss and higher sodium show that renal excretion is improving.
options.reason: Weight loss plus rising sodium suggests proportionally greater water loss, not proof that the prescribed intake should be reduced. Any fluid change remains team-directed.

options.text: Give sterile water through the feeding tube and lower the warmer setting now to replace the presumed insensible loss.
options.reason: The nurse should not add free water or independently change the thermal environment. Those changes require evaluation and orders based on the complete trend.

options.text: Report possible net water loss, verify the intake, output, and weight data, and ask the team to reassess prescribed fluids and environmental losses.
options.reason: This recommendation integrates the serial trend with thin skin, tachypnea, radiant heat, and immature renal concentration while preserving team-directed changes.

options.text: Treat the pattern as fluid overload and prepare for a diuretic because the sodium is above the unit reference range.
options.reason: The newborn has weight loss, increased urine output, no edema, and no crackles. The supplied pattern does not support fluid overload or an independently initiated diuretic.

refs.label: Week 5 High-Risk Newborn Instructor Notes — Preterm infant monitoring, including intake, output, daily weight, and electrolyte balance.
Week 5 High-Risk Newborn Student Lecture — slide 5, preterm fluid and electrolyte vulnerability.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — chapter 27, printed pp. 192–193: preterm fluid administration, daily weight, intake/output, and hydration assessment.

limitations: The reference-range categories and expected weight trajectory are case-specific; no universal sodium cutoff, weight-loss percentage, urine-output threshold, or monitoring interval is created.
The case supports reporting and team reassessment, not an independent fluid-rate, humidity, warmer, enteral-water, or medication change.
The item tests general preterm fluid vulnerability and does not duplicate the furosemide-response decision in sf1-q285.

questions.objective: Distinguish secondary amenorrhea after pregnancy exclusion and prioritize cause-directed endocrine evaluation.
questions.stem: A 23-year-old patient reports no menstrual periods for 4 months. Menarche occurred at age 12, cycles were previously regular, and pregnancy testing is negative. The patient also reports new milky nipple discharge. Which nursing summary should guide follow-up?
questions.clue: The patient menstruated regularly before the current 4-month interruption, and the added symptom points toward an endocrine cause that still needs evaluation.
questions.rationale: This is secondary amenorrhea because menstruation occurred previously and regular cycles have now stopped for more than 3 months. Once pregnancy is excluded, the history should guide a cause-directed evaluation. New milky nipple discharge raises concern for hyperprolactinemia; medication review and clinician-ordered prolactin and thyroid testing belong in the initial evaluation. A prior history of menses argues against labeling this primary amenorrhea, and empiric cycle treatment or prolonged reassurance should not replace evaluation.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must combine prior cycle history, duration, pregnancy exclusion, and a new endocrine clue to classify the pattern and choose the next step rather than repeat the pregnancy-first decision.

options.text: Classify this as secondary amenorrhea and arrange cause-directed evaluation, including medication review and clinician-ordered prolactin and thyroid studies.
options.reason: Previously regular menses followed by more than 3 months without menstruation is secondary amenorrhea. After pregnancy exclusion, the milky discharge makes focused endocrine evaluation, including prolactin, appropriate.

options.text: Classify this as primary amenorrhea and prioritize imaging for a congenital outflow obstruction before reviewing medications or endocrine causes.
options.reason: Primary amenorrhea describes failure to begin menstruation. This patient menstruated regularly for years, so a primary anatomic pathway does not fit the supplied history.

options.text: Treat this as normal cycle variation because pregnancy is excluded, and reassess only if the absence of menses reaches 6 months.
options.reason: More than 3 months without menses after previously regular cycles warrants evaluation; the new nipple discharge is an additional reason not to delay.

options.text: Request medication to induce withdrawal bleeding now, and evaluate endocrine causes only if menses do not resume after treatment.
options.reason: Inducing bleeding before evaluating the cause can obscure the diagnostic problem. The endocrine clue should be assessed rather than deferred behind empiric treatment.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — Menstrual Disorders: Amenorrhea.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing — Infertility: assessment of gynecologic history and hormone levels.
American Society for Reproductive Medicine — Current evaluation of amenorrhea: a committee opinion (2024), Secondary Amenorrhea and Laboratory Tests sections.

limitations: The item tests classification and the next evaluation branch after pregnancy exclusion; it does not repeat the existing pregnancy-first decision.
Milky nipple discharge raises concern for hyperprolactinemia but does not establish a pituitary diagnosis.
No laboratory threshold, imaging sequence, medication choice, or treatment regimen is prescribed.

questions.objective: Select age-appropriate osteoporosis screening for a postmenopausal patient before a fragility fracture occurs.
questions.stem: A 68-year-old postmenopausal patient has no known osteoporosis, no history of a fragility fracture, and has never had bone-density screening. Which plan should the nurse recommend at the wellness visit?
questions.clue: The patient is an asymptomatic woman older than 65 who has not yet been screened.
questions.rationale: Menopause-related estrogen loss accelerates bone loss and increases fracture risk. Current preventive guidance recommends osteoporosis screening for women age 65 years or older, using central dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) bone mineral density with or without fracture-risk assessment. Screening is appropriate before a fracture or pain occurs. Serum calcium, risk discussion alone, or an assumption of osteoporosis based only on menopause does not substitute for the recommended bone measurement.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a direct age-based preventive screening recommendation to an otherwise uncomplicated postmenopausal visit.

options.text: Arrange osteoporosis screening with a DXA bone-density measurement now, with fracture-risk assessment added if the clinician uses it.
options.reason: Women age 65 years or older should be screened for osteoporosis with DXA bone mineral density, whether or not a fracture-risk tool is also used.

options.text: Use a serum calcium level as the screening test, and reserve DXA for a result below the laboratory reference range.
options.reason: Serum calcium is not a substitute for bone-density screening and does not determine whether age-based DXA screening is indicated.

options.text: Defer bone-density screening until the patient reports bone pain, loss of height, or a low-impact fracture.
options.reason: The purpose of screening is to identify osteoporosis and fracture risk before a fragility fracture or other late manifestation occurs.

options.text: Treat the postmenopausal history as proof of osteoporosis and begin a bone medication before obtaining a bone-density measurement.
options.reason: Menopause increases risk but does not itself diagnose osteoporosis. The case supports screening, not an unmeasured diagnosis or an independently selected treatment.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — Menopause and osteoporosis.
U.S. Preventive Services Task Force — Osteoporosis to Prevent Fractures: Screening, final recommendation statement (January 14, 2025).

limitations: The screening recommendation applies to women age 65 years or older without known osteoporosis or a prior fragility fracture; the case does not address secondary osteoporosis.
No diagnosis, medication, supplement dose, hormone-therapy plan, or treatment threshold is supplied.
The item tests the distinct menopause bone-health branch, not vasomotor symptoms, hormone selection, or postmenopausal bleeding.

questions.objective: Teach correct pelvic-floor muscle exercise technique for stress urinary incontinence.
questions.stem: A patient reports small urine leaks when coughing and sneezing and is starting pelvic-floor muscle exercises. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Effective Kegel exercises isolate, contract, and fully relax the pelvic-floor muscles; routine interruption of urination is not the exercise plan.
questions.rationale: Leakage with coughing or sneezing is a stress-incontinence pattern, and pelvic-floor muscle training can reduce these leaks. Correct teaching helps the patient identify the pelvic floor by imagining prevention of passing gas, then squeeze, hold briefly, and fully relax while keeping the abdomen and thighs relaxed. Repeatedly stopping the urine stream can prevent complete bladder emptying and raise infection risk, so it is not routine practice. Bearing down increases downward pressure rather than strengthening the pelvic floor.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must select several compatible technique elements and reject two commonly confused actions rather than identify Kegel exercises by name alone.

options.text: Identify the target muscles by imagining that you are trying to prevent passing gas.
options.reason: The muscles used to prevent passing gas are pelvic-floor muscles and provide a safe way to identify the intended contraction.

options.text: Squeeze the pelvic-floor muscles, hold briefly as taught, and then fully relax them before repeating.
options.reason: Kegel training uses deliberate contraction followed by complete relaxation; the clinician can individualize hold time and repetitions.

options.text: Keep the abdomen and thighs relaxed so the effort stays focused on the pelvic floor.
options.reason: Tightening surrounding muscles can increase pressure on the bladder and reduces isolation of the intended pelvic-floor contraction.

options.text: Practice during every urination by repeatedly stopping and restarting the urine stream.
options.reason: Interrupting urine flow may help identify the muscles initially, but doing it routinely can interfere with emptying and increase bladder-infection risk.

options.text: Bear down as if having a bowel movement during each contraction to strengthen the support muscles.
options.reason: Bearing down is the opposite of the inward pelvic-floor contraction and increases downward pressure rather than training the target muscles.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — Pelvic floor dysfunction, Kegel exercises, and urinary incontinence.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing — Prenatal Care and Postpartum Client Education: Kegel exercise teaching.
National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases — Kegel Exercises, How do I do Kegel exercises? (last reviewed November 2021).

limitations: The symptom pattern is limited to uncomplicated stress leakage; the item does not diagnose prolapse, retention, infection, or another incontinence subtype.
Hold time, repetition count, frequency, and progression should be individualized rather than treated as a universal prescription.
The item tests basic exercise teaching and does not duplicate the existing pessary refitting decision.

questions.objective: Use private, nonjudgmental, non-directive communication to support a patient receiving abortion care.
questions.stem: A patient who is scheduled for abortion care says, “I have made my decision, but I am anxious. I do not want anyone judging me or trying to change my mind.” Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The patient is asking for emotional safety and information without pressure or imposed values.
questions.rationale: Therapeutic abortion counseling is voluntary, private, person-centered, respectful, and non-directive. The nurse should invite the patient's concerns, listen, answer questions in understandable language, and avoid imposing personal values or requiring another person's involvement. Minimizing emotion, predicting a particular emotional outcome, or directing the decision does not meet the patient's stated need.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner identifies the one response that combines privacy, open-ended listening, understandable information, and respect for the patient's decision.

options.text: “Tell me what is worrying you. We can talk privately, and I will answer your questions without trying to direct your decision.”
options.reason: This response protects privacy, invites the patient's concerns, and offers nonjudgmental, non-directive support.

options.text: “You should bring a partner or family member so we can be certain that someone else agrees with your decision.”
options.reason: Support persons may be included if the patient wants them, but requiring another person's agreement undermines privacy and autonomy.

options.text: “Try not to focus on your anxiety now; the important thing is to complete the appointment before discussing emotions.”
options.reason: This dismisses the patient's expressed anxiety instead of using therapeutic communication and answering current concerns.

options.text: “I will explain why this is the best choice for you so that you can feel more confident about going through with it.”
options.reason: The nurse should not direct the decision or present a personal judgment about which choice is best for the patient.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — Elective Abortion: emotional considerations, counseling, and therapeutic communication.
World Health Organization — Abortion care guideline, Service Delivery Recommendation 5: Provision of counselling (3.2.2–3.2.3); second edition published August 24, 2025.

limitations: The item is limited to therapeutic communication and emotional support from the instructor-note passages on those topics.
It does not test abortion method, gestational timing, medications, complications, consent law, jurisdiction-specific requirements, or contraception.
The scenario does not claim a universal emotional response or require counseling when a patient declines it.

questions.objective: Escalate a persistent gynecologic warning-sign cluster for diagnostic evaluation without assigning an unsupported diagnosis.
questions.stem: A 47-year-old patient reports persistent vulvar itching and irritation with a new raised, discolored area of vulvar skin. The symptoms have been present for 3 weeks and are not normal for the patient. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The symptoms are new, have persisted longer than 2 weeks, and include both irritation and a skin change, but they do not establish a specific cause.
questions.rationale: Persistent vulvar itching or irritation and a new vulvar skin or color change are warning signs that require diagnostic follow-up when they are new, last 2 weeks or longer, and are not normal for the patient. These findings can have causes other than cancer, so the nurse should arrange timely clinical evaluation without naming a malignancy or treating the pattern as proof of one. Self-treating and delaying care, substituting routine cervical screening, or beginning cancer-specific teaching before diagnosis does not match the evidence provided.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must recognize persistence and clustering as the discriminator while avoiding both under-triage and unsupported diagnostic overreach.

options.text: Arrange timely clinician evaluation of the persistent vulvar symptoms and skin change rather than treating them as simple irritation.
options.reason: New vulvar itching or irritation with a skin or color change lasting more than 2 weeks warrants diagnostic evaluation even though the cause is not yet known.

options.text: Recommend an over-the-counter anti-itch cream and wait until the next annual visit unless vaginal bleeding begins.
options.reason: Symptom relief may later be appropriate, but self-treatment should not delay evaluation of persistent vulvar irritation with a new skin change.

options.text: Schedule routine cervical screening as the sole evaluation because it checks for the gynecologic causes of vulvar symptoms.
options.reason: Preventive cervical screening does not evaluate the full range of causes of persistent vulvar symptoms or a focal vulvar skin change.

options.text: Begin cancer-specific teaching because persistent itching and a discolored vulvar area confirm a vulvar malignancy.
options.reason: The pattern requires evaluation but does not confirm malignancy; diagnosis-specific teaching would be premature before the cause is established.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — Disorders of the reproductive tract: symptoms that must always have follow-up.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Symptoms of Gynecologic Cancers (September 5, 2024; accessed September 17, 2026).

limitations: The item tests escalation of persistent vulvar irritation with a focal skin or color change and deliberately does not diagnose infection, dermatosis, dysplasia, or malignancy.
It excludes already-tested vaginal-infection differentiation, postmenopausal bleeding, changed endometriosis pain, acute adnexal pain, and chronic abnormal-uterine-bleeding sampling decisions.
The case supports timely diagnostic evaluation but does not specify a test sequence, diagnosis, emergency pathway, or treatment.

questions.objective: Select developmentally appropriate pedestrian and wheeled-activity injury prevention for a preschool child.
questions.stem: At a 5-year well-child visit, a caregiver explains that the child rides a bicycle and scooter and walks with the family through a busy apartment parking lot. Which plans should the nurse reinforce? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: A preschool child can practice safety rules while an adult still provides close supervision and consistent protective equipment.
questions.rationale: Preschool injury prevention combines active adult supervision near vehicles, repeated practice of pedestrian rules, safer play locations, and consistent activity-appropriate protective equipment. Being able to recite a rule does not establish readiness to cross a parking lot alone, and a short ride does not remove the risk of a fall or head injury.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate developmental supervision, pedestrian behavior, environmental planning, and protective equipment across one family routine. This is level 2 application rather than recall of a single rule.

options.text: An adult will stay close enough to intervene whenever the child plays or crosses near moving or parked vehicles.
options.reason: Preschool children need close supervision outdoors near traffic hazards even while they are learning pedestrian rules.

options.text: We will practice stopping back from the curb and looking left, right, and left again before crossing together.
options.reason: Repeated supervised practice of a concrete crossing sequence is developmentally appropriate pedestrian teaching.

options.text: For every ride or skating session, use a properly fitted, fastened helmet for that activity and add other protective equipment when appropriate.
options.reason: Every-ride helmet use is supported; other protective equipment should be matched to the activity rather than treated as universal for every bicycle ride.

options.text: We will choose an outdoor play area away from curbs and parked cars whenever possible.
options.reason: Separating play from traffic and parked vehicles reduces exposure to a hazard that a preschool child cannot reliably judge.

options.text: Once the child can recite the crossing steps, the child may cross the parking lot alone while I watch from a window.
options.reason: Verbal recall does not replace close adult supervision in a busy parking lot, where vehicle movement and visibility can change quickly.

options.text: The helmet can be skipped for short driveway rides because vehicles are moving slowly there.
options.reason: Falls can occur during short rides and at low vehicle speeds, so location or duration does not justify inconsistent helmet use.

refs.label: Week 6 Exam 2 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes - preschool and school-age injury-prevention sections.

ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11 - chapters 5 and 6, injury prevention for preschool and school-age children (verified supplied-text passages, printed pp. 27 and 31; no original PDF review).

limitations: The item does not define a universal age for independent street crossing or substitute for local traffic law and caregiver judgment.
No sport-specific fitting protocol, certification standard, or legal requirement is inferred.
The apartment setting and family routine are fictional case facts used to test the supplied safety principles.

questions.objective: Interpret expected granulation during secondary-intention healing and distinguish it from wound infection.
questions.stem: A 9-year-old has an open lower-leg wound that was debrided 9 days ago and is healing by secondary intention. During the ordered dressing change, the nurse sees moist beefy-red tissue filling the wound from the base, scant serosanguineous drainage, and slight pinpoint bleeding with gentle cleansing. The child is afebrile and has no spreading redness, swelling, purulent drainage, or increasing pain. Which interpretation and action are most appropriate?
questions.clue: Granulation develops during fibroplasia and can bleed easily; infection is suggested by a different change pattern.
questions.rationale: The timing and appearance are consistent with expected granulation during the fibroplasia phase of a wound healing from the edges inward. The nurse should document the findings, continue the prescribed protective dressing, and monitor the trend. Purulence, spreading erythema, edema, increased temperature, or worsening pain would support infection concern, but none is present here.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must interpret several local findings together rather than treating red tissue or slight bleeding as infection in isolation. This is level 2 clinical judgment.

options.text: Recognize expected granulation during fibroplasia, document the findings, and continue the prescribed protective dressing while monitoring for change.
options.reason: Moist red tissue filling from the base with slight easy bleeding at day 9 fits granulation, and the case lacks the supplied infection findings.

options.text: Treat the red tissue and pinpoint bleeding as infection, stop the dressing plan, and request antibiotics before the next assessment.
options.reason: The expected granulation pattern is being mistaken for infection despite absent purulence, spreading erythema, edema, fever, and increasing pain.

options.text: Identify the wound as entering maturation and leave it open to dry so a thick scab can replace the moist tissue.
options.reason: The wound is showing active granulation during fibroplasia, not a pale mature scar, and drying conflicts with the ordered protective approach.

options.text: Reclassify the wound as primary-intention healing and request immediate edge approximation because the base is red.
options.reason: A debrided open wound healing from the base and edges is not primary-intention healing, and redness of viable granulation does not establish a need for immediate closure.

refs.label: Week 7 Exam 2 Child with Integumentary Disorders Instructor Notes - wound healing phases, intentions, granulation, and infection findings.

ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11 - chapter 31 wound-infection findings and chapter 32 burn-wound granulation/infection comparison (verified supplied-text passages, printed pp. 202 and 210; no original PDF review).

limitations: The case distinguishes an expected healing pattern from the supplied infection findings; it does not rule out infection in every child with granulation tissue.
No culture, antibiotic, debridement, or closure protocol is selected.
The wound type, timing, drainage, and examination findings are fictional case facts.

questions.objective: Explain how an ordered moisture-retentive absorbent dressing protects a wound healing by secondary intention.
questions.stem: A child's shallow open wound is healing by secondary intention. The wound-care order specifies a moisture-retentive dressing that can absorb drainage. The caregiver asks why the wound should not be left uncovered to dry. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The ordered dressing has more than one function: it manages the wound environment as well as outside exposure.
questions.rationale: The supplied wound-care teaching promotes a moist, crust-free environment and describes dressings as protection from infection and trauma, a way to minimize pain, and a means of absorbing drainage. The nurse should explain those functions without claiming that one dressing type or change interval is appropriate for every wound.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner matches an explicit order to the core functions of wound dressings and rejects common drying misconceptions. This is level 1 application.

options.text: The dressing helps preserve a moist healing surface, protects the tissue from trauma and contamination, and manages drainage as ordered.
options.reason: This explanation accurately combines the supplied moisture, protection, and drainage functions of an ordered wound dressing.

options.text: The goal is to dry the wound quickly under the dressing so a thick crust forms before tissue grows from the edges.
options.reason: The course source promotes a moist, crust-free environment rather than intentional drying and thick scab formation.

options.text: Because the dressing absorbs drainage, assess the amount on its outer surface rather than inspecting the wound bed at scheduled changes.
options.reason: Absorption does not replace ordered assessment of the wound bed and surrounding skin; the dressing and wound still require reassessment.

options.text: The dressing's main function is to compress the wound until drainage stops, so its moisture-retentive property is incidental.
options.reason: Some dressings provide compression when prescribed, but this order identifies moisture retention and absorption; adding compression would invent a treatment.

refs.label: Week 7 Exam 2 Child with Integumentary Disorders Instructor Notes - factors that promote healing and functions and types of dressings.

ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11 - chapter 32 prescribed burn-wound assessment, cleansing, dressings, and skin coverings (verified supplied-text passages, printed pp. 208-210; no original PDF review).

limitations: The item explains the functions of the dressing already ordered; it does not authorize the nurse or caregiver to select a product independently.
No universal dressing material, moisture level, debridement method, or change frequency is prescribed.
The wound description and order are fictional case facts.

questions.objective: Support individualized symptom tracking and lifestyle care for recurrent symptoms compatible with irritable bowel syndrome without promising a cure.
questions.stem: A 13-year-old has recurrent abdominal discomfort, bloating, and alternating hard and loose stools. Growth is stable, and there is no fever, bleeding, nocturnal awakening, or weight loss. After evaluation, the clinician says the pattern is compatible with irritable bowel syndrome and schedules follow-up. The family asks what to do next. Which nursing response is best?
questions.clue: The source describes a functional disorder managed by symptoms, dietary changes, lifestyle education, and support rather than a guaranteed cure.
questions.rationale: A symptom-and-stool record can help the child and clinician review the pattern. Possible food and lifestyle triggers and any treatment change should be discussed through an individualized plan and reassessed at follow-up. Teaching should set realistic symptom-management goals, avoid unnecessary broad restriction, and preserve reassessment when the pattern changes.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must use reassuring case findings without minimizing symptoms, then choose a longitudinal individualized plan over cure claims or unsupervised treatment. This is level 2 application.

options.text: Keep a symptom-and-stool record, discuss possible food and lifestyle triggers with the clinician, and use follow-up to individualize the plan.
options.reason: This plan supports pattern review, clinician-guided individualized management, and reassessment while preserving realistic expectations.

options.text: Start a gluten- and dairy-free diet now, then use follow-up mainly to decide whether additional foods should also be removed.
options.reason: Removing multiple food groups before individualized evaluation can be unnecessarily restrictive and can create nutritional and food-relationship burdens.

options.text: Match each loose or hard stool with an over-the-counter antidiarrheal or laxative, and report the results at the scheduled follow-up.
options.reason: Selected symptom-directed medicines may have a role in a clinician-guided plan, but unsupervised alternating treatment across changing stool patterns is not appropriate.

options.text: Continue the usual routine without recording symptoms, because stable growth provides enough information to judge the plan at the scheduled follow-up.
options.reason: Stable growth is reassuring, but it does not replace symptom-pattern information needed for individualized follow-up and reassessment.

questions.objective: Recognize the prediagnostic vomiting and dehydration pattern of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
questions.stem: A 5-week-old is evaluated for vomiting that has become progressively more forceful after feedings. The vomit is milk-colored without green fluid, and the infant appears hungry again after vomiting. The caregiver reports fewer wet diapers; assessment finds dry mucous membranes and decreased skin turgor. Which condition best fits this pattern?
questions.clue: Consider the infant's age, the progressive nonbilious projectile pattern, persistent hunger, and dehydration.
questions.rationale: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis usually appears in the first weeks of life as gastric-outlet obstruction. Vomiting becomes projectile as obstruction worsens, remains nonbilious because the obstruction is proximal to the duodenum, and can cause persistent hunger and dehydration. The diagnosis still requires clinical evaluation and is commonly supported by ultrasound.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner identifies one classic prediagnostic pattern and distinguishes it from reflux, intussusception, and distal obstruction. This is level 1 recognition in a patient-care vignette.

options.text: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
options.reason: Progressive nonbilious projectile vomiting in the first weeks of life with hunger and dehydration is the supplied pyloric-stenosis pattern.

options.text: Uncomplicated physiologic reflux
options.reason: Physiologic reflux is typically effortless and should not explain progressively projectile vomiting with reduced urine and dehydration findings.

options.text: Intussusception
options.reason: The case lacks the supplied episodic severe pain, sausage-shaped mass, and bloody mucus stool pattern of intussusception.

options.text: A distal intestinal obstruction
options.reason: An obstruction distal to the stomach is more concerning when vomiting is bilious; the nonbilious progressive gastric-outlet pattern points elsewhere.

questions.objective: Connect initial Hirschsprung obstruction with rectal-biopsy confirmation and possible staged surgical care.
questions.stem: A newborn has not passed meconium by 48 hours and develops progressive abdominal distention and bilious vomiting. There is no fever, diarrhea, or poor perfusion. A contrast study suggests a distal colonic obstruction. The family asks how Hirschsprung disease is confirmed and why a temporary ostomy was mentioned. Which explanation by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The disorder reflects absent ganglion cells, and definitive care may require more than one surgical stage.
questions.rationale: Hirschsprung disease causes mechanical obstruction because a bowel segment lacks ganglion cells and cannot provide normal motility. Rectal biopsy confirms the absence of ganglion cells. Definitive care removes or bypasses the affected segment; some children require a temporary ostomy before a later pull-through procedure. The stable obstructive presentation in this stem is intentionally separate from the already tested enterocolitis emergency branch.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must link the newborn obstruction pattern to tissue confirmation and explain why staged surgery may be used without misclassifying the case as enterocolitis. This is level 2 integration.

options.text: A rectal biopsy confirms absent ganglion cells; the affected bowel is treated surgically, and a temporary ostomy may be used before a later pull-through procedure.
options.reason: This accurately connects the disease mechanism with the supplied confirmatory test and possible staged surgical plan without making an ostomy universal.

options.text: The contrast study alone confirms the diagnosis; if an enema produces stool, surgery is usually no longer needed.
options.reason: Imaging can support evaluation, but the supplied confirmatory procedure is rectal biopsy, and temporary stool passage does not restore missing ganglion cells.

options.text: The rectal biopsy checks for intestinal infection; an ostomy is considered only when fever and explosive diarrhea prove enterocolitis.
options.reason: The biopsy is used to confirm absent ganglion cells, and a temporary ostomy can be part of staged care without the enterocolitis findings omitted from this case.

options.text: Ganglion cells often mature after birth, so repeat imaging is used before deciding whether the obstruction will resolve without surgery.
options.reason: Hirschsprung disease is a congenital absence of ganglion cells; waiting for maturation does not address the structural cause of the obstruction.
