questions.objective: Use an ordered oxygen target and preserve protocol-triggered retinopathy screening through transfer
questions.stem: A newborn born at 27 weeks and 980 g has received supplemental oxygen for 18 days. The pulse-oximetry waveform is reliable, and saturation is 97% to 98% on an oxygen setting that has been unchanged for an hour. A standing order authorizes oxygen titration to this newborn's prescribed range of 90% to 94%. The newborn is otherwise stable and will transfer to a step-down nursery tomorrow. The unit retinopathy-of-prematurity protocol flags the newborn for screening, but the chart has no retinal examination result or scheduled plan. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Address both present oxygen exposure and the time-sensitive screening handoff without inventing a universal target or examination date.
questions.rationale: After confirming a reliable signal, the nurse should use the newborn-specific standing order to titrate oxygen toward the prescribed range and reassess the response. Both excessive and overly restricted oxygen exposure can cause harm, so 'less oxygen' is not an independent goal. This newborn also meets the supplied unit protocol for ROP screening. The missing plan should be escalated through the neonatal and ophthalmology pathway, and transfer should not break continuity: the current ocular status, required next examination, timing, and responsible receiving service must be explicitly communicated and arranged before departure. Screening eligibility and timing depend on gestational age, birth weight, clinical risk, postmenstrual age, retinal findings, and protocol—not on a universal oxygen-duration cutoff.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate a current oxygen value with a patient-specific order and a separate transfer-related screening omission while rejecting two appealing universal rules, supporting level 2.

options.text: Verify the sensor and waveform, then titrate oxygen under the standing order toward the prescribed 90% to 94% range and reassess.
options.reason: The signal is reliable and saturation remains above this newborn's ordered range. The standing order authorizes bounded titration with reassessment rather than an unbounded oxygen reduction.

options.text: Lower oxygen until saturation stays below the prescribed range because minimizing oxygen exposure is always the safest way to prevent ROP.
options.reason: Overly restricted oxygen can also cause harm. The nurse should target the supplied patient-specific range, not deliberately create hypoxemia in pursuit of less exposure.

options.text: Notify the neonatal team of the missing screening plan and activate the unit's ROP pathway for ophthalmology coordination.
options.reason: The case states that the unit protocol flags this infant. A missing examination or schedule requires timely coordination rather than an independently invented date.

options.text: Remove the ROP flag because oxygen has been used for fewer than 30 days, and reconsider screening only if oxygen continues past that point.
options.reason: A universal oxygen-days cutoff is not the screening rule. Gestational age, birth weight, clinical risk, postmenstrual age, and the unit protocol determine the pathway.

options.text: Before transfer, confirm the required next eye examination is specifically arranged and send its timing and current ocular status to the receiving team.
options.reason: ROP examinations and follow-up are time-sensitive. A concrete plan and direct transfer of the ocular record protect continuity when the infant changes facilities.

options.text: Schedule the first retinal examination for day 30 of oxygen therapy for every preterm newborn, regardless of gestational age or unit protocol.
options.reason: The nurse should not create a universal examination day. Initial and follow-up timing are protocol- and ophthalmology-directed using gestational and retinal information.

questions.objective: Distinguish trisomy 21 suspicion from confirmation and support respectful diagnostic communication
questions.stem: A term newborn has hypotonia, a flat nasal bridge, upward-slanting palpebral fissures, small ears, and a cardiac murmur. Prenatal cell-free DNA screening reported a high chance of trisomy 21, but no amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling was performed. The newborn is stable, and the family has not yet discussed the postnatal findings with the neonatal team. Which nursing plan is most appropriate?
questions.clue: Separate screening and clinical suspicion from laboratory confirmation while protecting how the family receives the information.
questions.rationale: The prenatal cell-free DNA result is a screening result, and the physical cluster supports clinical suspicion; neither alone establishes a confirmed postnatal diagnosis. The nurse should accurately document the screening history and findings, notify the neonatal team, and support postnatal karyotype testing. Karyotype confirms the chromosomal diagnosis and can identify a translocation relevant to genetic counseling. The team should discuss the concern promptly in a private setting, preferably with the family's chosen support person present, using the newborn's name and balanced, current, respectful, person-first language. The family should not receive a fixed prognosis because manifestations and outcomes vary, and suspicion need not be hidden until the final report is available.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must reconcile prenatal screening, a suggestive phenotype, the correct confirmatory study, and family-centered communication in one plan, supporting level 2.

options.text: Record trisomy 21 as confirmed from the screening result and appearance, then tell one parent at the bedside that no further diagnostic testing is needed.
options.reason: Cell-free DNA is screening, and appearance supports suspicion rather than laboratory confirmation. The family also deserves a coordinated private discussion rather than a unilateral definitive statement.

options.text: Document the screening history and findings as concern for trisomy 21, notify the team, support postnatal karyotype, and coordinate a private, balanced family discussion.
options.reason: This plan preserves the suspicion-versus-confirmation boundary, obtains the recommended chromosomal confirmation, and supports respectful family-centered communication.

options.text: Avoid discussing the concern until the final chromosome report returns, then provide written information without arranging a private conversation or family support.
options.reason: Concern can be discussed promptly and honestly while identified as unconfirmed. Waiting in silence and relying only on written material do not meet the family's communication and support needs.

options.text: Ask the team to replace karyotype with chromosomal microarray and explain that all newborns with these findings have the same cardiac and developmental outcome.
options.reason: Microarray does not replace karyotype for distinguishing nondisjunction from a translocation in this setting, and trisomy 21 manifestations and outcomes are not uniform.

American Academy of Pediatrics clinical report — Health Supervision for Children and Adolescents With Down Syndrome; newborn evaluation and communicating the diagnosis.

limitations: The findings and prenatal screen establish concern, not a definitive nursing diagnosis or an individual prognosis.
The item does not prescribe cardiac treatment, a complete Down syndrome newborn evaluation, reproductive-risk estimates, or the content and timing of genetic counseling beyond team coordination.
Trisomy 18 prognosis and treatment decisions are outside this slot; no diagnosis alone determines whether treatment is withheld or provided.

questions.objective: Coordinate routine aftercare, partner management, and follow-up for treated uncomplicated cervical gonorrhea.
questions.stem: A nonpregnant adult with clinician-confirmed uncomplicated cervical gonorrhea received the prescribed recommended treatment today. Chlamydia testing is negative, and there are no findings of pelvic inflammatory or disseminated infection. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: This is a treated cervical infection with chlamydia excluded; routine retesting, test-of-cure rules, and partner care have different purposes.
questions.rationale: For uncomplicated cervical gonorrhea treated with a recommended regimen, the patient should avoid sexual activity for 7 days after treatment and until partners have been treated. Recent partners need evaluation, testing, and presumptive treatment. Retesting at 3 months is recommended because repeat infection is common, even when partner treatment is reported. A routine test of cure is not required for uncomplicated urogenital or rectal infection treated appropriately, whereas pharyngeal infection requires a 7- to 14-day test of cure. Antichlamydial therapy is added when chlamydia has not been excluded; this patient's negative result removes that indication.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must keep five related decisions separate: abstinence, partner care, reinfection retesting, site-specific test of cure, and chlamydia status.

options.text: Avoid sexual activity for 7 days after treatment and until recent sex partners have also been treated.
options.reason: This interval and partner-treatment condition reduce immediate transmission and reinfection after gonorrhea treatment.

options.text: Refer recent sex partners for evaluation, testing, and presumptive treatment even if they have no symptoms.
options.reason: Gonorrhea can be asymptomatic, and recent partners need prompt evaluation and treatment to interrupt transmission and reduce reinfection.

options.text: Schedule repeat gonorrhea testing in 3 months even if the patient believes every partner completed treatment.
options.reason: Three-month retesting looks for repeat infection and remains recommended regardless of the patient's belief about partner treatment.

options.text: A routine test of cure is not needed for this appropriately treated cervical infection; pharyngeal infection follows a different test-of-cure plan.
options.reason: Test of cure is unnecessary after recommended treatment of uncomplicated urogenital or rectal infection, but pharyngeal gonorrhea requires testing 7 to 14 days after treatment.

options.text: Begin antichlamydial therapy now because every gonorrhea diagnosis requires treatment for chlamydia whether or not testing is negative.
options.reason: Antichlamydial therapy is added when chlamydia has not been excluded. The stem provides a negative chlamydia result, so universal added treatment is not supported.

options.text: Return in 7 to 14 days for a mandatory test of cure because all gonorrhea infection sites use the same follow-up schedule.
options.reason: The 7- to 14-day test-of-cure recommendation applies to pharyngeal gonorrhea, not every appropriately treated uncomplicated cervical, urethral, or rectal infection.

questions.objective: Match clinician-confirmed late latent syphilis (>1 year's duration) to the stage-appropriate benzathine penicillin G course and serologic follow-up.
questions.stem: A nonpregnant adult has clinician-confirmed late latent syphilis (>1 year's duration). The patient has no penicillin allergy and no neurologic, ocular, or otic symptoms. HIV testing has been ordered, and a long-term sex partner is being referred for evaluation. Which treatment and follow-up plan should the nurse anticipate?
questions.clue: Late latent syphilis requires a longer course and a longer serologic follow-up schedule than primary, secondary, or early latent infection.
questions.rationale: Late latent syphilis in a nonpregnant adult without penicillin allergy is treated with clinician-prescribed benzathine penicillin G totaling 7.2 million units, administered as three 2.4-million-unit IM doses at 1-week intervals. Quantitative nontreponemal serology is repeated at 6, 12, and 24 months and compared with the treatment-time titer. A single dose is the regimen for primary, secondary, or early latent infection, not late latent disease. Treponemal antibody tests commonly remain reactive and are not used to monitor treatment response. In the absence of neurologic, ocular, or otic findings, routine CSF evaluation should not be inserted before stage-appropriate therapy.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a clinician-confirmed stage to both regimen duration and the correct response-monitoring test while resisting early-stage and routine-CSF distractors.

options.text: Coordinate three 2.4-million-unit IM doses of benzathine penicillin G at 1-week intervals and quantitative nontreponemal testing at 6, 12, and 24 months.
options.reason: This is the recommended total 7.2-million-unit course and follow-up schedule for late latent syphilis.

options.text: Coordinate one 2.4-million-unit IM dose of benzathine penicillin G and repeat quantitative serology at 6 and 12 months.
options.reason: A single dose matches primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis, not the clinician-confirmed late latent stage in this case.

options.text: Coordinate three weekly benzathine penicillin G doses, then use repeat treponemal antibody results at 6, 12, and 24 months to determine response.
options.reason: The three-dose course fits the stage, but treatment response is followed with quantitative nontreponemal titers; treponemal tests often remain reactive after adequate therapy.

options.text: Delay the benzathine penicillin G course until routine CSF testing excludes asymptomatic neurosyphilis, then select the injection schedule from the CSF result.
options.reason: With no neurologic, ocular, or otic findings, routine CSF testing is not a prerequisite to stage-appropriate latent-syphilis treatment.

questions.objective: Explain the distinct purposes and limits of vaccination and lesion treatment when an adult already has anogenital HPV warts.
questions.stem: A nonpregnant, immunocompetent 24-year-old with newly diagnosed external anogenital warts has not received HPV vaccine. The clinician has discussed vaccination and lesion-treatment options. The patient asks, “If the warts are removed and I get vaccinated, will the virus be gone so I cannot pass it to anyone?” Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: Vaccination prevents new infection; lesion treatment removes visible warts. Neither action proves eradication of established HPV.
questions.rationale: HPV vaccination can prevent new infections with vaccine-covered types but does not treat established HPV or existing warts. Wart treatment targets visible lesions and symptoms; it does not eradicate the virus. Warts can recur, particularly during the first 3 months after treatment, and HPV can still be transmitted even when no warts are visible. The patient should continue the routine cervical-screening plan and return for treatment effects, nonresponse, worsening, or atypical lesions. HPV testing is not used to diagnose genital warts or prove that the infection has cleared.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner identifies the direct prevention-versus-treatment distinction and corrects the linked cure and transmission misconceptions.

options.text: “Wart treatment does not eradicate HPV, and vaccination prevents new infections rather than treating this one; recurrence and transmission can still occur.”
options.reason: This correctly separates lesion treatment from viral eradication and vaccination from treatment while preserving the possibility of recurrence and transmission.

options.text: “Yes. Removing every visible wart eradicates HPV, and vaccination then prevents the treated infection from recurring or being transmitted.”
options.reason: Removing visible lesions does not eradicate HPV, and vaccination does not treat the established infection or guarantee against recurrence or transmission.

options.text: “Vaccination should be postponed until an HPV test becomes negative because visible warts mean the vaccine cannot protect against any other HPV type.”
options.reason: Established infection does not make vaccination a treatment, but an eligible patient can still gain protection against vaccine-covered types not previously acquired.

options.text: “A negative HPV test after treatment proves the infection is cleared and allows the routine cervical-screening plan to be discontinued.”
options.reason: HPV testing is not recommended to diagnose genital warts or prove clearance, and established warts do not replace the patient's routine cervical-screening plan.

questions.objective: Choose developmentally appropriate complementary-food progression using readiness cues, single-ingredient introduction, and safe texture and preparation.
questions.stem: A 6-month-old sits with support, holds the head steady, reaches for food, opens the mouth when food approaches, and swallows a small amount of smooth puree without pushing it back out. Breast milk or formula remains the infant's main nutrition. Which plans should the nurse reinforce as complementary foods begin? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Use the infant's developmental readiness and feeding skills, then progress one new food and texture step at a time with close supervision.
questions.rationale: The infant is about 6 months old and shows multiple readiness cues. Current CDC guidance supports starting one single-ingredient food at a time, waiting 3 to 5 days before another new food, and offering textures prepared for the child's developmental skill while an adult watches closely. Texture can progress gradually as feeding skills develop, while breast milk or formula remains the primary source of nutrition through the first year. A rigid food sequence is unnecessary, and age alone does not establish readiness.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate age, several readiness cues, safe preparation, supervision, texture progression, and the current food-introduction interval while rejecting age-only and rigid-sequence rules. This is level 2 application.

options.text: Offer one single-ingredient smooth or mashed food, then wait 3 to 5 days before introducing another new food.
options.reason: A single-ingredient introduction with a 3-to-5-day observation interval reflects current CDC guidance and allows the caregiver to notice a reaction to a new food.

options.text: Prepare food in a soft texture and safe size, offer small portions slowly, and supervise continuously during feeding.
options.reason: Developmentally safe preparation, small portions, slow feeding, and direct supervision reduce feeding and choking risk as the infant learns new oral skills.

options.text: Progress gradually from smooth or mashed foods toward thicker and more varied textures as the infant's skills improve.
options.reason: Texture should advance with the child's feeding abilities rather than remain fixed or jump immediately to foods that require more mature skills.

options.text: Continue breast milk or formula as the primary nutrition while complementary foods are added during the first year.
options.reason: Complementary foods are added gradually; the supplied ATI source keeps breast milk or formula as the primary nutrition through the first year.

options.text: Treat the infant's sixth-month birthday as sufficient readiness even if head control or swallowing skills later appear inconsistent.
options.reason: Starting solids depends on developmental readiness as well as being about 6 months old; age by itself is not enough.

options.text: Follow a required sequence in which cereal must come first and fruits, vegetables, and meats must be introduced in a fixed order.
options.reason: Current CDC guidance does not require foods to be introduced in a particular order.

questions.objective: Choose the age-appropriate milk transition at 12 months and prevent milk from displacing a varied, nutrient-rich diet.
questions.stem: At a 12-month well-child visit, the caregiver reports that the child eats a variety of family foods and is finishing the remaining infant formula. The caregiver asks what milk plan to use next and says, "If milk is healthy, I may offer it whenever my child refuses food." Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: At 12 months, milk can become one part of a varied diet; it should not become a replacement for that diet.
questions.rationale: At 12 months, pasteurized, unsweetened whole cow's milk can be introduced as part of a varied diet. Milk is not a substitute for meals, and excessive reliance on it can reduce appetite for other nutrient-rich foods and contribute to inadequate iron intake. Cow's milk should not be used as the main drink before 12 months. Lower-fat milk and plant beverages require individualized consideration because one rule or product does not fit every child.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must combine the age boundary, milk type, food-displacement risk, and limits of universal lower-fat or plant-beverage advice. This is level 2 application.

options.text: At 12 months, pasteurized, unsweetened whole cow's milk can be introduced as part of the varied diet; avoid using milk to replace meals or crowd out nutrient-rich foods.
options.reason: This plan applies the current 12-month transition and keeps milk in its proper role within, rather than in place of, a varied diet.

options.text: Cow's milk should have replaced breast milk or formula as the main drink by 10 months so the child becomes accustomed to it before the first birthday.
options.reason: Cow's milk as a main drink is not recommended before 12 months.

options.text: Every child should change directly to low-fat cow's milk at 12 months, regardless of growth pattern or cardiovascular risk history.
options.reason: Whole milk is the usual 12-month transition; lower-fat selection is individualized rather than a universal rule for every 12-month-old.

options.text: Any plant beverage can replace cow's milk without checking the nutrition label because all plant beverages provide equivalent protein, calcium, and vitamin D.
options.reason: Plant beverages vary substantially in nutrient content, so label review and individualized guidance are needed.

questions.objective: Recognize infant seborrheic dermatitis as cradle cap and select gentle scalp cleansing and scale-loosening care.
questions.stem: A 4-month-old has adherent greasy scales and crusted areas on the scalp. The infant is afebrile and comfortable, with no spreading redness, tenderness, or drainage. Which teaching should the nurse provide?
questions.clue: The common infant form of seborrheic dermatitis is managed by softening and gently loosening scalp scales.
questions.rationale: Seborrheic dermatitis of the infant scalp is commonly called cradle cap. Current AAP and AAD guidance supports mild fragrance-free baby shampoo, gentle scalp massage, and a soft brush or comb for scales that have loosened. A small amount of mineral oil, petrolatum, or another supported non-food-based oil can soften stubborn scales and should be washed out afterward. Medicated shampoo should be used only with pediatric-clinician direction.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner identifies a classic uncomplicated cradle-cap presentation and matches it to the supplied gentle scale-loosening care. This is level 1 application.

options.text: Use mild fragrance-free baby shampoo, gently massage and brush or comb loosened scales, and wash out a small amount of mineral oil or petrolatum used for stubborn scales; use medicated shampoo only if the clinician directs.
options.reason: This follows current gentle-care guidance: mild baby shampoo, gentle removal of loosened scales, supported scale softening with the product washed out, and clinician direction before medicated shampoo.

options.text: Use a medicated dandruff shampoo with each bath as the initial home treatment, and change to mild baby shampoo only after all visible scales have cleared.
options.reason: Current infant guidance starts with mild baby shampoo and directs caregivers to consult the pediatric clinician before using a medicated shampoo because it may irritate infant skin.

options.text: Massage olive oil into the scalp after bathing and leave it between washes so the scales remain soft; shampoo only when a thick layer starts to build.
options.reason: The reviewed dermatology guidance favors a small amount of non-food-based oil for stubborn scales before cleansing and directs washing it out rather than leaving an oil layer on the scalp.

options.text: Wash with mild baby shampoo, then use a fine-tooth comb to lift scales that are still firmly attached so the entire patch is cleared during each bath.
options.reason: A brush or comb should remove only scales loosened by shampooing and softening; forcefully lifting attached scales can injure the scalp and increase infection risk.

The item applies to the uncomplicated fictional presentation; spreading inflammation, drainage, pain, fever, or diagnostic uncertainty would require clinical reassessment.

questions.objective: Prevent fecal-oral gastroenteritis spread and support hydration and age-appropriate nutrition without BRAT or high-sugar drinks.
questions.stem: A 4-year-old with uncomplicated infectious gastroenteritis has been evaluated and will receive home care with follow-up. The child is alert, is drinking, and has no bloody stool, bilious vomiting, severe abdominal pain, or signs of severe dehydration. Which caregiver instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Protect hydration and usual nutrition while interrupting fecal-oral spread in the home.
questions.rationale: Home teaching for uncomplicated gastroenteritis includes commercially prepared oral rehydration solution when replacement is needed, small frequent amounts if vomiting limits intake, and return to the child's usual balanced, age-appropriate foods as tolerated. High-sugar drinks do not have the appropriate electrolyte composition and can worsen diarrhea. Soap-and-water handwashing and cleaning contaminated surfaces and laundry reduce fecal-oral spread. Antidiarrheal medication should not be started independently without clinician guidance.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must coordinate hydration, nutrition, medication safety, hand hygiene, and environmental cleaning rather than choosing a single symptom treatment. This is level 2 application.

options.text: Use a commercially prepared oral rehydration solution when fluid replacement is needed, offering small frequent amounts if vomiting limits intake.
options.reason: Commercial oral rehydration solution provides an appropriate glucose-electrolyte mixture; smaller frequent amounts can improve tolerance when vomiting occurs.

options.text: Resume the child's usual balanced, age-appropriate foods as tolerated rather than limiting intake to bananas, rice, applesauce, and toast.
options.reason: Current pediatric guidance supports early return to the usual age-appropriate diet and does not recommend a nutritionally restrictive BRAT-only plan.

options.text: Wash hands with soap and water after toileting or helping the child and before preparing or eating food.
options.reason: Soap-and-water hand hygiene at these fecal-oral transition points is a core infection-prevention measure.

options.text: Clean and disinfect stool- or vomit-contaminated surfaces promptly and wash soiled clothing or linens without shaking them.
options.reason: Environmental cleaning and careful laundry handling reduce household contamination and further spread.

options.text: Replace oral rehydration solution with fruit juice, soda, or sports drinks because their sugar provides faster hydration.
options.reason: These high-sugar drinks do not provide the appropriate electrolyte balance and can worsen diarrhea.

options.text: Begin an over-the-counter antidiarrheal and continue it until stools are normal without first contacting the child's clinician.
options.reason: The caregiver should seek clinician guidance rather than independently selecting an antidiarrheal for a child.

American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org - Diarrhea in Children: What Parents Need to Know.
CDC - How to Prevent Norovirus (updated January 13, 2025).

limitations: The item applies to a child already evaluated for uncomplicated home care and does not provide a replacement volume or IV-fluid protocol.
No antidiarrheal, antimicrobial, or organism-specific treatment is selected.
The item does not delay reassessment for reduced urine, lethargy, poor perfusion, blood in stool, bilious emesis, severe pain, or other worsening findings.

questions.objective: Choose an individualized lactose-management plan using symptom-guided tolerance, label review, lower-lactose or lactose-free options, and calcium and vitamin D adequacy.
questions.stem: A school-age child with clinician-diagnosed lactose intolerance develops bloating, gas, and loose stools after some dairy foods. There has been no hives, wheezing, facial swelling, or breathing difficulty. The family has removed every dairy product, and a diet review suggests low calcium and vitamin D intake. Which plan should the nurse recommend?
questions.clue: Lactose tolerance varies; symptom control must be balanced with adequate calcium and vitamin D.
questions.rationale: Most people with lactose intolerance can tolerate some lactose. Management should identify the child's symptom threshold, use label review and tolerated lower-lactose or lactose-free choices, and preserve calcium and vitamin D intake with pediatric clinician or dietitian guidance. Complete dairy elimination is not automatically required. Hives, wheezing, swelling, or breathing difficulty suggest an allergic process rather than the usual digestive symptoms of lactose intolerance and require a different safety response.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must correct an overly restrictive diet while preserving symptom control and nutrient adequacy and distinguishing digestive intolerance from milk allergy. This is level 2 application.

options.text: Work with the pediatric clinician or dietitian to find the child's tolerated amount, review labels, use tolerated lower-lactose or lactose-free foods, and maintain adequate calcium and vitamin D.
options.reason: This individualized plan reflects variable lactose tolerance while protecting the child's calcium and vitamin D intake.

options.text: Keep every dairy-derived food out of the diet permanently, even if small portions cause no symptoms, and do not replace their calcium or vitamin D.
options.reason: Universal complete avoidance is often unnecessary and can leave important nutrient gaps.

options.text: Stop reading ingredient lists when the front label says nondairy because lactose-containing ingredients are always identified only by the word lactose.
options.reason: Ingredient lists can identify lactose-containing components with terms such as milk, whey, curds, milk by-products, or dry milk solids, so front-label wording alone is not enough.

options.text: Teach that future hives, wheezing, or facial swelling after milk are expected lactose-intolerance symptoms that can be managed by simply reducing the portion.
options.reason: Those findings raise concern for allergy rather than routine lactose intolerance and require prompt clinical guidance, not a smaller lactose portion.

Week 7 Exam 2 GI Dysfunction lecture - lactose-intolerance GI symptom cues, slide 13.

National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases - Symptoms and Causes of Lactose Intolerance.
American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org - Calcium: The Bone Builder Kids and Teens Need.

limitations: The supplied instructor note's universal avoidance and routine breastfeeding-parent dairy restriction are not keyed because current government and AAP guidance supports individualized tolerance.
The lecture graphic's rash and shortness-of-breath claims are excluded as lactose-intolerance findings; allergy warning signs are treated as a distinct safety concern.
No supplement dose, universal tolerated amount, diagnostic test, or plant-beverage equivalence is prescribed.

questions.objective: Support an otherwise healthy infant with colic using safe soothing, illness assessment, and a safe caregiver respite plan.
questions.stem: A 7-week-old has been evaluated for recurrent evening episodes of difficult-to-console crying with a red face, clenched fists, and legs drawn toward the abdomen. Feeding, growth, and wet diapers are normal, and there is no fever, vomiting, lethargy, or poor feeding. The clinician says the pattern is compatible with colic. The exhausted caregiver says, "When nothing works, I feel like I might lose control." Which response and plan by the nurse are best?
questions.clue: Support the caregiver without promising a cure, and make the next step safe if frustration is rising.
questions.rationale: Colic occurs in an otherwise healthy infant and has no single reliably effective cure. The nurse should acknowledge caregiver strain, review safe soothing after basic needs and illness signs are checked, and give a concrete respite plan: place the infant safely in the crib, step away briefly, and contact a support person. The caregiver should never shake or hit the infant. New fever, poor feeding, vomiting, dehydration, lethargy, or other illness findings require clinical evaluation rather than automatic attribution to colic.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must respond therapeutically to caregiver distress while coordinating colic recognition, safe soothing, safe sleep placement, respite, abuse prevention, and red-flag reassessment. This is level 2 application.

options.text: Validate the strain. If soothing fails and frustration rises, place the infant safely in the crib, step away briefly, and get help; never shake or hit, and report new illness signs.
options.reason: This plan validates the caregiver, protects the infant during escalating frustration, provides safe respite, and keeps red-flag reassessment in view.

options.text: Tell the caregiver to keep holding and soothing the infant continuously, even when anger is rising, because stepping away will worsen attachment.
options.reason: An overwhelmed caregiver may safely place the infant in the crib and step away briefly; insisting on continued holding can increase danger when control is slipping.

options.text: Start scheduled gas drops and gripe water as the main plan because colic is caused by trapped gas.
options.reason: No single treatment reliably cures colic, and AAP parent guidance does not support promising benefit from gas drops or gripe water.

options.text: Change formula or remove all dairy from the breastfeeding caregiver's diet immediately, even though growth and feeding are normal and no clinician has identified an indication.
options.reason: A broad dietary restriction or formula change is not a universal colic treatment and should not be initiated without an individualized indication.

refs.label: Week 7 Exam 2 Child with GI Alterations Instructor Notes - colic recognition, soothing, course, and caregiver-fatigue scope.
Week 7 Exam 2 GI Dysfunction lecture - colic recognition cues, slide 16.
American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org - Abdominal Pain in Infants: 8 Possible Reasons Your Baby's Tummy Hurts.
American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org - Responding to Your Baby's Cries.

limitations: The clinician has already evaluated the fictional infant; the item does not define a diagnostic crying-duration threshold or replace assessment for illness, injury, feeding problems, or dehydration.
No gas drop, gripe water, probiotic, formula, or elimination-diet regimen is recommended.
The safe-respite instruction is brief and conditional; it does not mean leaving the infant unattended for a prolonged period.

questions.objective: Distinguish prenatal screening from diagnostic testing and connect a positive screening result with gestationally appropriate, preference-sensitive next steps.
questions.stem: At 11 weeks of pregnancy, a patient receives a positive cell-free DNA screening result for trisomy 21 and says, “This proves the baby has Down syndrome, so I need a test that tells me for sure.” Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The blood test estimates chance; testing placental or fetal cells provides a more definite answer, and one diagnostic route is available in the current gestational window.
questions.rationale: Cell-free DNA is a screening test: a positive result means the pregnancy has an increased chance of the screened condition, not that the condition is confirmed. The nurse should support genetic counseling and discussion of diagnostic testing. At 11 weeks, chorionic villus sampling is within its usual 10-to-13-week window; amniocentesis is usually performed later, beginning around 15 weeks. The patient retains the right to accept or decline screening and diagnostic testing after informed counseling.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must classify the result, match the diagnostic option to the current gestational age, and preserve informed choice rather than treating screening as confirmation.

options.text: “This result raises the chance of trisomy 21 but does not confirm it. Genetic counseling can help you consider diagnostic testing such as CVS now or amniocentesis later, and the choice is yours.”
options.reason: This accurately identifies cell-free DNA as screening, links the 11-week timing to CVS and later timing to amniocentesis, and supports informed patient choice.

options.text: “Because cell-free DNA is diagnostic, the next step is to plan care for a confirmed trisomy 21 pregnancy rather than perform another test.”
options.reason: Cell-free DNA is a screening test with possible false-positive and false-negative results; it does not establish a fetal diagnosis.

options.text: “Repeat the same cell-free DNA test today; two positive screening results provide the same certainty as sampling placental or fetal cells.”
options.reason: Repeating a screening test does not convert it into diagnostic testing or provide the same information as CVS or amniocentesis.

options.text: “An anatomy ultrasound at 18 to 22 weeks will prove whether trisomy 21 is present, so an invasive diagnostic option is unnecessary.”
options.reason: Ultrasound can identify structural findings but does not replace diagnostic chromosome testing when the patient wants a more definite answer.

refs.label: Assessment of the High-Risk Pregnancy Patient course presentation — prenatal screening, diagnostic testing, and nursing counseling.
Maternal-Child Nursing Care — prenatal genetic screening and diagnostic testing.
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists — Prenatal Genetic Screening Tests (last reviewed October 2025).
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists — Prenatal Genetic Diagnostic Tests.

limitations: The item addresses screening-versus-diagnostic purpose, usual timing, and informed choice; it does not predict a fetal diagnosis or test accuracy for an individual patient.
The example is limited to an 11-week positive cell-free DNA screen and does not prescribe which diagnostic test the patient must choose.
Procedure-specific risks, specimen analysis, and pregnancy-management decisions after a diagnostic result are outside this item.

questions.objective: Prepare and teach a patient for second-trimester amniocentesis using the correct route, monitoring, Rh prophylaxis, and postprocedure warning signs.
questions.stem: A patient at 18 weeks of pregnancy who reports fetal movement every day is scheduled for genetic amniocentesis. The patient is A negative, has a negative antibody screen, and has signed the procedure consent. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Amniocentesis is an ultrasound-guided transabdominal procedure that can expose an unsensitized Rh-negative patient to fetal blood; assessment continues after the sample is obtained.
questions.rationale: Genetic amniocentesis is usually performed at 15 to 20 weeks by inserting a needle through the abdomen under ultrasound guidance. Nursing safeguards include baseline maternal assessment and fetal heart rate, support for ultrasound guidance, and postprocedure reassessment. An unsensitized Rh-negative patient should receive Rh immune globulin after amniocentesis as ordered to reduce sensitization risk. The patient should report fluid leakage, bleeding, fever or chills, contractions, or decreased fetal movement. A transcervical placental-tissue route describes one approach to chorionic villus sampling, not amniocentesis, and fluid leakage should not be dismissed as routine.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies several standard procedure safeguards in a multi-select format while distinguishing amniocentesis from CVS and identifying reportable complications.

options.text: Record baseline maternal vital signs and fetal heart rate, and prepare to support ultrasound guidance during the transabdominal procedure.
options.reason: Baseline assessment and ultrasound-guided needle placement are core safeguards for amniocentesis.

options.text: Reassess fetal heart rate and maternal status after the procedure according to the unit protocol.
options.reason: Postprocedure reassessment helps identify an immediate change after an invasive prenatal procedure.

options.text: Anticipate Rh immune globulin after the procedure as ordered because the patient is unsensitized and Rh negative.
options.reason: Amniocentesis can expose an Rh-negative patient to fetal red blood cells, so Rh immune globulin is recommended when the patient is not already sensitized.

options.text: Teach the patient to report vaginal bleeding, fluid leakage, fever or chills, contractions, or decreased fetal movement.
options.reason: These findings can signal postprocedure complications and require prompt follow-up rather than routine observation at home.

options.text: Explain that a catheter will pass through the cervix to collect placental tissue because this is the usual route for amniocentesis at 18 weeks.
options.reason: Amniocentesis obtains amniotic fluid through a transabdominal needle; placental tissue obtained by a transcervical or transabdominal route describes CVS.

options.text: Reassure the patient that a small continuous leak of clear fluid is expected and does not need to be reported unless pain develops.
options.reason: Possible amniotic-fluid leakage after the procedure should be reported; absence of pain does not make continued leakage routine.

refs.label: Assessment of the High-Risk Pregnancy Patient course presentation — amniocentesis and CVS.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing — prenatal diagnostic procedures and amniocentesis nursing care.
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists — Prenatal Genetic Diagnostic Tests.
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists — The Rh Factor: How It Can Affect Your Pregnancy.

limitations: The case assumes a clinician has already determined the indication and obtained informed consent; the nurse does not independently select or perform the procedure.
Rh immune globulin applies to an unsensitized Rh-negative patient and remains subject to the clinician's order and local protocol.
Exact observation time, activity restrictions, bladder preparation, medication dose, and laboratory analysis are not standardized by this item.

questions.objective: Prepare and communicate the time-sensitive hepatitis B postexposure prophylaxis plan for a newborn of an HBsAg-positive parent.
questions.stem: A laboring patient has a confirmed positive hepatitis B surface antigen result. The anticipated newborn weight is 3,200 g, and the newborn admission orders do not mention hepatitis B prophylaxis. Which action should the nurse take?
questions.clue: The birth exposure is already known, so prophylaxis should be ready before delivery and should not wait for symptoms or another maternal test.
questions.rationale: A newborn of an HBsAg-positive parent requires single-antigen hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin within 12 hours of birth. They should be administered at different injection sites, such as separate limbs, and the date and time should be documented. The nurse should promptly communicate the positive result and missing plan to the newborn team so both products are available. Maternal viral-load testing may guide maternal antiviral therapy, but it does not replace or delay newborn prophylaxis.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner applies a direct, time-critical birth prophylaxis rule and recognizes an omitted newborn order as a coordination problem requiring immediate escalation.

options.text: Notify the newborn clinician now and prepare single-antigen hepatitis B vaccine plus HBIG for administration at separate sites within 12 hours after birth, with administration times documented.
options.reason: Both products are required promptly for an infant born to an HBsAg-positive parent, and advance communication prevents a time-sensitive omission.

options.text: Prepare hepatitis B vaccine alone before discharge because HBIG is needed only if the newborn later develops jaundice.
options.reason: HBIG is part of immediate postexposure immunoprophylaxis; it is not reserved for a symptomatic newborn.

options.text: Wait for the maternal hepatitis B viral-load result before alerting the newborn team or requesting prophylaxis orders.
options.reason: A confirmed positive HBsAg result is sufficient to trigger the newborn vaccine-plus-HBIG plan; viral-load testing must not delay it.

options.text: Prepare HBIG alone at birth and postpone the first hepatitis B vaccine dose until the routine two-month immunization visit.
options.reason: Postexposure protection for this newborn requires both HBIG and the birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours.

refs.label: High-Risk Pregnancy course materials — hepatitis B newborn prophylaxis.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing — care of the newborn exposed to hepatitis B.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Clinical Overview of Perinatal Hepatitis B (September 18, 2025).
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Hepatitis B Perinatal Vaccine Information (August 27, 2025).

limitations: The item addresses a term-size newborn whose parent has confirmed positive HBsAg; schedules differ for some low-birth-weight and unknown-status situations.
It tests immediate birth prophylaxis and communication, not maternal antiviral selection, vaccine-series completion, or postvaccination serologic testing.
The named related item tests a different perinatal infection and does not supply the hepatitis B decision.

questions.objective: Plan respectful equipment, assistance, positioning, and assessment support for a laboring patient with obesity.
questions.stem: A laboring patient with a BMI of 52 kg/m² is stable, and the fetal heart rate signal has already been verified as interpretable. The nurse is preparing for position changes, repeated assessments, and possible transfer to the operating room. Which actions should be included in the care plan? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Plan before movement or an urgent transfer: match equipment to the patient, protect staff and patient during repositioning, and include the patient in dignified positioning decisions.
questions.rationale: Obesity can make positioning, transfers, blood-pressure measurement, physical assessment, and access to fetal assessment more difficult. Safe planning includes confirming the capacity and availability of beds, stretchers, operating tables, and transfer equipment; using a blood-pressure cuff selected from the patient's measured arm; arranging trained help and assistive devices before movement; and asking about comfortable positions while protecting privacy. Standard-capacity equipment should not be assumed safe for labor-room movement until an operating-room transfer is scheduled, and cuff selection should not be based on BMI alone.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must assemble a coordinated, dignity-preserving plan across equipment, staffing, positioning, and assessment while avoiding weight-based restriction and reactive preparation.

options.text: Confirm in advance that the bed, stretcher, operating table, and transfer equipment have appropriate dimensions and weight capacities.
options.reason: Advance capacity checks reduce delay and equipment-related injury during routine movement or an urgent transfer.

options.text: Use a blood-pressure cuff sized to the patient's measured arm rather than defaulting to the standard adult cuff.
options.reason: Correct cuff sizing is necessary for a clinically useful blood-pressure measurement and should be planned before repeated assessments.

options.text: Arrange enough trained staff and appropriate lift or transfer aids before major repositioning or transport.
options.reason: Planned assistance and equipment protect both the patient and staff and reduce rushed manual handling.

options.text: Ask which positions feel secure and effective, explain needed adjustments, and maintain privacy during exposure and movement.
options.reason: Patient-centered positioning and privacy protect dignity while allowing the team to complete safe labor assessments.

options.text: Use standard-capacity equipment for labor-room repositioning and reserve capacity-matched transfer equipment only if an operating-room transfer is later scheduled.
options.reason: Capacity and fit must be confirmed before any equipment is used, including routine labor-room repositioning; safe planning cannot wait until a transfer is scheduled.

options.text: Choose the largest available blood-pressure cuff from the patient's BMI, then repeat unexpected readings with that cuff for consistency.
options.reason: Cuff size should be based on the patient's measured arm and device specifications, not inferred from BMI or selected merely for consistency.

refs.label: High-Risk Labor and Delivery Instructor Notes — physical challenges, positioning, and fetal assessment for the laboring patient with obesity.
Maternal-Child Nursing Care — care planning, equipment, and transfer needs for pregnant patients with obesity.

limitations: The fetal signal is explicitly already verified, so the item does not repeat the signal-confirmation decision in h80-q005.
Equipment dimensions, weight capacities, staff numbers, and transfer techniques must follow patient measurements, manufacturer specifications, and local policy.
The item does not prescribe a route of birth, anesthetic plan, or mobility restriction based on BMI alone.

questions.objective: Use a low Bishop score to recognize an unfavorable cervix and coordinate cervical ripening before treating the cervix as ready for oxytocin or amniotomy.
questions.stem: A nulliparous patient at 39 weeks 3 days is admitted for a planned induction. The fetus is cephalic, the tracing is reassuring, membranes are intact, there is no prior uterine surgery, and the Bishop score is 3 with a closed, firm, posterior cervix and a high presenting part. Which nursing summary should guide the initial plan?
questions.clue: The score describes readiness of the cervix, not simply the need for stronger contractions.
questions.rationale: A Bishop score below 6 suggests that the cervix may not be ready for labor. With a closed, firm, posterior cervix and a high presenting part, the nurse should communicate that the cervix is unfavorable and confirm the clinician's cervical-ripening plan before proceeding as though oxytocin or amniotomy alone were the initial step. Ripening may use medication or a mechanical device selected by the clinician, with maternal and fetal monitoring. A low Bishop score is not by itself an automatic indication for cesarean birth or cancellation of an otherwise appropriate induction.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must interpret the composite cervical assessment and choose the appropriate induction phase rather than equating induction with immediate oxytocin or membrane rupture.

options.text: The cervix is unfavorable; verify the cervical-ripening plan and required monitoring before proceeding as though the cervix is ready for oxytocin or amniotomy.
options.reason: The low score and cervical findings indicate limited readiness, so the initial induction plan should address ripening rather than skip that assessment.

options.text: The low score means contractions are the only missing factor, so begin oxytocin without first addressing cervical readiness.
options.reason: The Bishop score evaluates cervical and presenting-part readiness, not only contraction strength; this cervix is closed, firm, posterior, and high.

options.text: The cervix is favorable for immediate amniotomy because an intact membrane is the reason the score is low.
options.reason: Membrane status is not a Bishop component, and amniotomy is generally considered when the cervix is dilated and the head is down in the pelvis.

options.text: A Bishop score of 3 makes vaginal birth unsafe, so prepare for cesarean birth without attempting cervical ripening.
options.reason: A low score predicts an unfavorable cervix; it is not, by itself, a contraindication to induction or an indication for cesarean birth.

refs.label: High-Risk Labor and Delivery course materials — Bishop score, cervical ripening, amniotomy, and oxytocin.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing — cervical readiness and induction of labor.
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists — Labor Induction (last reviewed November 2025).

limitations: The case excludes prior uterine surgery and does not select a specific ripening medication or device; those choices require clinician orders and patient-specific contraindication review.
The item tests readiness and sequencing, not management of tachysystole, removal of dinoprostone, or TOLAC induction safety.
A Bishop score supports planning but does not guarantee induction success or determine route of birth by itself.

questions.objective: Use late-term gestational age and current surveillance findings to explain ongoing monitoring and induction planning before meconium or another complication appears.
questions.stem: A patient at 41 weeks 2 days has reliable pregnancy dating, reports usual fetal movement, and has a reassuring nonstress test and amniotic-fluid assessment today. An induction is planned for tomorrow. The patient asks, “If today's tests are reassuring, why not wait until there is meconium before doing anything?” Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: A reassuring surveillance result describes the current assessment; meconium is a possible complication, not a prerequisite for discussing delivery.
questions.rationale: Pregnancy from 41 weeks to 42 weeks is late term, and fetal and maternal risks rise as gestation advances. Surveillance at or after 41 weeks may be performed weekly or twice weekly, and induction may be recommended at 41 weeks. A reassuring nonstress test and fluid assessment are useful for the current point in time but do not guarantee that conditions will remain unchanged. The nurse should reinforce the planned induction, prescribed surveillance and movement awareness, and return precautions rather than wait for meconium, decreased fluid, or a nonreassuring assessment to begin planning.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate gestational age with the time-limited meaning of reassuring surveillance and explain proactive management without treating meconium as the trigger.

options.text: “Today's results are reassuring for now, but risk increases as pregnancy continues past 41 weeks. Keep the induction plan, continue prescribed surveillance and movement awareness, and report warning signs rather than waiting for meconium.”
options.reason: This accurately explains the limited time horizon of surveillance and the reason to plan delivery before a complication is evident.

options.text: Ask whether the induction can be postponed for one week because today's reassuring tests lower the need for scheduled surveillance unless fetal movement decreases.
options.reason: Today's results are reassuring but time-limited. They do not support a one-week delay or replacing the prescribed surveillance plan with symptom-triggered testing alone.

options.text: Keep tomorrow's induction only if the repeat fluid assessment becomes low; otherwise defer delivery planning until 42 weeks because that is when postterm pregnancy begins.
options.reason: The postterm label begins at 42 weeks, but late-term risks and management planning begin earlier. Normal fluid alone does not erase the reason for an already planned 41-week induction.

options.text: Recommend replacing induction with a scheduled cesarean because advancing gestational age makes labor a less appropriate option despite reassuring testing.
options.reason: Late-term gestation supports surveillance and delivery planning but does not, by itself, make labor inappropriate or require cesarean birth.

refs.label: High-Risk Labor and Delivery course materials — post-dates pregnancy, surveillance, and induction planning.
Maternal-Child Nursing Care — late-term and postterm pregnancy assessment and management.
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists — When Pregnancy Goes Past Your Due Date (last reviewed March 2026).

limitations: The case uses a reassuring assessment, reliable dating, and an already planned induction; urgent management would change with nonreassuring findings or another complication.
The item tests counseling before meconium appears and does not duplicate h80-q045's intrapartum meconium-trajectory reassessment.
Exact surveillance frequency and induction timing remain individualized by the obstetric clinician and local protocol.

questions.objective: Use a multidomain high-risk intake to connect actionable environmental, nutritional, and access findings with workable support.
questions.stem: At a first prenatal intake at 10 weeks, a patient has stable vital signs and no acute symptoms. The patient reports using solvent cleaners during long shifts in a poorly ventilated auto-body shop, skipping meals near the end of each month because food runs out, and losing pay whenever a prenatal visit is scheduled during work hours. Which nursing actions should be included in the initial plan? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Match each disclosed risk with focused assessment and active coordination that the patient can realistically use.
questions.rationale: A high-risk intake extends beyond current vital signs. The nurse should clarify the workplace exposure and protections, assess the nutrition and food-access problem, and coordinate accessible care and social support with the patient's participation. These actions address environmental, sociodemographic, and access domains without prescribing employment decisions or postponing action.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must sort three actionable domains from a stable presentation and pair each with a proportionate, collaborative response. This is level 2 application rather than simple risk-factor recall.

options.text: Clarify the cleaner names, frequency and route of exposure, ventilation, and protective equipment, then coordinate review with the obstetric and occupational-health teams.
options.reason: The disclosed solvent exposure is an environmental finding that warrants a more specific exposure history and coordinated risk review; the nurse should not independently prescribe whether the patient can work.

options.text: Assess usual intake and food availability and, with the patient's agreement, complete a referral to nutrition and food-support services with a follow-up plan.
options.reason: Skipping meals because food runs out is an actionable nutrition and social-needs finding. Active linkage and follow-up are more useful than education that assumes reliable food access.

options.text: Ask which scheduling changes are feasible and coordinate clustered visits or telehealth for suitable services while preserving required in-person care.
options.reason: Lost wages are a structural access barrier. Shared planning can improve access, but remote care should be used only for services that can be completed safely that way.

options.text: Provide workplace chemical-safety handouts and ask the patient to discuss changes with the employer; obtain a detailed exposure history only if symptoms develop.
options.reason: Written information can supplement care, but the ongoing solvent exposure warrants focused assessment and coordinated review now rather than waiting for symptoms or shifting the decision entirely to the employer.

options.text: Arrange telehealth for all remaining prenatal visits to reduce lost wages, then address food access and solvent exposure after the scheduling barrier is resolved.
options.reason: Access adaptations should preserve required in-person services and should not postpone action on the concurrent nutrition and environmental risks identified at intake.

refs.label: Assessment of High Risk Pregnancy bonus lecture — multidomain risk assessment and nursing-role diagrams.
ACOG Clinical Consensus No. 8 — Tailored Prenatal Care Delivery for Pregnant Individuals (comprehensive needs assessment, social-needs coordination, and accessible care delivery).

limitations: The item does not establish a toxic exposure limit or independently direct work restriction; product-specific review and local occupational resources remain necessary.
Telehealth and social-support availability vary, and required in-person prenatal services must still be completed.
The item samples environmental, nutrition, and access domains; it does not claim that one vignette completes the full high-risk intake.

questions.objective: Provide nonstigmatizing, age-specific assessment and counseling for a pregnant adolescent while preserving individualized support.
questions.stem: A pregnant 16-year-old presents for an initial prenatal visit with an aunt. The aunt answers most questions, while the patient becomes quiet when mood, substance use, safety, and available support are mentioned. The patient has no urgent symptoms. Which nursing approach is best?
questions.clue: Private time is a routine part of adolescent care, and confidentiality has both protections and defined limits.
questions.rationale: The nurse should normalize private conversation time, explain confidentiality and its limits, and invite the adolescent to describe concerns, risks, and desired support in respectful, open-ended language. Age can guide how communication and support are delivered, but it should not replace individualized assessment or automatically exclude a chosen support person from the rest of care.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must preserve adolescent autonomy and safety while avoiding both caregiver domination and age-based assumptions. This is level 2 communication and care-management application.

options.text: Normalize private time, explain confidentiality and its limits, then assess the patient's concerns and ask whom the patient wants involved in support.
options.reason: This creates routine private space for sensitive assessment, accurately frames confidentiality, and lets the patient guide support-person involvement.

options.text: Ask the aunt to remain for the full history so she can confirm details, then offer the patient a private follow-up call if sensitive concerns arise.
options.reason: Caregiver input may be useful with the patient's agreement, but substituting a later call for routine private time can prevent disclosure during the visit and keeps the aunt in control of the initial history.

options.text: Interview the patient alone, promise that everything discussed will remain confidential, then invite the aunt back for support planning.
options.reason: Private time is appropriate, but confidentiality cannot be promised as absolute because safety, mandatory-reporting, and other legal or policy limits may apply.

options.text: Ask the aunt which services the patient needs, then privately confirm that plan with the patient to avoid repeating sensitive questions.
options.reason: The patient should be assessed directly with open-ended questions and should guide support planning; asking the aunt to define needs first can suppress the adolescent's own concerns and preferences.

refs.label: Week 4 High-Risk Pregnancy Instructor Notes — adolescent pregnancy and support considerations.
ACOG Committee Opinion No. 803 — Confidentiality in Adolescent Health Care.

limitations: Minor-consent, confidentiality, mandatory-reporting, portal, and billing rules vary by jurisdiction and institution; the nurse must follow applicable law and policy.
Confidentiality is not promised as absolute, and immediate safety or legally reportable concerns can require disclosure.
This vignette tests the care approach, not a complete prenatal screening schedule or a judgment about the aunt.

questions.objective: Differentiate NST and contraction-stress-test purpose and interpret a supplied positive CST result.
questions.stem: A contraction stress test is performed after an earlier nonreactive nonstress test. During a 10-minute period, four contractions occur and late fetal heart-rate decelerations follow three of them. Baseline variability remains moderate. Which interpretation and nursing response are most appropriate?
questions.clue: CST results are labeled by the fetal heart-rate response to contractions, not by NST acceleration terminology.
questions.rationale: A CST evaluates the fetal heart-rate response to uterine contractions. Late decelerations after at least half of adequate contractions constitute a positive, concerning result. Moderate variability does not erase that contraction-linked pattern. The nurse should promptly communicate the result and continue the ordered evaluation while the obstetric clinician determines next steps.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must resist substituting NST labels for CST interpretation and must avoid turning a concerning test result into an independent delivery order. This is level 2 interpretation and escalation.

options.text: Interpret the CST as positive and concerning for uteroplacental insufficiency; promptly notify the obstetric clinician and continue the ordered fetal evaluation.
options.reason: Late decelerations after three of four contractions meet the supplied positive-CST pattern. The nurse escalates the result without independently selecting definitive delivery management.

options.text: Interpret the CST as negative because moderate variability remains present between contractions.
options.reason: A negative CST has no late decelerations. Moderate baseline variability is reassuring information but does not cancel recurrent late decelerations linked to most contractions.

options.text: Interpret the tracing as a nonreactive NST and extend monitoring to look for two accelerations.
options.reason: Reactive and nonreactive describe the NST response to fetal movement. This supplied test is a CST and must be interpreted from the response to contractions.

options.text: Interpret the CST as positive and begin arranging immediate delivery without clinician review because a positive result dictates one universal route and timing.
options.reason: The result requires prompt evaluation, but it does not by itself authorize the nurse to select delivery timing or route without the full clinical context and obstetric plan.

refs.label: Assessment of High Risk Pregnancy bonus lecture — antepartal fetal surveillance overview.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — nonstress and contraction stress testing.
ACOG — Special Tests for Monitoring Fetal Well-Being (reviewed January 2026).

limitations: The item supplies an adequate contraction pattern and tests only positive-versus-negative CST interpretation.
A positive CST is concerning but does not independently determine delivery timing, route, or the remainder of the evaluation.
Contraindications to inducing contractions are outside this vignette and must be assessed before a real CST.

questions.objective: Use bleeding, cervical, and ultrasound findings to identify incomplete early pregnancy loss and anticipate an individualized management path.
questions.stem: At 10 weeks' gestation, a patient reports cramping, moderate vaginal bleeding, and passage of some tissue. Vital signs are stable; there is no fever or uterine tenderness. The cervix is open, and ultrasound confirms that some pregnancy tissue remains in the uterus. Which interpretation and anticipated plan are most accurate?
questions.clue: Some tissue has passed, some remains, and the patient has no supplied instability or infection.
questions.rationale: Passage of some tissue with an open cervix and retained intrauterine tissue is an incomplete early pregnancy loss. Because this patient is stable and has no evidence of infection, management can be individualized among expectant, medication, and uterine-evacuation approaches after clinician counseling and patient preference. Urgent surgical management becomes more likely with hemorrhage, hemodynamic instability, infection, or another clinical indication.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate three diagnostic domains and separate stable-management options from the hemorrhagic emergency already represented elsewhere. This is level 2 pattern recognition and care planning.

options.text: Incomplete early pregnancy loss; anticipate clinician counseling about expectant, medication, or uterine-evacuation management based on findings and patient preference.
options.reason: The open cervix, partial passage, and retained tissue establish the incomplete pattern. In a stable patient without infection, more than one management route can be appropriate.

options.text: Threatened loss; anticipate discharge with observation because an open cervix and retained tissue do not change the diagnosis.
options.reason: Threatened loss is characterized by bleeding with a closed cervix and no confirmed partial expulsion. The supplied findings instead identify incomplete loss.

options.text: Complete loss; anticipate no further assessment because passage of any tissue means the uterus is empty.
options.reason: Ultrasound directly shows retained tissue, so the loss is not complete. Passage of some tissue alone cannot establish complete evacuation.

options.text: Missed loss; anticipate that expectant or medication management is inappropriate because surgery is always required.
options.reason: The active bleeding, open cervix, partial passage, and retained tissue fit incomplete rather than missed loss. Stable early pregnancy loss does not require one universal surgical route.

refs.label: Week 4 High-Risk Pregnancy Instructor Notes — spontaneous-abortion patterns and management.
Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition — spontaneous-abortion classification and management options.
ACOG — Early Pregnancy Loss (diagnosis and treatment options).

limitations: Ultrasound has already confirmed the loss and retained tissue; the item does not teach criteria for confirming pregnancy viability when findings are uncertain.
No medication regimen, aspiration technique, or Rh-immune-globulin decision is generalized from this case.
The patient is explicitly stable and without infection; hemorrhagic-shock stabilization remains a separate decision.

questions.objective: Use onset relative to 20 weeks and postpartum persistence to distinguish gestational from chronic hypertension.
questions.stem: A patient had normal blood-pressure readings before pregnancy and through 24 weeks. Hypertension was first confirmed at 30 weeks without proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, renal or liver dysfunction, pulmonary edema, headache, or visual symptoms. Blood pressure remains hypertensive at 13 weeks postpartum. Which classification should the nurse communicate for follow-up?
questions.clue: Classify the pregnancy presentation by when hypertension began, then reconsider the label when it does not resolve postpartum.
questions.rationale: New hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria or severe-feature findings is initially classified as gestational hypertension. Persistence well beyond the postpartum interval expected for a transient gestational disorder supports reclassification and ongoing evaluation as chronic hypertension. The case intentionally supplies no end-organ pattern requiring a preeclampsia or HELLP interpretation.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must use two time points and update the classification rather than anchoring on either the prenatal label or the postpartum reading alone. This is level 2 longitudinal interpretation.

options.text: The pregnancy presentation was initially gestational hypertension; persistence at 13 weeks postpartum supports chronic-hypertension evaluation and longitudinal care.
options.reason: The hypertension began after 20 weeks without a supplied preeclampsia pattern, but it has not resolved by 13 weeks postpartum. That chronology supports transition from the provisional gestational label to chronic-hypertension follow-up.

options.text: The disorder was chronic hypertension throughout pregnancy because any postpartum persistence proves that it began before 20 weeks.
options.reason: The record documents normal pressure through 24 weeks and first confirmed hypertension at 30 weeks. Later persistence can change the ultimate classification but cannot rewrite the documented onset.

options.text: The disorder remains gestational hypertension indefinitely because it was first detected after 20 weeks.
options.reason: The prenatal onset supports the initial gestational label, but persistence beyond the expected postpartum resolution interval requires reassessment for chronic hypertension.

options.text: The postpartum persistence establishes preeclampsia even though no proteinuria or other end-organ findings were present.
options.reason: Persistence of hypertension alone does not supply the proteinuria or organ-dysfunction pattern used to identify preeclampsia. The key distinction here is gestational versus chronic hypertension.

refs.label: Week 4 High-Risk Pregnancy Instructor Notes — gestational and chronic hypertension chronology.
ACOG — Preeclampsia and High Blood Pressure During Pregnancy.
2025 ACC/AHA Multisociety Guideline for High Blood Pressure in Adults — hypertension and pregnancy classification.

limitations: The 13-week postpartum time point is chosen so that persistence is beyond both the course's six-week teaching point and the approximately 12-week threshold used in contemporary U.S. summaries.
The item excludes severe-range urgency, preeclampsia, HELLP syndrome, and medication selection.
Classification supports clinician evaluation and longitudinal follow-up; it does not authorize the nurse to diagnose a secondary cause or alter treatment independently.

questions.objective: Use maternal diabetes and fetal size to prepare surveillance for birth injury and non-glucose newborn transition risks.
questions.stem: A patient with pregestational diabetes has an estimated fetal weight above the 90th percentile near term. The birth and newborn teams are developing a coordinated plan, and the newborn glucose pathway is already included. Which additional preparations or surveillance should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Look beyond glucose to the mechanical risks of large size and the respiratory, calcium, and bilirubin-related transition risks associated with maternal diabetes.
questions.rationale: Maternal diabetes and suspected large fetal size warrant preparation for difficult shoulder delivery and focused assessment for birth injury. Infants of diabetic parents also require close respiratory-transition assessment and risk-focused surveillance for hypocalcemia, polycythemia, and hyperbilirubinemia according to clinical findings and local orders. Large size does not prove lung maturity, and risk alone does not justify prophylactic treatment without assessment or an order.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must deliberately exclude the already-addressed glucose pathway and integrate intrapartum mechanical risk with several non-glucose newborn transition domains. This is level 2 anticipatory care planning.

options.text: Confirm that the birth team is prepared for shoulder dystocia and preserve the exposure history for a focused newborn examination for clavicle or brachial-plexus injury.
options.reason: Suspected macrosomia increases difficult-delivery and birth-trauma risk. Team readiness and a focused postbirth examination connect the prenatal finding to safe maternal-newborn care.

options.text: Assess respiratory rate, work of breathing, and oxygenation during transition and escalate grunting, retractions, or persistent tachypnea.
options.reason: Newborns of patients with pregestational diabetes have an increased risk of respiratory problems, so focused transition assessment is appropriate.

options.text: Include hypocalcemia, polycythemia, and hyperbilirubinemia in the newborn handoff and follow the newborn service's ordered examinations and laboratory surveillance.
options.reason: These are recognized non-glucose risks for infants of diabetic parents. Surveillance should follow the infant's findings and the local newborn plan rather than automatic treatment.

options.text: Treat the large estimated size as evidence of mature lungs and omit additional respiratory-transition observation.
options.reason: Large size does not establish lung maturity. Maternal diabetes can coexist with neonatal respiratory difficulty despite macrosomia.

options.text: Begin phototherapy and intravenous calcium prophylactically after birth even if assessment and ordered laboratory findings are normal.
options.reason: Risk calls for focused assessment and ordered surveillance, not automatic treatment without a clinical or laboratory indication and prescribing plan.

refs.label: Week 4 High-Risk Pregnancy Instructor Notes — diabetes in pregnancy outcomes.
Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition — infant-of-diabetic-mother birth injury and transition risks.
ACOG — Pregnancy With Type 1 or Type 2 Diabetes.
ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 216 — Macrosomia.

limitations: Estimated fetal weight is imprecise and does not independently determine delivery route or timing.
The item assumes glucose monitoring is already planned and does not test glucose thresholds, frequency, feeding treatment, or serial interpretation.
Laboratory surveillance and treatment must follow the newborn's clinical findings, clinician orders, and local protocol; risk alone does not justify prophylactic therapy.

questions.objective: Respond to parvovirus B19 exposure in pregnancy with prompt testing coordination and proportionate follow-up rather than reassurance or automatic fetal-harm assumptions.
questions.stem: At 17 weeks, a daycare teacher reports close contact 3 days ago with a child whose illness was confirmed as parvovirus B19. The patient has no rash or joint pain and asks, “Does this mean the baby is infected, and should I quit work?” Which plan is most appropriate?
questions.clue: Exposure is not the same as infection; establish immunity or recent infection before assigning a surveillance pathway.
questions.rationale: A known parvovirus B19 exposure during pregnancy warrants prompt contact with the obstetric clinician. Antibody testing can help determine immunity and recent or past infection.
