Exposure does not prove maternal infection or fetal harm, and most maternal infections are mild. If infection is confirmed, the obstetric team may prescribe additional visits, blood tests, and ultrasound monitoring. The nurse should not impose a fixed surveillance schedule or automatic workplace exclusion without the clinical and occupational assessment.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must separate exposure from confirmed infection and choose staged evaluation and follow-up rather than either delayed reassurance or an unverified universal surveillance plan.

options.text: Contact the obstetric clinician for ordered antibody testing; exposure is not infection, and confirmed infection requires prescribed follow-up.
options.reason: This establishes immunity or recent infection first, gives proportionate reassurance, and preserves clinician-directed follow-up if infection is confirmed.

options.text: Wait for the routine anatomy ultrasound; antibody testing is unnecessary unless that scan later shows fetal hydrops.
options.reason: Known exposure should be reported now. Waiting for a fetal complication delays the maternal immunity and infection assessment that guides follow-up.

options.text: Treat the exposure as confirmed fetal infection and arrange the same weekly Doppler schedule through birth before obtaining antibody results.
options.reason: Exposure does not establish maternal or fetal infection, and no single fixed surveillance schedule should be imposed before the clinician evaluates the test results and gestational context.

options.text: Recommend leave from daycare for the rest of pregnancy; workplace exclusion makes maternal antibody testing unnecessary.
options.reason: Automatic exclusion does not replace prompt clinical evaluation. Work decisions should be individualized with the obstetric and occupational-health teams.

refs.label: Week 4 High-Risk Pregnancy Instructor Notes — parvovirus heading.
Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition — parvovirus B19 fetal risk and workplace considerations.
CDC — Parvovirus B19 in Pregnancy (December 17, 2025).

limitations: The item does not equate exposure with infection and does not claim that every maternal infection causes fetal harm.
The clinician determines the antibody interpretation and frequency or type of additional blood tests and ultrasound monitoring.
No universal occupational exclusion, Doppler schedule, invasive procedure, or treatment is prescribed.

questions.objective: Use pregnancy TB risk factors and a positive infection test to coordinate timely evaluation for active disease without assigning a diagnosis or regimen.
questions.stem: At 12 weeks, a patient reports recent close household contact with a relative treated for pulmonary tuberculosis and was born in a country where TB is common. The patient has no cough, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. A risk-based interferon-gamma release assay is positive. Which nursing response is best?
questions.clue: A positive infection test cannot distinguish latent infection from active disease, and pregnancy is not a reason to postpone the distinction.
questions.rationale: TB blood and skin tests can be used during pregnancy when risk factors are present. A positive infection test shows TB infection but does not determine whether infection is latent or active. The patient needs prompt medical evaluation for TB disease, which can include history, examination, chest radiography, and bacteriologic testing as indicated. Absence of symptoms does not establish latent infection, and evaluation should not be deferred because of pregnancy. Treatment timing and regimen differ for latent infection and active disease and remain clinician- and TB-program-directed.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must combine risk-based testing with correct interpretation of a positive result and sequence further evaluation without prematurely labeling disease or selecting treatment.

options.text: Explain that the test shows TB infection, not active disease; promptly coordinate the ordered evaluation, including chest radiography as indicated.
options.reason: A positive blood test requires evaluation to distinguish latent infection from active TB disease. Needed evaluation is not universally delayed because the patient is pregnant.

options.text: Document active TB from the positive blood test and begin teaching one standard multidrug regimen before further evaluation.
options.reason: A positive infection test alone does not diagnose active TB disease, and the nurse should not select a regimen before diagnostic and specialist evaluation.

options.text: Classify the result as latent TB because the patient has no symptoms, schedule postpartum treatment, and omit chest imaging during pregnancy.
options.reason: Absence of symptoms does not complete the evaluation or prove latent infection. A positive test still requires medical assessment for active disease, which may include chest radiography.

options.text: Repeat the blood test after 20 weeks before arranging any evaluation because testing and chest imaging are unreliable in early pregnancy.
options.reason: TB blood and skin testing can be used during pregnancy, and no universal 20-week delay should postpone evaluation of a positive result or compatible symptoms.

refs.label: Week 4 High-Risk Pregnancy Instructor Notes — tuberculosis heading.
Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition — risk-based prenatal tuberculin testing.
CDC — Tuberculosis Clinical Care and Treatment During Pregnancy (April 17, 2025).
CDC — Clinical and Laboratory Diagnosis for Tuberculosis (January 31, 2025).

limitations: The case supplies recognized exposure and epidemiologic risks; it does not advocate universal TB testing for every pregnant patient.
A positive infection test is not labeled as active or latent TB until medical evaluation is complete.
The item does not select a chest-imaging protocol, drug regimen, treatment duration, or timing of latent-infection treatment; those decisions require clinician and TB-program guidance.

questions.objective: Escalate a persistent abdominal and early-satiety warning-sign cluster for diagnostic evaluation without assigning an unsupported diagnosis.
questions.stem: A 47-year-old patient reports new abdominal bloating, constipation, and feeling full after only a few bites. The symptoms have occurred almost daily for 3 weeks and are not normal for the patient. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: Several new warning signs have persisted longer than 2 weeks, but the presentation does not establish a specific cause.
questions.rationale: Persistent bloating, constipation, and early satiety are warning signs that need diagnostic follow-up when they are new and last 2 weeks or longer. These symptoms may have benign or serious causes, so the nurse should arrange timely clinical evaluation without naming a cancer or treating the cluster as proof of one. Waiting for bleeding, substituting routine cervical screening, or beginning cancer-specific teaching before diagnosis does not match the evidence provided.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must recognize persistence and clustering as the discriminator while avoiding both under-triage and unsupported diagnostic overreach.

options.text: Arrange timely clinician evaluation of the persistent symptom cluster rather than attributing it to constipation alone.
options.reason: New bloating, constipation, and early satiety lasting more than 2 weeks warrant diagnostic evaluation even though the cause is not yet known.

options.text: Recommend fiber and an over-the-counter laxative, and wait until the next annual visit unless vaginal bleeding begins.
options.reason: Constipation care may later be appropriate, but it should not delay evaluation of several persistent warning signs that are new for the patient.

options.text: Schedule routine cervical screening as the sole evaluation because it checks for the gynecologic causes of these symptoms.
options.reason: Preventive cervical screening does not diagnose the full range of causes of persistent abdominal, bowel, or satiety symptoms.

options.text: Begin cancer-specific teaching because this symptom cluster confirms an advanced reproductive-tract malignancy.
options.reason: The symptoms require evaluation but do not confirm malignancy; diagnosis-specific teaching would be premature before the cause is established.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — Disorders of the reproductive tract: symptoms that must always have follow-up.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Symptoms of Gynecologic Cancers (September 5, 2024).

limitations: The item tests the residual persistent abdominal and early-satiety symptom-cluster decision and remains distinct from the current vulvar-focused cov1-gyn-005.
The item deliberately does not name or distinguish a specific malignancy and excludes already-tested postmenopausal bleeding, acute torsion, and chronic abnormal-uterine-bleeding sampling decisions.
The case supports timely diagnostic evaluation but does not specify a test sequence, diagnosis, or treatment.

questions.objective: Use age, cervical history, risk exclusions, and patient preference to select due preventive cervical screening while preserving consent.
questions.stem: An asymptomatic 36-year-old patient with a cervix has no history of cervical precancer, immunocompromise, or diethylstilbestrol exposure. The last cervical cancer screening was cytology alone 6 years ago. The patient says, "I want preventive care, but explain each step and stop if I ask." Which plan by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The patient is average risk, the prior cytology interval has elapsed, and agreement to preventive care does not remove control over the examination.
questions.rationale: This average-risk patient is due for cervical cancer screening because the last cytology was 6 years ago. For ages 30 through 65, current final USPSTF guidance supports cytology alone, primary high-risk HPV testing, or cotesting at their recommended intervals. The nurse should review the available guideline-based strategy with the clinician and patient, explain the collection, and confirm ongoing consent. Screening is preventive even when symptoms are absent, does not need to occur annually, and is not replaced by a routine pelvic examination or unrelated cancer screening.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must combine age, cervix and risk history, elapsed screening time, valid strategy selection, and ongoing consent rather than acting on one isolated screening label.

options.text: Explain that cervical screening is due, review the recommended test options, and confirm consent before and during specimen collection.
options.reason: The elapsed interval makes screening due, while informed consent and shared decision-making remain part of selecting and performing the preventive service.

options.text: Schedule annual cytology and collect the specimen during the pelvic examination unless the patient signs a refusal form.
options.reason: Average-risk adults do not require annual cytology, and consent must be voluntary and ongoing rather than presumed unless a formal refusal is signed.

options.text: Defer cervical screening because the patient has no symptoms and restart screening only if abnormal bleeding or discharge develops.
options.reason: Cervical screening is intended for asymptomatic people; waiting for symptoms would replace prevention with delayed diagnostic evaluation.

options.text: Use a routine pelvic examination as the screening test and reserve cytology or HPV testing for an abnormal examination finding.
options.reason: A pelvic examination does not substitute for guideline-based cervical cytology or high-risk HPV testing.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — General Women's Health Promotion and Maintenance.
U.S. Preventive Services Task Force — Cervical Cancer: Screening, current final recommendation (August 21, 2018).
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists — Informed Consent and Shared Decision Making in Obstetrics and Gynecology.

limitations: The item applies current final guidance to an explicitly average-risk patient with a cervix; high-risk surveillance is excluded.
The course note's obsolete age wording is not used, and the item does not claim that every gynecologic visit requires a pelvic examination.
No abnormal-result management, colposcopy pathway, breast screening interval, or colorectal screening interval is tested.

questions.objective: Compare hepatitis A, B, and C transmission and vaccination to select pregnancy-appropriate prevention and screening actions.
questions.stem: A patient at 12 weeks of pregnancy reports recent injection drug use, has not received hepatitis A or B vaccine, and has never been screened for hepatitis B or C. Which teaching should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Compare each virus by its main route, vaccine availability, and pregnancy-specific screening or prevention need.
questions.rationale: Hepatitis A spreads mainly by the fecal-oral route and vaccination is recommended during pregnancy when exposure risk or risk of severe outcome is present. Hepatitis B spreads through blood, semen, and other body fluids; vaccination is available, and pregnancy is not a contraindication when vaccination is indicated. Hepatitis C is primarily bloodborne, has no vaccine, and screening is recommended during each pregnancy. Hepatitis A does not become chronic, and neither a hepatitis C vaccine nor symptom-based waiting is an appropriate response to possible blood exposure.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate three viruses, distinguish overlapping blood-exposure risks, and apply vaccine and pregnancy boundaries across multiple plausible statements.

options.text: Hepatitis A spreads mainly by the fecal-oral route, and the clinician should assess the need for hepatitis A vaccination during this pregnancy.
options.reason: Injection drug use increases hepatitis A risk, and CDC recommends HepA vaccination during pregnancy when infection risk or risk of severe outcome is present.

options.text: Hepatitis B can spread through blood and sexual body fluids, and indicated hepatitis B vaccination does not need to wait until after pregnancy.
options.reason: HBV is transmitted through infectious blood and body fluids, a vaccine is available, and pregnancy is not a contraindication to indicated HepB vaccination.

options.text: Hepatitis C is primarily bloodborne, has no vaccine, and screening should be arranged during this pregnancy.
options.reason: The patient's injection exposure is relevant to HCV, no vaccine exists, and CDC recommends HCV screening during each pregnancy.

options.text: Hepatitis A commonly becomes chronic, so lifelong viral-load monitoring is the main preventive plan.
options.reason: Hepatitis A is an acute infection and does not progress to chronic infection; vaccination and exposure prevention are the relevant strategies.

options.text: Hepatitis B vaccine should be postponed until after delivery because pregnancy is a contraindication.
options.reason: Pregnancy is not a contraindication to HepB vaccination, and this unvaccinated patient has a current risk factor.

options.text: A hepatitis C vaccine should be given now, and testing is needed only if jaundice develops.
options.reason: No hepatitis C vaccine exists, and the absence of symptoms does not remove the need for pregnancy screening or exposure evaluation.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — Hepatitis A, B, and C.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Clinical Overview of Viral Hepatitis (August 29, 2025).
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Guidelines for Vaccinating Pregnant Women (August 22, 2025).

limitations: The item is limited to the three hepatitis types explicitly named in the accepted course notes.
The nurse coordinates screening and vaccination assessment and does not diagnose infection, select immune globulin, or prescribe an antiviral regimen.
The pregnancy, vaccination history, screening history, and injection-drug exposure are fictional case facts.

questions.objective: Coordinate routine HIV screening and PrEP evaluation for an adult with ongoing sexual exposure risk.
questions.stem: A 27-year-old patient has never had HIV screening and reports ongoing vaginal sex without condoms with a partner who has HIV. The partner's current viral suppression status is unknown. The patient's last sexual contact was 2 weeks ago, there are no symptoms of acute HIV infection, and the patient asks how to reduce future risk. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The patient needs current HIV status established and a prevention plan designed for continuing, rather than isolated, exposure risk.
questions.rationale: Routine HIV screening is recommended even without disclosed risk, and this patient's ongoing exposure makes prompt testing especially important. PrEP is for people without HIV who may be exposed through sex, so HIV status must be evaluated before initiation. The nurse should arrange testing now and, if HIV is excluded, coordinate PrEP evaluation with condom and STI-prevention counseling. Waiting for symptoms misses asymptomatic infection, starting PrEP without HIV testing is unsafe, and repeated use of postexposure prophylaxis is not the planned strategy for continuing exposure.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must sequence testing before PrEP while distinguishing ongoing prevention from delayed symptom-based testing and episodic postexposure care.

options.text: Arrange HIV testing now and, if HIV is excluded, coordinate PrEP evaluation with counseling about condoms and other STI prevention.
options.reason: Current HIV status must be established before PrEP, and the ongoing exposure pattern supports prompt prevention counseling and PrEP evaluation.

options.text: Wait for fever, rash, or lymph-node swelling before testing, because screening during an asymptomatic period is not useful.
options.reason: HIV can be asymptomatic, and routine plus risk-based screening should not wait for symptoms.

options.text: Begin PrEP without HIV testing because the partner's diagnosis already establishes the medication choice.
options.reason: HIV testing is required before PrEP so unrecognized infection is not managed with an incomplete prevention regimen.

options.text: Use postexposure prophylaxis after each future sexual contact instead of developing a preexposure prevention plan.
options.reason: Postexposure prophylaxis is an urgent time-limited response to a recent exposure, whereas PrEP is the appropriate prevention pathway to evaluate for continuing risk.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — HIV screening, counseling, and prevention.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Clinical Testing Guidance for HIV (August 17, 2026).
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Clinical Guidance for PrEP (April 30, 2026).

limitations: The item does not select a PrEP product, dose, laboratory panel, or follow-up interval; the clinician completes the required baseline evaluation.
The two-week interval places the described contact outside a routine 72-hour PEP initiation scenario, but exact testing interpretation remains clinician-directed.
No claim is made about the partner's transmission risk because current viral suppression is explicitly unknown.

questions.objective: Compare permanence, onset of contraceptive reliability, and follow-up after tubal surgery versus vasectomy.
questions.stem: A patient and partner are comparing laparoscopic tubal sterilization with vasectomy. They understand that both methods are intended to be permanent and ask when each can be relied on for contraception. Which explanation by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The procedures share an intent of permanence but differ in how quickly contraceptive success can be relied on and confirmed.
questions.rationale: Laparoscopic and abdominal tubal surgery can be relied on immediately for contraception and do not require additional contraceptive protection for onset. Vasectomy is not immediately reliable because sperm can remain after the procedure; abstinence or a barrier method is needed until postvasectomy semen analysis confirms success. Counseling before either procedure should address intended irreversibility, alternatives, benefits, and risks. Wound healing or a fixed ejaculation count does not confirm vasectomy success, and routine imaging is not the confirmation pathway for tubal surgery.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must distinguish two permanent methods by onset and follow-up rather than treating the shared permanence label as evidence that their postprocedure instructions are identical.

options.text: Tubal surgery is reliable immediately; after vasectomy, use backup until postvasectomy semen analysis confirms success.
options.reason: Current guidance distinguishes immediate reliability after tubal surgery from delayed reliability after vasectomy until laboratory confirmation.

options.text: Both methods are reliable as soon as the incision has healed, so neither requires method-specific follow-up.
options.reason: Incision healing does not establish sperm clearance after vasectomy, which requires postvasectomy semen analysis before backup stops.

options.text: Vasectomy is reliable immediately, while tubal surgery requires three-month pelvic imaging before backup can stop.
options.reason: This reverses the supported onset distinction; tubal surgery is immediately reliable, while vasectomy requires semen-analysis confirmation.

options.text: Use a fixed ejaculation count after vasectomy and routine cervical screening after tubal surgery to confirm success.
options.reason: Ejaculation count is not a reliable clearance measure, and cervical screening does not confirm tubal occlusion or contraceptive effectiveness.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — Sterilization and informed consent.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — Chapter 1 Contraception, surgical sterilization methods (legacy fixed-count rules excluded).
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Permanent Contraception, U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations (November 18, 2024).

limitations: The item compares laparoscopic or abdominal tubal surgery with vasectomy and excludes discontinued transcervical sterilization devices.
No fixed ejaculation count, two-zero-sample rule, universal reversal success, or provider-specific semen-collection protocol is used.
The item tests onset and follow-up after informed method selection; it does not recommend one permanent method for every patient.

questions.objective: Coordinate indicated Rh follow-through and therapeutic grief support after pregnancy loss without blame or false reassurance.
questions.stem: After uterine evacuation for a pregnancy loss at 13 weeks, a patient is stable and preparing for discharge. The record shows Rh-negative blood type, a negative antibody screen, and a prescribed Rh immune globulin (RhIg) dose that has not yet been documented as given. The patient says, “I caused this by carrying groceries. Please do not just tell me everything will be fine.” Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Address the time-sensitive Rh plan and the patient's stated need for honest, individualized support.
questions.rationale: At 13 weeks, an unsensitized Rh-negative patient with pregnancy loss should receive the prescribed RhIg follow-through to reduce the chance of Rh sensitization affecting a future pregnancy. Grief care should acknowledge the loss, invite the patient's experience, and offer preferred resources without blame, minimizing language, or promises about emotional recovery or a future pregnancy.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must coordinate a gestational-age-specific medication follow-through and select therapeutic grief responses in the same discharge encounter. This is level 2 integrated care.

options.text: Reconcile the pending order and arrange administration of the prescribed RhIg before discharge according to the obstetric protocol.
options.reason: The patient is Rh negative, unsensitized, and experienced loss at 13 weeks. The nurse should close the documented medication gap rather than assume that removal of pregnancy tissue ends the sensitization concern.

options.text: Say, “I am sorry this happened. Would you like to tell me what you are thinking or what support would feel helpful right now?”
options.reason: This response acknowledges the loss, avoids blame and false reassurance, and lets the patient define immediate emotional needs.

options.text: Offer follow-up with the obstetric team and, according to the patient's preferences, bereavement counseling or a pregnancy-loss support resource.
options.reason: Grief responses vary. Offering continued care and optional resources supports the patient without imposing one way to grieve.

options.text: Remove RhIg from the discharge plan because prophylaxis is no longer useful once the pregnancy tissue has been evacuated.
options.reason: Evacuation does not erase potential fetal red-cell exposure. The supplied 13-week, Rh-negative, unsensitized scenario supports completing the prescribed RhIg plan.

options.text: Reassure the patient that another pregnancy will happen soon and will make this loss easier to forget.
options.reason: This predicts a future pregnancy and emotional course that cannot be guaranteed, while minimizing the patient's current loss and explicit request for honest support.

refs.label: Week 4 High-Risk Pregnancy Instructor Notes — pregnancy-loss grief and Rh considerations.
ACOG — Early Pregnancy Loss (RhIg guidance updated September 2024).
ACOG — Finding Emotional Support After Pregnancy Loss (reviewed February 2025).

limitations: The 13-week scenario is intentionally outside the less-than-12-week range in which current ACOG guidance suggests forgoing routine Rh testing and RhIg prophylaxis; it does not restore a universal early-loss rule.
The item assumes a valid patient-specific RhIg order and does not generalize a dose, product, or timing protocol.
The item tests supportive communication and referral, not diagnosis or treatment of a grief-related mental health disorder.

questions.objective: Use current GBS-screen status and prolonged rupture at term to implement the prescribed intrapartum prophylaxis plan.
questions.stem: A patient at 39 weeks is in labor. The current pregnancy record has no vaginal-rectal GBS screening result. Membranes ruptured 19 hours ago, temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), and there are no findings suggesting intraamniotic infection. A urine culture obtained for dysuria last week was negative, and the intrapartum protocol contains an active penicillin prophylaxis order for an eligible patient with unknown GBS status. The patient has no penicillin allergy. Which action should the nurse take?
questions.clue: A negative urine culture is not the current vaginal-rectal GBS screen, and rupture duration matters when status is unknown.
questions.rationale: At term, unknown GBS status plus rupture of membranes for 18 hours or more is an indication for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis. The unrelated negative urine culture does not establish negative vaginal-rectal colonization. The nurse should implement the prescribed protocol promptly without waiting to guarantee a fixed number of doses; absence of fever and other findings does not create a separate intraamniotic-infection treatment indication.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must reject an incidental negative test, combine unknown current screen status with a 19-hour rupture interval, and use the supplied prophylaxis order. This is level 2 evidence selection and care implementation.

options.text: Start the prescribed intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis now and document the unknown current GBS status and 19-hour rupture interval.
options.reason: Unknown status with rupture for at least 18 hours at term meets the supplied prophylaxis criterion, and the current order can be implemented.

options.text: Withhold prophylaxis because the negative urine culture serves as a negative GBS screening result for this pregnancy.
options.reason: A urine culture obtained for dysuria is not the recommended vaginal-rectal GBS screening culture and does not resolve the unknown screening status.

options.text: Delay prophylaxis until the team confirms that exactly two antibiotic doses can be completed before birth.
options.reason: The course's two-dose shorthand is not a universal prerequisite. Indicated prophylaxis should begin promptly, and necessary obstetric care is not delayed solely to complete a fixed number of doses.

options.text: Replace GBS prophylaxis with broad-spectrum treatment for intraamniotic infection because rupture has exceeded 18 hours.
options.reason: Prolonged rupture increases GBS risk but does not by itself establish intraamniotic infection. The stem supplies no fever or other infection findings requiring that different treatment pathway.

refs.label: Week 4 High-Risk Pregnancy Instructor Notes — group B streptococcus.
ACOG Committee Opinion No. 797 — Prevention of Group B Streptococcal Early-Onset Disease in Newborns.
ACOG — Group B Strep and Pregnancy (reviewed April 2025).

limitations: The prophylaxis indication is bounded to term labor, unknown current GBS status, and rupture for 19 hours with an active protocol order.
The item does not select a regimen for penicillin allergy, suspected intraamniotic infection, preterm labor, prior affected newborn, or GBS bacteriuria.
No fixed number of doses or minimum exposure interval is presented as a condition for beginning indicated prophylaxis or proceeding with necessary obstetric care.

questions.objective: Recognize possible birth-trauma phrenic-nerve injury and escalate persistent respiratory distress
questions.stem: After a difficult shoulder-dystocia birth, a newborn has a flaccid right arm with an absent right Moro response. Airway positioning and prescribed oxygen have been provided, but tachypnea and retractions persist. Breath sounds are present bilaterally, and chest and abdominal movement appear asymmetric. Which plan should the nurse follow?
questions.clue: Decide whether the respiratory and arm findings should be managed as separate problems or as one birth-trauma pattern requiring prompt evaluation.
questions.rationale: Birth-trauma phrenic-nerve injury can occur with an ipsilateral brachial-plexus injury and impair movement of one hemidiaphragm. The nurse should integrate the difficult birth, arm findings, persistent respiratory distress, and asymmetric movement; continue prescribed respiratory support and serial assessment; and promptly report concern for clinician-directed diagnostic evaluation. Treating the findings as separate routine problems, anchoring first on a pulmonary-transition diagnosis, or delaying the integrated handoff to collect another trend can postpone evaluation of possible diaphragm dysfunction.
questions.difficultyReason: The alternatives all continue care or escalate some portion of the case. The learner must integrate the birth mechanism, ipsilateral plexus pattern, persistent distress, and asymmetric movement to choose the prompt combined handoff, supporting level 2.

options.text: Continue prescribed support, document the arm and respiratory findings as separate problems, and request routine respiratory and orthopedic reviews.
options.reason: Both reviews may ultimately contribute, but separating the findings and using routine timing misses an integrated birth-trauma pattern that warrants prompt evaluation for associated phrenic-nerve injury.

options.text: Continue respiratory assessment and prescribed support, report possible phrenic-nerve injury promptly, and prepare for clinician-directed diagnostic evaluation.
options.reason: The difficult birth, ipsilateral plexus pattern, persistent distress, and asymmetric movement support prompt integrated escalation while prescribed respiratory support and serial assessment continue.

options.text: Report the persistent distress as a pulmonary-transition problem and ask that diaphragm-specific evaluation be considered only if the lung assessment is unrevealing.
options.reason: A pulmonary assessment can be appropriate, but anchoring on transition and postponing the diaphragm concern fails to integrate the associated arm and movement findings in the initial handoff.

options.text: Continue prescribed support and collect another interval of oxygen-saturation and movement trends before reporting a possible nerve-related breathing problem.
options.reason: Serial trends should continue, but the existing persistent distress and asymmetric pattern are already sufficient for prompt reporting; another observation interval should not precede escalation.

refs.label: Week 5 High-Risk Newborn Instructor Notes — phrenic-nerve birth injury and diaphragmatic paralysis.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing, edition 11 — chapter 27, printed pp. 197–198: birth-trauma assessment and care.
Maternal Child Nursing Care, 7th ed. — chapter 25, birth injuries: phrenic-nerve injury.
Canadian Paediatric Society — The evaluation and management of neonatal brachial plexus palsy.
Journal of Pediatric Surgery — Diaphragmatic paralysis after phrenic nerve injury in newborns.

limitations: The case raises concern for phrenic-nerve injury; it does not diagnose diaphragmatic paralysis from respiratory distress or asymmetry alone.
No positioning rule, imaging order, ventilatory prescription, operative candidacy rule, or plication timing is created.
The item tests integration, continued prescribed support, serial assessment, and prompt escalation rather than Erb-palsy limb management or a generic pulmonary-transition pathway.

questions.objective: Coordinate time-sensitive congenital-CMV confirmation and follow-up
questions.stem: A 10-day-old newborn is small for gestational age and has petechiae, jaundice, microcephaly, and hepatosplenomegaly. The newborn passed the birth hearing screen, and no cytomegalovirus evaluation has been started. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Recognize the pattern, protect the congenital diagnostic window, and do not let one reassuring screening result close follow-up.
questions.rationale: The multisystem pattern should be reported as concern for congenital CMV without diagnosing from appearance. Confirmation uses PCR within 2 to 3 weeks after birth; under the clinician's plan, saliva PCR is obtained promptly and a positive saliva result is confirmed with urine. Newborn IgG or IgM does not establish congenital CMV, and saliva PCR alone is not the complete confirmation pathway. If infection is confirmed, hearing and vision follow-up remains important even after a reassuring birth hearing screen because hearing loss can emerge or progress. Testing, surveillance intervals, and antiviral decisions remain clinician-directed.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must assemble a three-part recognition, specimen-confirmation, and longitudinal follow-up plan while distinguishing three clinically plausible but incomplete CMV-specific alternatives, supporting level 2.

options.text: Report the complete pattern as concern for congenital CMV and request clinician-directed evaluation without documenting CMV as confirmed.
options.reason: The pattern is compatible but overlaps other conditions. Reporting the integrated findings initiates evaluation without converting phenotype into a diagnosis.

options.text: Use a positive saliva PCR as final confirmation because the compatible physical pattern makes urine confirmation unnecessary.
options.reason: Saliva is a preferred initial specimen, but a positive saliva PCR should be confirmed with urine even when the clinical pattern is compatible.

options.text: After testing is ordered, facilitate PCR before 3 weeks of age using the saliva collection and urine-confirmation pathway.
options.reason: Testing within 2 to 3 weeks preserves the congenital diagnostic window, and urine confirmation completes the pathway after a positive saliva result.

options.text: Add newborn CMV IgG and IgM to the PCR plan and use concordant antibody results to determine whether infection was congenital.
options.reason: Newborn antibody results do not establish congenital CMV or its timing. Timely PCR with the appropriate confirmation specimen is the relevant pathway.

options.text: If congenital CMV is confirmed, ensure ongoing hearing and vision follow-up despite the reassuring birth hearing screen.
options.reason: Confirmed congenital CMV can be followed by delayed or progressive hearing loss and warrants continued hearing and vision monitoring.

options.text: If the birth hearing screen was normal, use routine well-child surveillance unless caregivers later notice a hearing or vision change.
options.reason: A reassuring birth screen does not replace planned longitudinal monitoring after confirmed congenital CMV; waiting for caregiver-detected change can miss evolving impairment.

refs.label: Week 5 High-Risk Newborn Instructor Notes — TORCH complex and congenital complications.
Maternal Child Nursing Care, 7th ed. — chapter 25, congenital infections and cytomegalovirus.
CDC — Clinical Overview of CMV and Congenital CMV: newborn testing and monitoring.

limitations: The findings support concern but do not diagnose congenital CMV or distinguish it from every other congenital infection.
The item does not prescribe universal CMV screening, an antiviral drug, dose, duration, or a fixed hearing or vision surveillance interval.
Testing, interpretation, treatment, and specialty follow-up remain clinician- and protocol-directed.

questions.objective: Use exposure and newborn findings to facilitate congenital-toxoplasmosis confirmation
questions.stem: A 2-day-old newborn has hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications, and a retinal finding concerning for chorioretinitis. During pregnancy, the parent frequently ate undercooked game and changed cat litter without gloves. The clinician orders infant Toxoplasma IgG, IgM, and IgA testing. Which nursing plan is most appropriate?
questions.clue: Prompt collection is appropriate, but antibody results obtained this early require specialty interpretation and may require directed repeat testing.
questions.rationale: The exposure plus ocular and CNS findings raises concern for congenital toxoplasmosis but does not independently confirm it. The nurse should collect the ordered infant IgG, IgM, and IgA specimens promptly, report the complete pattern, and facilitate specialty-laboratory confirmation and team interpretation. At 2 days of age, detection of IgM before day 5 or IgA before day 10 can reflect maternal-blood contamination. That caveat does not make prompt collection wrong; it makes independent interpretation unsafe and clinician-directed repeat testing important when indicated. Negative early tests can also occur, and a stable initial course does not eliminate later ocular disease.
questions.difficultyReason: Each alternative uses part of the neonatal serology pathway. The learner must reconcile prompt complete collection with the age-dependent contamination caveat, specialty confirmation, and possible directed repeat testing, supporting level 2.

options.text: Collect infant IgG now, defer IgM and IgA until after day 10, and then send the later antibody set for specialty interpretation.
options.reason: The contamination caveat does not require withholding the clinician-ordered early specimens. Prompt complete collection is appropriate, with specialty interpretation and repeat testing when directed.

options.text: Collect the ordered infant IgG, IgM, and IgA, report the full pattern, send specimens for specialty confirmation, and anticipate repeat testing if directed.
options.reason: This preserves prompt complete testing while accounting for specialized interpretation and the possibility that very early IgM or IgA results need clinician-directed repeat confirmation.

options.text: Run the complete antibody set locally and use specialty confirmation only when the local IgM and IgA results disagree with each other.
options.reason: All specimens from neonates suspected of congenital toxoplasmosis should enter the specialty-confirmation pathway; agreement between early local results does not remove interpretation limits.

options.text: Collect IgM and IgA but omit IgG because maternal transfer makes IgG unhelpful in the neonatal confirmation pathway.
options.reason: Maternal IgG complicates interpretation, but current neonatal guidance still calls for infant IgG, IgM, and IgA testing with specialty interpretation.

options.text: Collect all three antibodies and close the specialty pathway if the early results are negative and the newborn remains clinically stable.
options.reason: False-negative early results can occur, and clinical stability does not exclude congenital infection or later ocular disease. Team-directed confirmation and follow-up should continue.

refs.label: Week 5 High-Risk Newborn Instructor Notes — TORCH complex and toxoplasmosis.
Maternal Child Nursing Care, 7th ed. — chapter 25, congenital toxoplasmosis.
CDC DPDx — Toxoplasmosis: clinical presentation and neonatal antibody confirmation (last reviewed May 5, 2025).

limitations: The exposure and findings raise suspicion but do not independently diagnose congenital toxoplasmosis.
Detection of infant IgM before day 5 or IgA before day 10 can reflect maternal-blood contamination; the item does not direct the learner to interpret an early positive result as definitive.
The item does not prescribe a fixed repeat-testing schedule, treatment drugs, doses, durations, or a universal follow-up interval.
Specimen selection is supplied by the clinician's order; confirmation, interpretation, repeat testing, treatment, and specialty follow-up remain team-directed.

questions.objective: Recognize urgent neonatal-HSV concern and activate evaluation and treatment pathways
questions.stem: A 12-day-old newborn is brought to the emergency department for poor feeding and a brief focal seizure. The nurse observes several clustered vesicles on an erythematous base. The birth record contains no clinically evident maternal herpes history. Which plan is the priority?
questions.clue: Compare plans that all escalate some aspect of the case; decide which one treats the skin-plus-CNS pattern as an immediate neonatal-HSV concern.
questions.rationale: Neonatal HSV can occur without a clinically evident maternal history and may present with skin-eye-mouth, CNS, or disseminated disease. A 12-day-old infant with vesicles, poor feeding, and a focal seizure requires a unified urgent HSV response. The nurse should immediately notify the neonatal clinician, coordinate pediatric-infectious-disease involvement, and prepare for the clinician-directed evaluation and systemic treatment pathway. Bacterial sepsis and seizure evaluation may occur in parallel, but they should not postpone HSV-specific escalation or treatment planning while confirmation is pending.
questions.difficultyReason: All alternatives initiate urgent assessment, consultation, or specimen work. The learner must integrate the age, vesicles, CNS finding, and unreliable negative maternal-history cue to avoid sequential or fragmented plans, supporting level 2.

options.text: Activate the neonatal seizure and bacterial-sepsis pathways first, then add HSV-specific evaluation if the initial cultures do not explain the presentation.
options.reason: Seizure and sepsis evaluation may be appropriate in parallel, but waiting for bacterial results postpones the HSV-specific response to a compatible skin-plus-CNS pattern.

options.text: Notify the neonatal clinician immediately, coordinate pediatric-infectious-disease evaluation, and prepare for the ordered systemic HSV treatment pathway.
options.reason: The age, vesicles, and neurologic finding warrant immediate unified HSV evaluation and treatment planning despite the absent maternal history.

options.text: Notify the neonatal clinician, prioritize lesion sampling and dermatology review, and defer systemic treatment planning until CNS testing confirms HSV.
options.reason: Lesion sampling can contribute, but a focal seizure raises CNS concern now. Systemic treatment planning should not wait for confirmation or proceed as a skin-only problem.

options.text: Request a broad neonatal-infection evaluation, but assign HSV lower priority unless additional vesicles appear because no maternal herpes was documented.
options.reason: A documented maternal history is often absent, and the current skin-plus-CNS pattern already gives HSV high priority without waiting for more lesions.

options.text: Begin the urgent HSV evaluation through the neonatal clinician and seek infectious-disease consultation only if initial virologic testing confirms infection.
options.reason: The evaluation should begin urgently, but delaying specialty involvement until confirmation creates unnecessary sequential care in a time-sensitive suspected neonatal-HSV case.

refs.label: Week 5 High-Risk Newborn Instructor Notes — TORCH complex and herpes simplex virus.
Maternal Child Nursing Care, 7th ed. — chapter 25, neonatal herpes patterns.
CDC Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines — Genital Herpes: neonatal herpes.

limitations: The pattern creates urgent concern but does not independently confirm neonatal HSV or its disease classification.
The item does not prescribe a specimen set, isolation protocol, acyclovir dose or duration, or maternal delivery-route decision.
Diagnostic testing, infectious-disease consultation, treatment, and escalation details remain clinician- and protocol-directed.

questions.objective: Recognize a congenital-rubella pattern and coordinate infection control, confirmation, and specialty follow-up
questions.stem: A 6-day-old term newborn who is small for gestational age has microcephaly, a generalized purpuric rash, bilateral cataracts, a patent ductus arteriosus, and an abnormal hearing screen. The parent reports an early-pregnancy febrile rash after international travel and has no clear record of rubella immunity. Which nursing plan is most appropriate?
questions.clue: The cluster is more informative than one anomaly, but recognition must lead to coordinated precautions and confirmation rather than a bedside diagnosis.
questions.rationale: The combined growth, CNS, skin, eye, cardiac, and hearing findings with a relevant maternal history form a compatible congenital-rubella pattern but do not independently confirm congenital rubella syndrome. The nurse should initiate ordered infection-control precautions and promptly coordinate neonatal-clinician, infection-prevention, public-health, confirmatory-testing, and specialty-follow-up pathways. Treating each anomaly separately, waiting for infant confirmation before infection-control coordination, or using phenotype or maternal serology as the sole confirmation method can delay appropriate containment and evaluation. The nurse does not independently choose a universal test panel or set the duration of precautions.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate a multi-organ newborn cluster with maternal travel history and distinguish the complete coordinated response from three partially appropriate but fragmented or prematurely closed plans, supporting level 2.

options.text: Initiate the ordered contact precautions and notify the neonatal clinician, but wait for infant confirmation before involving infection prevention, public health, or specialty services.
options.reason: Starting precautions and notifying the clinician are appropriate, but the compatible cluster warrants prompt coordinated infection-prevention, public-health, testing, and specialty pathways rather than sequential referral after confirmation.

options.text: Initiate ordered infection-control precautions and promptly coordinate clinician, infection-prevention and public-health notification, confirmatory testing, and specialty follow-up.
options.reason: This recognizes the compatible pattern without diagnosing it and activates the coordinated containment, confirmation, and organ-specific follow-up response.

options.text: Arrange cardiology, ophthalmology, and audiology consultations for separate anomalies while using standard precautions until maternal immunity is clarified.
options.reason: The specialty needs are real, but treating the findings as unrelated and delaying ordered infection-control coordination misses the congenital-infection pattern.

options.text: Use the classic phenotype to place the newborn on the congenital-rubella pathway and defer virologic confirmation unless public health specifically requests it.
options.reason: The phenotype raises strong concern but is not independently diagnostic. Clinician-directed infant confirmation belongs in the initial coordinated pathway rather than being conditional on a later request.

options.text: Notify infection prevention and public health, but limit confirmation to repeat maternal serology because the newborn findings already localize the infection.
options.reason: Maternal history contributes context, but the newborn still requires clinician-directed infant confirmation and specialty assessment; maternal serology alone does not close the case.

refs.label: Week 5 High-Risk Newborn Instructor Notes — TORCH complex, rubella, and Table 25.5 referral.
Maternal Child Nursing Care, 7th ed. — Table 25.5, congenital rubella, printed p. 2033.
CDC MMWR — Notes from the Field: Congenital Rubella Syndrome — Florida, 2025 (published March 5, 2026).

limitations: The supplied phenotype and maternal history are fictional and raise concern; they do not independently diagnose congenital rubella syndrome.
The item does not retest prenatal MMR contraindication, postpartum vaccination, or maternal exposure reporting.
No universal diagnostic panel, independent test order, or independently chosen type or duration of precautions is created.
Testing, infection-control details, public-health actions, and specialty follow-up remain clinician-, protocol-, and jurisdiction-directed.

questions.objective: Direct a stable possible ingestion to immediate Poison Control guidance without induced emesis, improvised decontamination, or delay for symptoms.
questions.stem: A caregiver finds a 3-year-old holding an open bottle of adult multivitamins. Several tablets are on the floor, and the caregiver cannot determine whether any were swallowed. The child is awake, breathing normally, able to swallow, and has no symptoms. Which instruction should the nurse give first?
questions.clue: The exposure is uncertain and the child is stable; expert substance-specific direction is needed before home treatment is attempted.
questions.rationale: A possible ingestion should not be managed by waiting for symptoms or guessing at a home treatment. Because the child is currently stable, the caregiver should call Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222 immediately, keep the product container available, provide the child's age and weight and known exposure details, and follow the poison expert's directions. Vomiting, activated charcoal, milk, food, or other decontamination should not be improvised. Collapse, seizure, trouble breathing, or inability to awaken would change the priority to calling 911 immediately.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must use the child's present stability to choose Poison Control before symptoms or home treatment while preserving the separate emergency boundary. This is level 2 triage application.

options.text: Call Poison Help at 1-800-222-1222 now, keep the bottle nearby, report the child's age, weight, timing, and possible amount, and follow the expert's directions.
options.reason: The child is stable but the product and dose still require immediate substance-specific assessment; the container and exposure details help the poison expert guide the next action.

options.text: Make the child vomit now, then call Poison Help only if tablets or pill fragments are seen in the vomit.
options.reason: Induced vomiting is not recommended and can cause harm. Poison Help should be contacted immediately rather than made conditional on what appears in vomit.

options.text: Give milk and an over-the-counter activated-charcoal product now, then call Poison Help after the home decontamination is complete.
options.reason: Milk and activated charcoal are not universal ingestion treatments. The caregiver should not improvise decontamination before receiving product-specific direction.

options.text: Observe the child at home until symptoms appear because calling before a symptom begins will not change the recommendation.
options.reason: Poison Help specifically advises not waiting for symptoms; early expert assessment uses the product, possible amount, timing, age, weight, and current condition.

refs.label: Week 6 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes — Poisoning prevention and treatment section.
Week 7 GI Instructor Notes — Injurious Agents/Poisons section.
ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11 — chapter 43, poisoning care and routine ipecac contraindication (verified supplied-text passage, printed p. 288; no original PDF review).
U.S. Health Resources and Services Administration Poison Help — What You Can Do (current page; no publication date shown).
National Capital Poison Center — First aid guidelines (current page; no publication date shown).

limitations: The fictional child is stable; collapse, seizure, trouble breathing, or inability to awaken requires immediate 911 activation.
No decontamination, dilution, antidote, observation interval, transport destination, or laboratory plan is prescribed.
The item does not assume the product contains iron or infer toxicity from an unknown dose.

questions.objective: Recognize a compatible pinworm pattern, collect the intended tape specimen correctly, and coordinate household treatment and hygiene to interrupt fecal-oral transmission.
questions.stem: A school-age child has intense perianal itching at night and restless sleep. A sibling now reports similar itching, and the clinician requests evaluation for pinworm infection. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Eggs are collected from the perianal skin before morning activities, and reinfection control involves the household rather than the symptomatic child alone.
questions.rationale: Nocturnal perianal itching is compatible with pinworm infection, which spreads by the fecal-oral route. CDC guidance directs the caregiver to press the sticky side of clear tape to the perianal skin first thing in the morning, before washing, toileting, or dressing, and repeat collection on three mornings. Handwashing, short clean nails, morning bathing, clean underwear, and careful hot laundering without shaking contaminated items reduce egg transfer. When infection is treated, the infected person, caregivers, and household members should follow the clinician-directed simultaneous treatment plan to limit reinfection. Stool culture is not the intended test, and household pets do not transmit human pinworms.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must reconcile the symptom timing with a precise current collection technique and then connect fecal-oral spread to household-wide control. This is level 2 application.

options.text: Press the sticky side of clear tape to the perianal skin first thing in the morning before bathing, toileting, or dressing, and repeat this on three mornings as directed.
options.reason: CDC's current collection method targets eggs on the perianal skin before morning activities remove or redistribute them and recommends three consecutive morning collections.

options.text: Wash hands with soap and warm water, keep fingernails short and clean, and discourage scratching and nail biting.
options.reason: These measures reduce transfer of eggs from the perianal area and contaminated surfaces to the mouth or other people.

options.text: Use morning bathing and clean underwear, and wash bedding, towels, and clothing in hot water without shaking them first.
options.reason: Morning hygiene removes eggs deposited overnight, while careful laundering limits redistribution of eggs into the household environment.

options.text: If pinworm infection is treated, have the infected child, caregivers, and household members follow the clinician's same-time treatment plan.
options.reason: Simultaneous clinician-directed treatment of the infected person, caregivers, and household members helps prevent repeated reinfection.

options.text: Collect a routine stool culture after the child has used the toilet because pinworm eggs are best recovered from the stool.
options.reason: The intended test is the perianal tape test before toileting or washing, not a routine stool culture.

options.text: Arrange treatment for household dogs and cats at the same time because pets commonly return human pinworms to children.
options.reason: Human pinworms do not come from household pets; treating pets would not address the fecal-oral household transmission route.

refs.label: Week 6 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes — communicable disease and intestinal parasite scope.
Week 7 GI Instructor Notes — Enterobiasis section; current CDC guidance controls specimen timing.
Week 7 GI Dysfunction lecture — Pinworms, slide 17.
ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11 — chapter 22, pinworm manifestations, fecal-oral spread, and tape testing (verified supplied-text passage, printed pp. 136–137; no original PDF review).
CDC — Diagnosing Pinworms (February 20, 2024).
CDC — Preventing Pinworm Infection (April 29, 2026).

limitations: Current CDC morning collection guidance supersedes the local notes' and supplied ATI text's bedtime placement technique.
The item does not diagnose the child from symptoms alone or select a medication, dose, contraindication, or repeat-dose schedule.
Household treatment is clinician-directed and conditional on the treatment plan; hygiene does not substitute for evaluation.

questions.objective: Teach age-appropriate brushing with fluoride toothpaste, bedtime-bottle avoidance, and current dental-home follow-up for a toddler.
questions.stem: At an 18-month well visit, a caregiver says, "I brush my child's teeth with water most nights, and a bottle of milk helps the child fall asleep. We have not seen a dentist yet." Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The toddler has erupted teeth, is younger than 3 years, and is already past the recommended time to establish a dental home.
questions.rationale: For a child younger than 3 years, the caregiver should brush erupted teeth twice daily with no more than a grain-of-rice-sized smear of fluoride toothpaste. Milk or juice should not remain in a bedtime bottle or be given after bedtime brushing; water is the safe drink if one is needed. A dental home should be established within 6 months after the first tooth erupts and no later than 12 months, so this toddler should be referred now. Follow-up intervals and systemic fluoride supplementation are individualized according to dental assessment, caries risk, total fluoride exposure, and the water supply rather than prescribed universally.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate toothpaste amount, caregiver technique, bedtime feeding risk, overdue dental-home timing, and individualized rather than automatic supplementation. This is level 2 application.

options.text: Brush twice daily with a grain-of-rice-sized smear of fluoride toothpaste, give only water after bedtime brushing, stop the milk bottle in bed, and establish a dental home now for individualized follow-up.
options.reason: This plan matches the child's age, reduces prolonged sugar exposure during sleep, and addresses the overdue dental home without imposing a universal recall or supplement plan.

options.text: Continue water-only brushing until the child can spit reliably, keep the bedtime milk for nutrition, and schedule the first dental visit when all primary teeth have erupted.
options.reason: A toddler younger than 3 can use a small smear of fluoride toothpaste with caregiver control; bedtime milk increases caries risk, and the dental visit is already overdue.

options.text: Use a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste once daily, replace bedtime milk with juice, and arrange dental care only if a visible cavity develops.
options.reason: A pea-sized amount is too much for this age, juice still exposes teeth to sugar, and preventive dental care should begin before visible disease appears.

options.text: Brush after the bedtime bottle, start a fluoride supplement for every toddler, and schedule dental cleaning every 6 months without assessing water fluoride or caries risk.
options.reason: Eliminating the bedtime bottle is preferable to retaining it, and supplements and recall intervals require individualized review rather than a universal plan.

limitations: The item does not prescribe a fluoride supplement or varnish schedule; total fluoride exposure, water source, caries risk, and professional assessment matter.
No universal six-month recall interval is keyed; the dental home individualizes follow-up.
The question addresses routine prevention and does not evaluate existing tooth decay, pain, trauma, or infection.

questions.objective: Prevent tick exposure, remove an attached tick correctly, and provide post-removal monitoring without treating exposure as a diagnosis.
questions.stem: The caregiver of a 7-year-old asks how to prevent tick bites during family hikes and what to do if an attached tick is found. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Prevention reduces exposure; prompt mechanical removal reduces attachment time; later symptoms—not the bite alone—guide reassessment.
questions.rationale: Current CDC guidance recommends EPA-registered repellents used according to the label, 0.5% permethrin on clothing and gear, avoidance of brush and tall grass when possible, and tick checks after outdoor exposure. An attached tick should be removed promptly with clean fine-tipped tweezers placed close to the skin and pulled with steady, even pressure without twisting. The bite area and hands are then cleaned. Petroleum jelly, heat, and nail polish can agitate the tick and should not be used. The caregiver should watch for rash or fever over the following days to weeks and report when and where the exposure occurred; a tick bite alone does not establish disease or justify automatic antibiotics.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must select a coherent before-exposure, removal, and after-care plan while rejecting two familiar but unsafe overreactions. This is level 2 application.

options.text: Use an EPA-registered repellent as directed and consider clothing and gear treated with 0.5% permethrin for tick exposure.
options.reason: Label-directed EPA-registered repellents and 0.5% permethrin-treated clothing or gear are CDC-supported exposure-reduction measures.

options.text: Stay near the center of trails when possible and perform a full-body tick check after returning from grassy, brushy, or wooded areas.
options.reason: Reducing contact with tick habitat and checking promptly after exposure can prevent attachment or shorten the time a tick remains attached.

options.text: Grasp an attached tick close to the skin with clean fine-tipped tweezers, pull with steady even pressure without twisting, then clean the hands and bite area.
options.reason: This is the recommended prompt removal technique and post-removal cleansing sequence.

options.text: Watch for rash or fever during the next several days to weeks and seek care if either develops, noting when and where the bite occurred.
options.reason: Later rash or fever warrants clinical evaluation with the exposure timeline and location; monitoring does not label the child with a tickborne disease.

options.text: Cover the tick with petroleum jelly or apply heat and wait for it to detach so that no mouthparts remain in the skin.
options.reason: CDC advises prompt mechanical removal and warns against petroleum jelly, heat, nail polish, or similar methods that can agitate the tick.

options.text: Begin leftover antibiotics after any tick bite because every attached tick transmits infection before it can be removed.
options.reason: Exposure does not establish infection, and antibiotics are not automatically indicated after every tick bite; individualized clinical assessment is required.
