Week 7 Children and Integumentary lecture — Lyme disease, slide 8.
ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11 — chapter 30, tick removal and cleansing (verified supplied-text passage, printed p. 197; no original PDF review).
CDC — Preventing Tick Bites (August 28, 2024).
CDC — What to Do After a Tick Bite (June 9, 2026).

limitations: The item does not diagnose Lyme disease or another tickborne illness from exposure alone.
No antibiotic prophylaxis or treatment product, dose, age cutoff, attachment-time threshold, or regional rule is supplied.
Repellents and permethrin products must be used according to their labels and child-specific restrictions.

questions.objective: Use symptom chronology together with migration, anorexia, localized tenderness, and movement-related pain to recognize concern for early appendicitis and initiate structured evaluation before perforation.
questions.stem: A 10-year-old reports abdominal pain that began near the umbilicus 10 hours ago, moved toward the right lower quadrant, and was followed several hours later by one episode of vomiting. The child has anorexia, low-grade fever, focal right-lower-quadrant tenderness, and pain with hopping. There is no sudden pain relief, generalized rigidity, or abdominal distention. Which interpretation and action are best?
questions.clue: Chronology contributes to the pattern, but pediatric appendicitis assessment depends on the full history, examination, and structured risk evaluation.
questions.rationale: Pain before vomiting can be part of a classic appendicitis history, but pediatric evidence shows that chronology alone has poor diagnostic performance. Here, migration toward the right lower quadrant, anorexia, focal tenderness, movement-related pain, fever, and vomiting after pain form a concerning preperforation cluster. The nurse should promptly notify the clinician, maintain NPO status under the acute-abdominal-pain pathway, and anticipate structured risk assessment, laboratory testing, and ultrasound or other imaging as clinically indicated. The absence of sudden relief followed by generalized pain, rigidity, or distention means the existing perforation-emergency pattern is not being retested; it does not make early appendicitis safe to dismiss.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate chronology with several historical and examination findings, avoid diagnosing from one clue, and act before a perforation pattern appears. This supports level 2.

options.text: Recognize a concerning early-appendicitis cluster, notify the clinician promptly, maintain NPO status per the acute-abdominal-pain pathway, and anticipate structured risk assessment, laboratory testing, and ultrasound as indicated.
options.reason: The combined migration, localized and movement-related pain, anorexia, fever, and vomiting chronology warrant prompt structured evaluation without declaring the diagnosis confirmed.

options.text: Classify the pattern as gastroenteritis because vomiting occurred, begin an oral-fluid challenge, and pursue appendicitis evaluation only if diarrhea does not develop.
options.reason: Vomiting does not establish gastroenteritis, and the localized migrating pain and examination findings require appendicitis evaluation before an oral challenge or discharge decision.

options.text: Continue observation without escalation until sudden pain relief is followed by generalized rigidity, because appendicitis requires a perforation pattern before evaluation is useful.
options.reason: Waiting for perforation signs delays evaluation of a concerning early pattern and increases risk; sudden relief followed by diffuse severe pain is a later emergency boundary.

options.text: Document confirmed nonperforated appendicitis from pain-before-vomiting chronology and request appendectomy without a full examination, risk assessment, laboratory testing, or imaging review.
options.reason: Chronology alone is not diagnostic in children, and definitive management follows integrated examination, risk assessment, testing, imaging, and surgical evaluation as indicated.

refs.label: Week 7 GI Instructor Notes — appendicitis symptom chronology, right-lower-quadrant findings, and perforation distinction.
Week 7 GI Dysfunction lecture — Appendicitis, slide 7.
ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11 — chapter 23, pediatric appendicitis assessment and care (verified supplied-text passage, printed pp. 145–146; no original PDF review).
Kitaoka et al. — Diagnostic performance of the classic symptom abdominal pain before vomiting for pediatric acute appendicitis (2024).
Children's Hospital of Philadelphia — Suspected Appendicitis Emergency Department Clinical Pathway (revised January 2026).

limitations: Pain-before-vomiting chronology is one clue and is not used alone to rule in or rule out appendicitis.
The item prompts structured evaluation but does not diagnose appendicitis or prescribe a specific laboratory, imaging, antibiotic, analgesic, or surgical regimen.
This is an early concern pattern and is distinct from sudden relief followed by generalized pain, rigidity, tachycardia, or other perforation findings.

questions.objective: Differentiate folic-acid prevention teaching from iron treatment and connect adequate folic acid to lower neural-tube-defect risk.
questions.stem: A patient taking prescribed oral iron for laboratory-confirmed iron-deficiency anemia is planning a pregnancy. The patient asks, “My iron tablet is enough to prevent defects of the baby's brain and spine, right?” Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: Iron and folic acid address different nutritional problems.
questions.rationale: Iron treats or prevents iron-deficiency anemia, whereas folic acid is the vitamin with evidence for reducing neural-tube-defect risk. Standard prevention teaching is to obtain 400 micrograms of folic acid daily before pregnancy and during early pregnancy from a vitamin or fortified food while also eating a balanced, folate-rich diet. A clinician may prescribe a different plan for a patient with specific high-risk factors.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner makes a direct teaching distinction between two commonly paired prenatal nutrients and connects folic acid to its prevention goal. This is level 1 application.

options.text: “Keep taking prescribed iron for anemia, and get 400 micrograms of folic acid daily before conception and during early pregnancy unless your clinician directs otherwise.”
options.reason: This keeps iron treatment and folic-acid prevention separate, provides the standard 400-microgram timing, and leaves individualized higher-risk dosing clinician-directed.

options.text: “Keep taking prescribed iron for anemia; because iron supports red-cell formation, count it toward the 400-microgram folic-acid goal when planning pregnancy.”
options.reason: Iron supports red-cell formation but cannot be counted toward a folic-acid amount or substituted for folic acid in neural-tube-defect prevention.

options.text: “Keep taking prescribed iron, and begin 400 micrograms of folic acid daily in the second trimester, when neural-tube prevention becomes relevant.”
options.reason: Neural-tube development occurs early, so prevention teaching starts before conception and continues in early pregnancy rather than beginning in the second trimester.

options.text: “Keep taking prescribed iron, and add 400 micrograms of folic acid daily if follow-up testing shows that the iron-deficiency anemia has not improved.”
options.reason: The folic-acid prevention plan is not contingent on the response to iron treatment; the two nutrients address distinct clinical goals.

refs.label: Week 4 High-Risk Pregnancy Instructor Notes — iron-deficiency and folic-acid-deficiency anemia.
CDC — Folic Acid: Facts for Clinicians (updated July 15, 2026).

limitations: The 400-microgram message is the standard prevention recommendation for people capable of pregnancy; higher-dose regimens for specific recurrence or medication risks remain clinician-directed.
The item does not replace individualized anemia evaluation or prenatal nutrition counseling.
The item does not claim that folic acid prevents every neural tube defect.

questions.objective: Distinguish low from excess amniotic fluid and connect an oligohydramnios pattern with its placental and growth context.
questions.stem: At 31 weeks, ultrasound shows a single deepest vertical pocket of amniotic fluid measuring 1.6 cm. Membranes are intact, both fetal kidneys and the bladder are visualized, estimated fetal weight is at the 6th percentile, and an umbilical-artery Doppler waveform is abnormal. Which interpretation and nursing plan are most appropriate?
questions.clue: The measured pocket is low, and the supplied growth and Doppler findings point toward the relevant context.
questions.rationale: A single deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm meets the supplied oligohydramnios criterion. With intact membranes, visualized urinary anatomy, fetal growth restriction, and an abnormal placental Doppler, uteroplacental insufficiency is an important context. The nurse should communicate the combined pattern and coordinate the prescribed high-risk surveillance or escalation rather than relabeling it as excess fluid or claiming one proven cause.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner integrates a quantitative fluid result with membrane, genitourinary, growth, and placental findings and avoids overclaiming causation. This is level 2 clinical interpretation.

options.text: Recognize oligohydramnios in a fetal-growth and placental context; report the combined findings and implement the prescribed enhanced surveillance plan.
options.reason: The pocket is below 2 cm, and the growth restriction plus abnormal Doppler support a placental-insufficiency context without proving one cause; the combined pattern requires coordinated follow-up.

options.text: Manage this as isolated oligohydramnios; report the fluid measurement and plan follow-up without incorporating the growth restriction or abnormal Doppler.
options.reason: The low fluid is not isolated: fetal growth restriction and an abnormal umbilical-artery Doppler materially change the risk context and surveillance plan.

options.text: Attribute the fluid and growth findings primarily to fetal urinary dysfunction; request renal-focused follow-up before escalating placental surveillance.
options.reason: Visualized kidneys and bladder do not support prioritizing a structural urinary explanation, while the abnormal Doppler and growth restriction require prompt placental-risk follow-through.

options.text: Document oligohydramnios and schedule routine fluid reassessment; treat the growth percentile and abnormal Doppler as secondary unless later fetal testing worsens.
options.reason: Deferring escalation underweights the concurrent fetal-growth and abnormal Doppler findings; those findings belong in the current high-risk surveillance decision.

refs.label: Week 4 High Risk Pregnancy lecture — amniotic abnormalities.
Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition — amniotic-fluid-volume assessment.
ACOG Committee Opinion No. 828 — Indications for Outpatient Antenatal Fetal Surveillance.

limitations: The item supplies ultrasound and Doppler findings and does not ask the learner to independently diagnose the underlying placental disorder.
No universal surveillance frequency, delivery threshold, or amnioinfusion decision is prescribed; those depend on the full maternal-fetal plan.
Chorioamnionitis escalation, post-rupture cord assessment, and intrapartum amnioinfusion safety remain outside this item.

questions.objective: Use chorion, amnion, and placental arrangement rather than zygosity alone to recognize a high-risk multifetal pregnancy.
questions.stem: At 12 weeks, an ultrasound report describes twins sharing one placenta and one amniotic sac. The referral note only says “identical twins.” Which nursing interpretation and follow-up are most appropriate?
questions.clue: Translate the shared placenta and shared sac into chorionicity and amnionicity before framing risk.
questions.rationale: Twins sharing one chorion/placenta and one amniotic sac are monochorionic-monoamniotic. This arrangement carries risks beyond the label “identical,” including shared-placenta complications and umbilical-cord complications within a shared sac. The nurse should preserve the ultrasound classification and coordinate individualized high-risk or maternal-fetal-medicine monitoring rather than using zygosity alone or selecting a birth route at 12 weeks.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must translate anatomic ultrasound information into the clinically meaningful risk arrangement and avoid relying on the less useful identical-twin label. This is level 2 interpretation.

options.text: Document monochorionic-monoamniotic twins and coordinate individualized maternal-fetal-medicine follow-up for complications related to shared placental circulation and a shared sac.
options.reason: One shared placenta/chorion and one shared amniotic sac define the monochorionic-monoamniotic arrangement, which needs risk-focused specialist monitoring.

options.text: Document monochorionic-diamniotic twins because the shared placenta establishes monochorionicity; plan surveillance as though each fetus has a separate sac.
options.reason: The report describes one shared sac, so diamniotic classification is incorrect and would omit the added shared-sac and cord-risk context.

options.text: Retain the identical-twin label while deferring chorion and amnion documentation; use standard twin follow-up until a complication appears.
options.reason: Zygosity does not replace arrangement-based classification; chorionicity and amnionicity affect risk framing and surveillance before a complication appears.

options.text: Document monochorionic-monoamniotic twins, but use routine dichorionic-twin monitoring unless cord entanglement or growth discordance is later identified.
options.reason: The classification is correct, but waiting for a complication before risk-focused monitoring underestimates shared-placenta and shared-sac risks.

refs.label: Week 4 High Risk Pregnancy lecture — multiple-gestation placentation and amnion diagram.
ACOG — Multiple Pregnancy (reviewed May 2025).
SMFM — Updated Checklists for Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy (2026).

limitations: The item tests arrangement-based risk recognition and referral continuity, not a fixed ultrasound, admission, birth-timing, or birth-route protocol.
The supplied one-placenta/one-sac report is assumed to be a qualified ultrasound determination.
Intrapartum reassessment of the second twin is outside this prenatal item.

questions.objective: Provide current U.S. shared-decision infant-feeding counseling for a patient with sustained HIV viral suppression on ART.
questions.stem: A U.S. patient at 36 weeks has taken antiretroviral therapy consistently, and every HIV RNA result for the past 4 months has been below 50 copies/mL. The patient asks whether breastfeeding can be considered. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
questions.clue: Separate the zero postnatal-transmission options from the less-than-1%-but-not-zero option, then preserve coordinated follow-up.
questions.rationale: Current NIH guidance recommends patient-centered counseling about formula, banked pasteurized donor milk, and breastfeeding when ART has been taken consistently and HIV RNA has remained below 50 copies/mL for at least 3 months before delivery. Formula or banked donor milk eliminates postnatal transmission through breastfeeding. With sustained suppression, breastfeeding transmission risk is less than 1% but not zero, and a breastfeeding plan requires coordinated maternal viral-load monitoring and infant prophylaxis/testing follow-up.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must replace an outdated categorical rule with a population-specific risk comparison and shared-decision follow-up plan without claiming zero risk. This is level 2 current-guidance application.

options.text: “Formula or banked pasteurized donor milk eliminates breastfeeding transmission. With sustained suppression, breastfeeding has a less-than-1% but nonzero risk and requires shared decision-making plus maternal-infant follow-up.”
options.reason: This accurately compares the feeding risks for the supplied suppressed population, supports shared decision-making, and preserves coordinated maternal and infant follow-up.

options.text: “Breastfeeding with sustained suppression can be supported; emphasize its benefits and continue the same routine maternal and infant follow-up planned for a patient using formula or banked donor milk.”
options.reason: Support is appropriate, but counseling must also state that risk is less than 1% rather than absent and arrange the additional maternal and infant follow-up required for breastfeeding.

options.text: “Because formula or banked pasteurized donor milk eliminates breastfeeding transmission, recommend replacement feeding first and defer discussing breastfeeding despite sustained suppression unless the patient declines both.”
options.reason: Replacement feeding does eliminate breastfeeding transmission, but withholding a balanced discussion is not the patient-centered shared decision-making recommended for this suppressed population.

options.text: “Discuss the less-than-1% breastfeeding risk and support either choice; begin added maternal viral-load and infant follow-up after HIV RNA becomes detectable or adherence concerns appear.”
options.reason: The risk statement is accurate, but a breastfeeding plan requires coordinated monitoring and infant follow-up from the outset, not only after viremia appears.

refs.label: Week 4 High-Risk Pregnancy Instructor Notes — HIV section (categorical feeding wording reconciled with current NIH guidance).
NIH ClinicalInfo — Preventing HIV Transmission During Infant Feeding (updated and reviewed June 25, 2026).

limitations: The counseling applies only to the supplied U.S. patient taking ART consistently with HIV RNA below 50 copies/mL for at least 3 months before delivery.
The item does not prescribe a fixed viral-load interval, maternal ART regimen, infant prophylaxis regimen, or infant testing schedule; those require the coordinated HIV-obstetric-pediatric plan.

If ART is not taken or suppression is not maintained, replacement-feeding recommendations differ; detectable HIV RNA during breastfeeding requires prompt team reassessment and temporary cessation or discontinuation according to current guidance.

questions.objective: Coordinate time-sensitive varicella exposure management for a susceptible pregnant patient while deferring live vaccination until postpartum.
questions.stem: At 18 weeks, a patient reports that the patient's child was diagnosed with chickenpox yesterday after several days of close household contact. Prenatal records show negative varicella IgG and no documented vaccination. The patient has no rash or fever. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Apply pregnancy-specific timing and nursing scope to each proposed action.
questions.rationale: Live varicella vaccine is contraindicated during pregnancy. A pregnant patient without evidence of immunity who has a significant exposure should be referred promptly for clinician or public-health evaluation of postexposure prophylaxis; when eligibility criteria are met, prescribed VariZIG is most useful when given as soon as possible. The nurse should not independently select or administer immune globulin. If the patient remains susceptible after pregnancy, postpartum varicella vaccination should be planned, and breastfeeding does not require delaying it.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate documented susceptibility, time-sensitive postexposure coordination, live-vaccine timing, and a staged postpartum series while rejecting plausible delayed or compressed follow-through. This is level 2 application.

options.text: Notify the obstetric clinician today and activate exposure follow-up so VariZIG eligibility can be evaluated and any prescribed dose given promptly.
options.reason: The patient lacks evidence of immunity and has a significant exposure during pregnancy. Prompt clinician or public-health evaluation preserves the window for provider-directed postexposure prophylaxis.

options.text: Withhold live varicella vaccine during pregnancy.
options.reason: Varicella vaccine is a live vaccine and is contraindicated during pregnancy.

options.text: Document a postpartum varicella vaccination plan if susceptibility remains, with follow-up for the second dose.
options.reason: A susceptible postpartum patient should receive the two-dose varicella series; vaccination can begin before discharge and is compatible with breastfeeding.

options.text: Schedule repeat varicella IgG at the next prenatal visit before deciding whether postexposure evaluation is needed.
options.reason: The record already documents susceptibility and a significant exposure. Repeating the titer at a routine visit would delay the time-sensitive evaluation for provider-directed prophylaxis.

options.text: Plan both varicella vaccine doses during the birth hospitalization so postpartum prevention is complete before discharge.
options.reason: The first dose can be given after delivery before discharge, but the second is given 4 to 8 weeks later; compressing both into the birth hospitalization is not appropriate.

refs.label: Week 4 High-Risk Pregnancy Instructor Notes — varicella-zoster heading.
Maternal Child Nursing Care, seventh edition — prenatal immunity assessment and postpartum varicella vaccination.
CDC — Clinical Guidance for People at Risk for Severe Varicella (April 24, 2024).
CDC — Varicella Vaccination for Specific Groups (June 26, 2024).

limitations: The case supplies negative varicella IgG, no documented vaccination, and significant household exposure; it does not define every evidence-of-immunity or exposure criterion.
The nurse coordinates prompt evaluation and order verification but does not independently prescribe VariZIG, select a dose, or choose antiviral therapy.
The item does not teach a congenital-varicella anomaly list or management of active maternal varicella disease.

questions.objective: Ensure timely execution of the prescribed infant ARV plan after documented perinatal HIV exposure
questions.stem: A newborn with documented in-utero HIV exposure is 3 hours old. The maternal HIV RNA and treatment history are already available in the chart, but the pediatric HIV plan says "awaiting final orders," and no infant antiretroviral medication has been prescribed. The newborn is stable. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.clue: Compare plans that all communicate or gather useful information; choose the sequence that protects the near-birth treatment goal without constructing the regimen.
questions.rationale: Newborns with in-utero or intrapartum HIV exposure should receive an appropriate clinician-selected antiretroviral plan as close to birth as possible, preferably within 6 hours. Maternal HIV RNA and treatment history inform risk-based regimen selection, so the nurse should actively contact the neonatal or pediatric HIV clinician about the missing order, direct the team to the available history, and coordinate medication access. A routine consult queue, pharmacy-first regimen framing, sequential obstetric-first escalation, or postponing the maternal risk data until after a first dose can all delay or misdirect the exposure-specific plan.
questions.difficultyReason: Every alternative communicates with a relevant service or advances part of the workflow. The learner must distinguish the correct immediate clinician, risk-information, and pharmacy sequence without selecting the regimen, supporting level 2.

options.text: Contact the neonatal or pediatric HIV clinician now about the missing order, direct the team to the available maternal history, and coordinate prompt pharmacy access.
options.reason: This actively resolves the missing exposure-specific order, supplies the maternal risk information needed for clinician selection, and supports timely access without the nurse choosing the regimen.

options.text: Send the maternal history through the routine pediatric HIV consult queue and continue newborn monitoring while awaiting the consultant's response.
options.reason: The information and consult are relevant, but a routine queue does not actively resolve a time-sensitive missing order when initiation is preferred near birth.

options.text: Ask pharmacy to identify an available standard prophylaxis option first, then contact the neonatal clinician with that option for authorization.
options.reason: Pharmacy coordination is useful, but medication availability should not drive regimen selection before the clinician applies the maternal RNA and treatment history to the infant's risk.

options.text: Escalate the missing order to the obstetric team first because maternal HIV RNA determines risk, then involve pediatric HIV if the order remains unresolved.
options.reason: The obstetric team may clarify maternal history, but the missing newborn order requires direct neonatal or pediatric HIV escalation rather than a sequential detour through maternal care.

options.text: Contact the neonatal clinician and pharmacy now, but route the maternal RNA and treatment history after the first dose so medication access is not delayed.
options.reason: Prompt contact is appropriate, but maternal RNA and treatment history inform the exposure-specific regimen and should guide the order before the first dose rather than follow it.

refs.label: Week 5 High-Risk Newborn Instructor Notes — TORCH complex and HIV course scope.
Maternal Child Nursing Care, 7th ed. — Table 25.5, Human Immunodeficiency Virus, printed p. 2031.
NIH ClinicalInfo — Antiretroviral Management of Infants With In Utero, Intrapartum, or Breastfeeding Exposure to HIV; Panel's Recommendations (updated and reviewed June 25, 2026).

limitations: The exposure, age, chart status, and missing order are fictional case facts; they do not define a universal regimen.
The 6-hour language is a preferred initiation goal, not a claim that later initiation has no benefit.
The item does not select an ARV drug, dose, duration, risk category, diagnostic test, testing schedule, or feeding plan.
The maternal RNA and treatment history are already present, so the key tests postbirth order execution rather than prenatal handoff or feeding counseling.

questions.objective: Recognize symptomatic congenital syphilis concern and activate evaluation and treatment before discharge
questions.stem: A newborn whose mother had reactive nontreponemal and treponemal syphilis tests at delivery has copious nasal discharge, a diffuse maculopapular rash, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly. The newborn RPR is 1:8 and the maternal delivery RPR is 1:16 using the same test and laboratory. Discharge was planned for later today. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Decide how the abnormal examination and lower paired titer should be weighted and sequenced in the immediate plan.
questions.rationale: Congenital-syphilis decisions use maternal infection and treatment, the newborn examination, and paired nontreponemal titers together. Rhinitis, rash, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly form an abnormal examination compatible with congenital syphilis, so a lower newborn RPR does not justify downgrading or postponing the response. The nurse should promptly report the integrated pattern, pause routine discharge, and prepare to implement and monitor the clinician-selected evaluation and penicillin-treatment pathway. Repeating titers, separating the organ findings into parallel consults, or leading the handoff with the lower titer should not precede or dilute that unified escalation.
questions.difficultyReason: The false choices all use clinically relevant data or consultations. The learner must integrate the abnormal examination with paired titers and distinguish immediate unified escalation from plausible but missequenced assessment plans, supporting level 2.

options.text: Report the findings immediately and pause routine discharge so the neonatal team can complete a congenital-syphilis evaluation and treatment plan.
options.reason: The maternal history plus compatible rhinitis, rash, jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly requires prompt unified evaluation before discharge despite the lower newborn titer.

options.text: Prepare to implement and monitor the prescribed penicillin-based pathway once the neonatal team has selected the evaluation and treatment plan.
options.reason: The abnormal examination supports urgent entry into the clinician-directed evaluation and penicillin-treatment pathway; the nurse prepares and monitors care without selecting it.

options.text: Lead the clinician handoff with the lower newborn RPR and ask the team to classify titer risk before emphasizing the physical findings.
options.reason: The paired titers belong in the handoff, but an abnormal compatible examination independently drives urgent concern; leading with the lower titer can inappropriately downgrade the symptomatic branch.

options.text: Keep the newborn for observation and request repeat paired titers before activating the congenital-syphilis evaluation and penicillin pathway.
options.reason: Inpatient observation is safer than discharge, but repeat titers are not a prerequisite when the current examination is compatible with congenital syphilis.

options.text: Escalate jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly through a hepatic consult and rhinitis and rash through an infection consult, then reconcile the plans after initial results.
options.reason: Those consultations may contribute, but splitting a coherent maternal-infection and multisystem pattern can delay the unified congenital-syphilis evaluation and treatment plan.

refs.label: Week 5 High-Risk Newborn Instructor Notes — TORCH complex and referral to Table 25.5.
Maternal Child Nursing Care, 7th ed. — Table 25.5, Congenital Syphilis, printed pp. 2030 and 2034.
CDC — Congenital Syphilis, STI Treatment Guidelines: Evaluation and Treatment of Neonates and Scenario 1 (page last reviewed July 22, 2021; rechecked September 17, 2026).

limitations: The maternal tests, paired RPR values, examination findings, and discharge plan are fictional case facts.
The item raises urgent concern but does not authorize the nurse to confirm congenital syphilis independently.
No full scenario algorithm, cerebrospinal-fluid or imaging panel, penicillin formulation, dose, route, duration, or follow-up schedule is selected.
The item tests the symptomatic newborn branch and does not retest maternal penicillin desensitization or the less-than-30-day maternal-treatment chronology in a normal-appearing newborn.

questions.objective: Apply current Zika travel, mosquito, sexual-transmission, testing, and pregnancy follow-up guidance after possible exposure.
questions.stem: A patient at 12 weeks of pregnancy and the patient's male partner returned yesterday from a location with an active CDC Zika Travel Health Notice. Neither has symptoms. Which teaching should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Possible exposure during pregnancy requires current risk-based prevention and clinical review even when no symptoms are present; testing does not clear sexual-transmission risk.
questions.rationale: Current CDC guidance uses the destination's active travel notice and risk classification rather than a permanent country list. The patient should contact the prenatal clinician with the exact itinerary so exposure and testing can be considered; testing is not automatic solely because an asymptomatic pregnant traveler was exposed. Both travelers should prevent mosquito bites for 3 weeks after return. Because the male partner also had possible exposure during the pregnancy, condoms or abstinence should be used for the rest of the pregnancy. If the clinical team determines that infection is confirmed or possible, serial fetal ultrasound assessment may be considered to monitor neuroanatomy and growth. A negative blood test does not establish that sexual transmission is impossible, and asymptomatic infection can still affect a fetus.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must coordinate four related actions while distinguishing risk-based testing from prevention and avoiding obsolete geography or a falsely reassuring negative-test rule.

options.text: Contact the prenatal clinician now with the exact itinerary so the current exposure and need for testing can be assessed individually.
options.reason: Asymptomatic exposure does not trigger universal testing, but pregnancy and an active travel notice warrant prompt clinician review using current exposure details.

options.text: Use an EPA-registered insect repellent and continue mosquito-bite precautions for 3 weeks after returning.
options.reason: CDC advises travelers returning from an active-notice or current/past-transmission area to prevent mosquito bites for 3 weeks; labeled EPA-registered repellents are appropriate during pregnancy.

options.text: Use condoms consistently or abstain from sex for the remainder of the pregnancy because the partner also had possible exposure.
options.reason: Sexual transmission can occur without symptoms, and pregnancy-specific prevention continues throughout the pregnancy when a partner may have been exposed.

options.text: If infection is considered confirmed or possible, expect the prenatal team to consider serial fetal ultrasound assessment of anatomy and growth.
options.reason: Possible or confirmed infection during pregnancy can prompt serial ultrasound surveillance focused on fetal anatomy, neuroanatomy, and growth.

options.text: A single negative blood test means condoms and other sexual precautions can be stopped immediately.
options.reason: Testing is not recommended to determine sexual-transmission risk because a negative result can be falsely reassuring and does not establish absence of virus in genital secretions.

options.text: Wait for fever or rash before notifying the prenatal team because infection without symptoms cannot affect the fetus.
options.reason: Many infections are asymptomatic, and pregnancy exposure still merits prevention and risk review because fetal effects can occur.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — Zika.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Recommendations for Travelers and People Living Abroad (August 7, 2026).
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — Clinical Considerations for Pregnant Women with Possible Zika Virus Infection (January 31, 2025).

limitations: The item anchors geography to an active CDC Zika Travel Health Notice and does not preserve a fixed destination list.
It tests prevention and escalation, not a laboratory algorithm, diagnosis, medication regimen, or guarantee of fetal outcome.
Serial fetal ultrasound is framed as a clinician-directed consideration only after infection is determined to be confirmed or possible.

questions.objective: Counsel about IVF embryo-transfer multiple-gestation risk and preserve specialist-directed individualization around a singleton goal.
questions.stem: A 31-year-old patient with a favorable prognosis is preparing for a first IVF embryo transfer and has several good-quality embryos available. The patient asks, "Would transferring two embryos improve the chance of success enough to outweigh the risk?" The fertility specialist has not finalized the transfer plan. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: More embryos can increase multiple-gestation risk, but the exact transfer plan belongs to an individualized specialist-patient decision.
questions.rationale: Transferring more than one embryo increases the risk of twin or higher-order multiple gestation. Infertility care aims for one healthy child at a time, and single-embryo transfer is an important risk-reduction strategy in favorable-prognosis cycles. The nurse should support a singleton-gestation goal and explain that the fertility specialist and patient individualize the plan using age, prognosis, embryo characteristics, medical context, prior treatment information, and preferences. The nurse should not prescribe a fixed embryo number, promise success, or defer risk counseling until pregnancy occurs.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must balance the patient's success concern with multiple-gestation risk, a singleton goal, and specialist-directed individualization rather than applying a universal embryo number.

options.text: More embryos raise multiple-gestation risk. Support a singleton goal and have the specialist individualize the plan using prognosis, embryo features, medical context, and preferences.
options.reason: This directly addresses the risk, supports one healthy child at a time, and preserves individualized specialist-patient decision-making.

options.text: Age and embryo features guide the plan; with favorable embryos, transferring two is the usual way to improve success, and multiple-gestation risk can be managed after implantation.
options.reason: Favorable prognosis supports careful risk reduction, not a default transfer of two or postponement of multiple-gestation counseling.

options.text: A singleton goal means exactly one embryo should be transferred in every IVF cycle; the specialist only needs to individualize the plan when no favorable embryo is available.
options.reason: Single-embryo transfer is an important strategy, but the nurse should not turn it into a universal rule or limit specialist individualization.

options.text: Transferring more embryos does not materially change multiple-gestation risk; the plan should emphasize the preferred pregnancy chance and defer risk counseling until pregnancy occurs.
options.reason: Embryo number is a major modifiable multiple-gestation risk, so counseling must occur before transfer rather than after implantation.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — Assisted reproductive therapies and nursing counseling/referral.
American Society for Reproductive Medicine and Society for Assisted Reproductive Technology — Guidance on the Limits to the Number of Embryos to Transfer (2021).
American Society for Reproductive Medicine — Multiple Gestation Associated with Infertility Therapy: A Committee Opinion (2022).

limitations: The favorable-prognosis facts are supplied for counseling context; the nurse does not prescribe the embryo number or guarantee implantation, live birth, or singleton pregnancy.
The item is limited to IVF embryo-transfer counseling and does not compare all ART modalities, infer ICSI from an image, or test medication toxicity or ovarian hyperstimulation.
Exact transfer limits depend on specialist assessment of age, prognosis, embryo characteristics, medical context, treatment history, and patient preferences.

questions.objective: Continue contraception during perimenopause and select a medically eligible pathway around migraine with aura, bleeding goals, and patient preference.
questions.stem: A 49-year-old patient has menstrual periods every 2 to 4 months and wants to avoid pregnancy. The patient has migraine with aura and asks for a combined estrogen-progestin pill to make bleeding more predictable. Which plan by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: Irregular cycles do not prove fertility has ended, age alone is not a universal contraindication, and migraine with aura specifically changes estrogen eligibility.
questions.rationale: Pregnancy remains possible during perimenopause, and contraception is still needed for a patient older than 44 who wants to avoid pregnancy. Irregular cycles or a single follicle-stimulating hormone result do not reliably prove definitive loss of fertility. Age alone does not exclude all intrauterine or hormonal methods, but migraine with aura makes combined hormonal contraception an unacceptable health risk under the 2024 U.S. MEC. The nurse should coordinate selection of a medically eligible non-estrogen option while incorporating bleeding goals, reversibility, and patient preference instead of imposing sterilization or a universal cutoff age.
questions.difficultyReason: The similarly complete plans require the learner to integrate ongoing fertility, the migraine-with-aura eligibility rule, bleeding goals, and patient preference without relying on option length or categorical wording.

options.text: Continue contraception; avoid combined hormonal methods because of migraine with aura, then compare eligible non-estrogen choices by bleeding goals and preference.
options.reason: This preserves contraception during ongoing pregnancy risk, applies the specific estrogen contraindication, and keeps method selection person-centered.

options.text: Continue contraception; use the requested combined pill because irregular cycles lower pregnancy risk, then reassess bleeding and migraine symptoms after three months.
options.reason: Irregular cycles do not end pregnancy risk, and migraine with aura makes combined hormonal contraception an unacceptable risk rather than a trial option.

options.text: Continue contraception; exclude every hormonal method because of migraine with aura, then compare only a copper IUD and permanent contraception by bleeding goals.
options.reason: Migraine with aura excludes combined hormonal methods, not every hormonal option; this plan unnecessarily narrows eligible person-centered choices.

options.text: Continue contraception; select a non-estrogen method solely for predictable bleeding, then address ongoing pregnancy risk and the patient's preferences at a later visit.
options.reason: Eligibility, continuing pregnancy risk, bleeding goals, and patient preference should be integrated in the current shared decision rather than separated.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — Perimenopausal contraception.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — When Contraceptive Protection Is No Longer Needed (November 19, 2024).
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, 2024: Summary of Classifications.

limitations: The item does not assign a universal age at which contraception must stop or use one FSH value to define infertility.
It identifies a combined-hormonal contraindication but does not select a specific non-estrogen method without fuller history and shared decision-making.
Irregular bleeding is framed as a perimenopausal pattern in the case; new heavy, persistent, or otherwise concerning bleeding would require separate evaluation.

questions.objective: Recognize a post-abortion hemorrhage pattern and direct immediate evaluation without inferring a cause or prescribing additional treatment.
questions.stem: Two days after a medication abortion, a patient calls the clinic and reports soaking more than two full-size pads each hour for the past 2 hours, worsening pelvic pain, and dizziness when standing. Which response by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: The bleeding exceeds a current aftercare danger threshold and is accompanied by worsening pain and a symptom of possible hemodynamic compromise.
questions.rationale: Heavy vaginal bleeding that soaks more than two pads per hour for two consecutive hours is a post-abortion danger sign. Worsening pelvic pain and orthostatic dizziness add urgency. The nurse should direct immediate in-person emergency evaluation and advise the patient not to drive. The cause could include hemorrhage, retained tissue, ectopic pregnancy, or another complication, but the phone findings do not establish which one. Waiting for a scheduled visit, recommending self-treatment, or prescribing another medication dose delays assessment. Fever, chills, foul-smelling discharge, or increasing abdominal or pelvic pain are additional infection or complication red flags that also require prompt evaluation.
questions.difficultyReason: The full bleeding threshold, worsening pain, and dizziness make immediate emergency escalation a foundational recognition decision; comparable alternatives test unsafe delay without adding an artificial level-2 discriminator.

options.text: Arrange immediate emergency evaluation, tell the patient not to drive because of dizziness, and activate emergency transport if a safe ride is unavailable.
options.reason: The threshold-level bleeding, worsening pain, and dizziness require immediate in-person assessment with safe transport.

options.text: Arrange an urgent same-day visit with the abortion provider, have another adult drive, and use emergency care only if another hour of heavy bleeding occurs.
options.reason: The current findings already meet an emergency threshold; adding another hour of observation could delay assessment of significant bleeding.

options.text: Have the patient lie down, drink fluids, track bleeding for one more hour, and then call the abortion provider if the dizziness or pain continues.
options.reason: Supportive measures do not make home observation appropriate when heavy bleeding is already accompanied by worsening pain and dizziness.

options.text: Use prescribed medicines only as directed, arrange evaluation the next morning with a support person, and seek emergency care sooner only if fainting occurs.
options.reason: Waiting until morning or until syncope occurs under-triages the present bleeding threshold and orthostatic symptoms.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — Elective abortion complications and follow-up.
ATI RN Maternal Newborn Nursing — Chapter 7, Bleeding During Pregnancy: post-abortion client education.
World Health Organization — Clinical Practice Handbook for Quality Abortion Care (June 15, 2023).

limitations: The item tests complication triage after medication abortion and does not test a medication regimen, gestational-age cutoff, or legal rule.
The scenario supports immediate evaluation but not a definitive diagnosis of hemorrhage source, retained tissue, infection, or ectopic pregnancy.
The WHO bleeding threshold is used as a danger sign, not as permission to delay care when other severe symptoms are present below that threshold.

questions.objective: Distinguish fibrocystic and fibroadenoma teaching patterns in already evaluated cases without treating either pattern as a diagnosis.
questions.stem: During follow-up teaching, the nurse reviews two patients whose breast findings have already received clinician examination and age-appropriate imaging. Patient A has diffuse bilateral tenderness and lumpiness that worsens before menses and improves afterward. Patient B has a discrete, firm, round, mobile, usually painless mass. Which explanation by the nurse is best?
questions.clue: Compare the two benign teaching patterns while preserving that examination and imaging—not palpation words alone—guide diagnosis and follow-up.
questions.rationale: Diffuse or bilateral lumpiness and tenderness that varies with the menstrual cycle is compatible with a fibrocystic-change pattern. A discrete firm or hard, round, mobile, usually painless mass is compatible with a fibroadenoma pattern. These descriptions help organize teaching but do not establish a diagnosis. Both patients should continue the clinician-directed plan, and any new, persistent, or changing finding still warrants reassessment based on age, risk, examination, and prior results.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must compare timing, distribution, texture, mobility, and pain across two already evaluated cases while rejecting both pattern reversal and diagnostic certainty.

options.text: A is compatible with fibrocystic change and B with fibroadenoma; neither pattern is a diagnosis, so both patients should continue the clinician-directed follow-up plan.
options.reason: This accurately distinguishes the two teaching patterns while preserving the role of completed evaluation and ongoing clinician-directed follow-up.

options.text: A is compatible with fibroadenoma and B with fibrocystic change; the cyclic and mobile findings establish which benign diagnosis is present, so follow-up can end.
options.reason: The patterns are reversed, and neither cyclic timing nor mobility alone establishes a diagnosis or ends follow-up.

options.text: Both patients are most compatible with fibroadenoma because benign masses can vary with the cycle; completed imaging means later pattern changes need no reassessment.
options.reason: Fibroadenoma is typically a discrete mass rather than diffuse cyclic lumpiness, and later changes still require clinician-directed reassessment.

options.text: A and B should both be described only as nonspecific masses; benign teaching patterns should not be discussed unless a biopsy proves one diagnosis and excludes every alternative.
options.reason: The patterns can guide bounded patient teaching after evaluation even though they are not diagnostic and do not replace follow-up.

refs.label: Week 6 GYN, Infertility, and STI Instructor Notes — Benign breast disorders.
Week 6 GYN, STIs, and Infertility Lecture — Fibrocystic changes and fibroadenoma.
National Cancer Institute — Benign and Precancerous Breast Lumps and Conditions (updated December 2, 2025).
American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists — Benign Breast Conditions.

limitations: The stem explicitly places both patients after clinician examination and age-appropriate imaging; the item tests pattern comparison rather than generic new-lump escalation.
Neither fibrocystic change nor fibroadenoma is diagnosed from timing or palpation features alone, and the item does not claim that a benign pattern excludes malignancy.
No universal imaging, biopsy, surveillance, or treatment sequence is prescribed; later new, persistent, or changing findings remain clinician-directed.

questions.objective: Integrate social-emotional, language, cognitive, and motor observations across time to identify a materially discordant developmental domain and initiate screening and evaluation rather than relying on one isolated milestone.
questions.stem: At a 4-year well visit, the nurse reviews a child's trajectory. Over the past year, the child has progressed from short phrases to telling stories in sentences, names several colors, draws a person with multiple body parts, and joins other children in pretend play. The caregiver reports that the child still cannot walk independently and moves by holding furniture or crawling. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's next action?
questions.clue: Compare the direction of progress across several domains and judge whether one domain is merely variable or markedly out of step with the rest of the trajectory.
questions.rationale: Development is monitored across social-emotional, language, cognitive, and motor domains and over time. This child shows ongoing gains in language, cognition, and social participation, but the absence of independent walking at age 4 is a marked gross-motor discordance, not a small variation within an otherwise even trajectory. The nurse should document the pattern, discuss it with the caregiver and clinician, complete or arrange standardized developmental screening, and facilitate timely evaluation. Milestone surveillance does not diagnose a cause, but it should not be replaced by reassurance or watchful waiting when a major concern is present.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must synthesize several age-linked observations, preserve evidence of strengths, and isolate a materially discordant motor trajectory without labeling the whole child globally delayed or diagnosing an etiology. This supports level 2.

options.text: Recognize a marked gross-motor discordance despite progress in other domains, document the trajectory, and arrange standardized developmental screening and timely evaluation.
options.reason: The child's language, cognitive, and social skills are progressing, but lack of independent walking is substantially out of step; surveillance should trigger screening and evaluation without assigning a diagnosis.

options.text: Document the motor concern and repeat developmental surveillance in 6 months, reserving standardized screening for lack of progress in another domain.
options.reason: Surveillance documents the concern, but a marked motor discordance warrants standardized screening and timely evaluation now rather than waiting for another domain to stall.

options.text: Describe global developmental delay and refer for broad services now, leaving standardized screening to the referral team despite the otherwise uneven pattern.
options.reason: Referral is timely, but the documented strengths do not support a global label; standardized screening and evaluation should clarify the specific discordant trajectory.

options.text: Refer for physical therapy for walking and continue routine developmental surveillance, treating the motor referral as sufficient before broader screening or diagnostic evaluation.
options.reason: Physical therapy may become part of care, but a therapy referral alone does not replace standardized screening and evaluation of the child's full developmental trajectory.

refs.label: Week 6 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes — developmental milestones and age-linked multidomain tables.
CDC — Milestones by 4 Years (May 15, 2026).
CDC — About Learn the Signs. Act Early. (February 16, 2026).

limitations: The milestone pattern prompts screening and evaluation but does not diagnose a neurologic, genetic, orthopedic, or environmental cause.
The item intentionally uses several domains and a longitudinal trajectory; it is not a request to memorize one complete milestone table.
Milestone surveillance and a checklist do not replace a validated screening tool or individualized clinical assessment.

questions.objective: Use respectful, nonstigmatizing assessment and collaborative nutrition and activity planning when body-image concerns or teasing threaten an adolescent's healthy participation.
questions.stem: A 14-year-old says, “Some teammates joke about my body. I want to skip lunch and quit every activity until I lose weight.” The adolescent denies dizziness, vomiting, laxative use, or self-harm. Which nursing response best supports healthy nutrition, activity, and body image?
questions.clue: Protect health and participation while addressing the stigma and potentially restrictive plan rather than centering the conversation on appearance or a target number.
questions.rationale: Weight-based teasing can worsen body image, reduce physical activity, and contribute to unhealthy eating behaviors. The nurse should respond privately with respectful, nonstigmatizing language; assess the teasing, emotional impact, safety, and emerging disordered-eating behaviors; and involve the adolescent in a plan for regular balanced meals and enjoyable, safe movement. The plan can include addressing bullying and identifying an activity setting where the adolescent feels supported. Public weigh-ins, punitive exercise, meal skipping, appearance-based praise, and unsupervised calorie restriction can deepen stigma and risk rather than promote sustainable health.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must integrate nutrition, activity, peer context, and body image while avoiding both restrictive dieting and forced sport participation. This is an applied level-2 counseling decision.

options.text: Acknowledge the teasing, assess mood and restrictive eating, and collaborate on regular balanced meals plus enjoyable activity in a safe, supportive setting.
options.reason: This response addresses stigma and emerging restriction while preserving nutrition, autonomy, and access to positive movement rather than making appearance the treatment target.

options.text: Address the teasing and maintain regular meals, but pause current sports and active hobbies until a weight-focused follow-up visit.
options.reason: Regular meals and attention to teasing help, but unnecessarily removing enjoyable movement may deepen disengagement and still centers care on weight.

options.text: Assess restrictive eating, mood, and safety, then set a scale-based weight target before helping the adolescent choose a more supportive activity setting.
options.reason: The assessment is useful, but making a scale target the organizing goal can reinforce stigma and postpones collaborative nutrition and participation planning.

options.text: Help the adolescent move to a supportive activity setting and address the teasing, but defer eating-behavior assessment unless physical symptoms appear.
options.reason: A safer activity setting and response to teasing are helpful, but stated meal restriction requires assessment now even when physical symptoms are absent.

refs.label: Week 6 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes — adolescent nutrition, fitness, sleep, emotional well-being, peers, and appearance.
ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11 — adolescent body image, nutrition, and physical activity passages (verified supplied text; no original PDF review).
American Academy of Pediatrics — The Role of the Pediatrician in the Promotion of Healthy, Active Living (March 2024).
American Academy of Pediatrics — Stigma Experienced by Children and Adolescents With Obesity (December 2017).

limitations: The fictional screening statements do not exclude an eating disorder, depression, or escalating bullying; further assessment and follow-up remain necessary.
No calorie prescription, weight-loss target, BMI diagnosis, sport clearance, or treatment regimen is supplied.
The item tests body-image-aware participation and balanced habits, not toddler meal structure, school food access, or sport emergency planning.

questions.objective: Prepare a preschool child for school entry through developmentally appropriate transition support, a consistent sleep routine, protected active play, and a family media plan.
questions.stem: The family of a 5-year-old starting kindergarten next month reports that the child is nervous about the new school, falls asleep late while watching videos in bed, and usually spends after-school time on a tablet instead of active play. Which anticipatory-guidance actions should the nurse recommend? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Build predictable routines and familiarity while preserving sleep, movement, play, and family connection rather than using media to manage each transition concern.
questions.rationale: School-transition guidance can reduce uncertainty by introducing the child to the school and classroom, discussing worries in concrete terms, and practicing the coming routine. Sleep is supported by a consistent bedtime sequence, gradual schedule adjustment before school, and removing or turning off screens before bed. A family media plan should protect time and places for sleep, active play, reading, hobbies, and family interaction. Enjoyable daily movement supports health and participation. Keeping videos in the bedtime routine or replacing active play with worksheets undermines the same transition goals.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must select a coherent anticipatory-guidance bundle across school readiness, sleep, media, and activity while rejecting superficially convenient strategies that worsen routines. This supports level 2.

options.text: Visit the school or classroom if possible, talk through what the day may look like, and invite the child to share specific worries.
options.reason: Familiarity, concrete preparation, and open discussion help the child anticipate the transition and allow the family to address particular concerns.

options.text: Begin shifting bedtime and wake time toward the school schedule, use the same calming bedtime routine, and keep screens out of the sleep setting before bed.
options.reason: A gradual schedule shift and predictable screen-free bedtime routine support adequate, consistent sleep before school begins.

options.text: Create a family media plan with screen-free times and places so videos do not replace sleep, active play, reading, hobbies, or family interaction.
options.reason: A family plan organizes media around developmental and health needs rather than treating one isolated minute limit as the entire intervention.

options.text: Schedule enjoyable active play most days and let the child help choose movement that is safe, social, and sustainable.
options.reason: Child-selected, enjoyable movement supports routine physical activity and participation without making exercise punitive.

options.text: Move the tablet out of bed but keep videos in the bedtime routine, postponing the sleep-schedule change until school starts.
options.reason: Moving the tablet helps the sleep setting, but bedtime media and a delayed schedule shift can still interfere with sleep preparation before school.

options.text: Visit the school and practice the morning routine, but replace after-school active play with extra readiness worksheets during the first month.
options.reason: School familiarity and routine practice help, but replacing active play neglects a developmentally important part of the child's health and transition plan.

refs.label: Week 6 Healthy Child Growth and Development Instructor Notes — preschool and school-age sleep, activity, media, and school-transition guidance.
ATI RN Nursing Care of Children, edition 11 — preschool and school-age sleep, play, nutrition, and activity passages (verified supplied text; no original PDF review).
American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org — Back-to-School Tips for Families (August 26, 2026).
American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org — Healthy Sleep Habits: How Many Hours Does Your Child Need? (August 7, 2026).
American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org — How to Make a Family Media Plan (January 20, 2026).

limitations: The item intentionally emphasizes routines and balanced participation rather than a universal numeric screen-time, sleep-hour, or exercise prescription.
Persistent sleep disturbance, severe anxiety, developmental concerns, bullying, or school refusal would require individualized assessment.
The guidance does not replace a school's transition plan or accommodations.

questions.objective: Protect an established gastrostomy site and tract through daily assessment and cleansing, stabilization, leakage and skin care, device-specific handling, and prescribed oral-skill support.
questions.stem: A caregiver is preparing to take home a child with a healed gastrostomy site and an established low-profile device. The child receives most nutrition through the tube and has an individualized speech-language pathology feeding plan. Which home-care instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Routine care protects dry intact skin, prevents traction, escalates persistent leakage or inflammation, and follows the child's device and feeding plans rather than a universal manipulation rule.
questions.rationale: Routine gastrostomy care includes daily observation, gentle cleansing according to the home plan, thorough drying, and securing extension tubing to prevent pulling. Leakage should not simply be hidden: a prescribed barrier or absorbent protection may protect the skin, while persistent or large leakage, pain, spreading redness, swelling, odor, drainage, or breakdown warrants clinical review. Rotation and other device manipulation are device- and placement-specific, so the caregiver should follow the current individualized instructions rather than rotate every gastrostomy or gastrojejunal device. Children who are tube-fed may also need continued oral hygiene and prescribed oral-motor or feeding practice to protect skills and safety; unapproved oral liquids should not be introduced.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must distinguish routine established-site care from fresh-tract emergencies and reject a familiar but unsafe universal rotation rule while preserving individualized oral-skill support. This supports level 2.

options.text: Inspect the site daily, clean it gently with water and mild soap or as directed in the home plan, and pat the skin dry.
options.reason: Daily assessment and gentle cleansing with careful drying help detect changes early and limit moisture-related skin injury.

options.text: Secure the extension tubing during use to reduce pulling, and follow the child's device-specific instructions for any rotation or position change.
options.reason: Stabilization protects the tract from traction, while rotation rules vary by device and placement and therefore must come from the individualized plan.

options.text: Use the prescribed skin barrier or absorbent protection for leakage and report persistent or large leakage, pain, spreading redness, swelling, drainage, odor, or skin breakdown.
options.reason: Barrier care can protect exposed skin, but ongoing leakage or inflammatory and breakdown findings require assessment rather than concealment.

options.text: Continue oral hygiene and only the oral-motor or feeding practice authorized in the child's feeding and speech-language pathology plan.
options.reason: Prescribed oral care and skill practice can support feeding development and safety without introducing oral intake that has not been cleared.

options.text: Rotate the low-profile button once daily when it moves easily, and continue that routine after a device replacement unless the caregiver notices pain.
options.reason: Easy movement does not establish that rotation is appropriate, and replacement can change the device or tract plan; handling must remain device-specific.

options.text: Place a folded absorbent dressing under the button for ongoing leakage and report it at the next scheduled visit if the skin remains intact.
options.reason: Absorbent protection may be prescribed temporarily, but ongoing leakage requires timely review rather than routine-visit delay even before visible skin injury appears.

refs.label: Week 7 GI Instructor Notes — gastrostomy site care, stabilization, leakage and skin protection, and oral-skill support.
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne — Nursing guidelines: Gastrostomy (first published August 2024).
Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne — Kids Health Info: Gastrostomy tube (written January 2024; updated July 2025).

limitations: The device is established and the tract healed; accidental dislodgement of a new or established tube requires the child's emergency replacement plan and prompt clinical direction.
No universal rotation, dressing, flush, balloon-volume, replacement, or device-specific schedule is prescribed.
Oral intake and oral-motor practice remain limited to the child's swallowing and feeding plan.

questions.objective: Characterize an infant's reported emesis by timing, appearance or color, force, and amount before distinguishing effortless spit-up from a concerning vomiting pattern.
questions.stem: During telephone triage, a caregiver says, “My 7-week-old vomited after feeding.” The infant is awake and breathing normally. Which set of follow-up questions gives the nurse the most useful initial characterization of the event?
questions.clue: Turn the caregiver's broad word “vomited” into observable features before assuming reflux, obstruction, infection, or feeding intolerance.
questions.rationale: Initial emesis assessment should translate a broad caregiver description into observable dimensions: timing in relation to feeding, appearance and color, effortless flow versus forceful or projectile expulsion, and estimated amount and repetition. Hydration and behavior questions add urgency context. Small milk-colored or curdled spit-up that flows easily is different from repeated forceful vomiting or green, bloody, or coffee-ground material, but the nurse should first gather the pattern rather than announce a diagnosis from one word. Feeding changes or home treatments should not precede characterization and red-flag assessment.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must choose a complete, neutral assessment set that separates several clinically meaningful dimensions without being drawn into premature diagnosis or management. This supports level 2.

options.text: Ask when it occurs relative to feeding; note the material's appearance and color, flow versus force, estimated amount and frequency; then ask about wet diapers and behavior.
options.reason: This set captures timing, appearance and color, force, volume and frequency, plus hydration and behavior context before interpreting the pattern.

options.text: Ask when it occurs relative to feeding; review bottle volume, formula preparation, burping, and feeding position; then ask about wet diapers and behavior.
options.reason: This set covers timing, feeding context, hydration, and behavior, but omits the material's appearance or color, observed force, and estimated amount and repetition.

options.text: Ask what the material looks like and its color; estimate amount and frequency from clothing or linens; then ask about wet diapers, behavior, and fever.
options.reason: This set covers appearance, amount, repetition, hydration, behavior, and fever, but it does not establish feeding timing or effortless versus forceful expulsion.

options.text: Ask when it occurs relative to feeding; describe the material's color and whether it flows or is forceful; then review feeding type, preparation, and recent changes.
options.reason: This set covers timing, color, force, and feeding context, but omits estimated amount and frequency plus hydration and behavior findings needed for urgency context.

refs.label: Week 7 GI Instructor Notes — infant emesis assessment by feeding timing, appearance, color, force, and volume.
American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org — Causes of Vomiting in Infants & Children (December 29, 2024).

limitations: The item tests initial characterization and does not diagnose reflux, pyloric stenosis, obstruction, infection, allergy, or another cause.
Green or bloody material, forceful or repeated vomiting, dehydration, lethargy, breathing difficulty, severe pain, fever in a young infant, or other acute concerns require prompt clinical escalation.
No formula change, thickening recipe, medication, imaging, or home-treatment plan is prescribed.

questions.objective: Complete a current vaccine-administration workflow that verifies the record and product-specific timing, screens for contraindications and precautions, supplies required information, separates injections, and documents each dose.
questions.stem: A 5-year-old arrives for a well visit with a dated vaccine record. The current schedule and standing orders indicate that three vaccines may be due. The child is afebrile and has only a mild runny nose. Which actions should the nurse take before, during, and after administration? Select all that apply.
questions.clue: Treat each planned vaccine as its own product and dose while completing the same safety sequence from record review through documentation.
questions.rationale: Safe vaccine administration begins by reconciling the dated record with current recommendations and confirming the correct product, indication, age, and interval for every planned dose. The nurse screens for vaccine-specific contraindications and precautions and provides the current required Vaccine Information Statement before each covered dose. Multiple vaccines given at one visit use separate syringes and separate sites; sites should be clearly mapped so each dose can be traced. Administration and VIS details are then entered in the permanent record. A minor illness such as an uncomplicated runny nose is not by itself a reason to defer every vaccine, and separately supplied vaccines must not be mixed in one syringe unless the product is specifically manufactured and approved as a combination vaccine.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must sequence several linked safeguards and distinguish product-specific verification from blanket deferral or improvised mixing. No schedule calculation or individual contraindication diagnosis is required, supporting level 2.

options.text: Reconcile the dated record with current recommendations and verify the ordered product, indication, age, and interval for each possible dose before preparation.
options.reason: A record review tied to current recommendations prevents unnecessary restarting, missed doses, and use of the wrong product or interval; this item does not require the learner to reproduce the full schedule.

options.text: Screen for contraindications and precautions separately for each planned vaccine and clarify any positive response before giving that dose.
options.reason: Contraindications and precautions can be vaccine-specific, so a standardized screen must be interpreted for each product rather than applied as an all-or-none label.

options.text: Give the current required Vaccine Information Statement for each covered vaccine before administration and record its edition date and the date provided.
options.reason: The current VIS is provided before each covered dose, and both the VIS edition date and the date it was given belong in the permanent record.

options.text: Use a separate syringe and a separate anatomic site for each vaccine, separate injection sites by at least 1 inch when possible, and map the sites for documentation.
options.reason: CDC guidance supports separate syringes and sites for vaccines given at the same visit, with at least 1 inch between sites when possible; mapping preserves dose-to-site traceability.

options.text: Postpone all three vaccines until the runny nose is completely gone because any current illness is a contraindication to vaccination.
options.reason: A mild illness is not automatically a contraindication. The nurse should complete the vaccine-specific screen instead of applying a blanket deferral.

options.text: Draw separately supplied vaccines into one syringe to reduce the number of injections when the same visit includes several routine products.
options.reason: Separately supplied vaccines should not be combined by the nurse; only a manufacturer-approved combination product is used as a combined vaccine.

questions.objective: Differentiate uncomplicated physiologic infant reflux from findings that require reassessment and preserve safe feeding and flat supine sleep practices.
questions.stem: A 3-month-old has small, painless spit-ups after feeds but feeds eagerly, has normal urine output, and continues to gain weight along the established curve. There is no blood or bile in the emesis, forceful vomiting, feeding refusal, cough, wheeze, choking, apnea, or breathing difficulty. Which teaching should the nurse provide?
questions.clue: Normal growth and painless post-feed regurgitation support physiologic reflux, but feeding support must remain separate from safe sleep positioning.
questions.rationale: Small painless spit-ups in a thriving infant without feeding, respiratory, bleeding, bilious, forceful-vomiting, or growth concerns are consistent with common physiologic gastroesophageal reflux. The caregiver can avoid overfeeding, use smaller more frequent feeds if recommended within the infant's daily nutrition plan, burp the infant, and hold the infant upright while awake for 20 to 30 minutes after feeding when practical. For every sleep, the infant still goes flat on the back on a firm sleep surface. Poor weight gain, feeding refusal, pain, choking, cough, wheeze, apnea, breathing difficulty, blood, bile, dehydration, or forceful vomiting requires prompt reassessment rather than being dismissed as routine reflux.
questions.difficultyReason: The learner must classify a reassuring growth-and-symptom pattern, choose nonpharmacologic feeding support, preserve safe sleep, and retain a red-flag boundary. This is level 2 application.

options.text: Treat this as common physiologic reflux; use clinician-directed smaller feeds, burping, and awake upright holding, keep sleep firm, flat, and supine, and seek reassessment for red flags.
options.reason: The infant is thriving without pathologic findings. This complete plan supports feeding tolerance, separates awake upright care from safe sleep, and preserves prompt follow-up for concerning changes.

options.text: Treat this as common physiologic reflux; thicken every feed without clinician review, use upright awake positioning, keep sleep firm, flat, and supine, and seek reassessment for red flags.
options.reason: The classification, awake positioning, safe sleep, and follow-up are appropriate, but feed thickening should not be started independently; any feeding change needs clinician direction and individualized nutrition review.

options.text: Treat this as GERD despite normal growth; use clinician-directed feeding support and awake upright holding, keep sleep firm, flat, and supine, and seek reassessment for red flags.
options.reason: The care plan is otherwise safe, but normal growth and the absence of feeding, respiratory, bleeding, bilious, dehydration, pain, or forceful-vomiting findings do not establish pathologic GERD.

options.text: Treat this as common physiologic reflux; use appropriate feeding support and awake upright holding, keep sleep firm, flat, and supine, and reserve earlier reassessment for faltering weight gain.
options.reason: The classification, feeding support, awake positioning, and sleep plan are appropriate, but non-weight red flags also require earlier reassessment; faltering growth is not the sole trigger.
